aaron.notes: Aaron functions in the NT as shorthand for the entire Old Covenant priestly system. Hebrews 5:4 anchors Christ's high priesthood in the pattern that no one takes the honor except by divine call, citing Aaron's appointment. Luke 1:5 identifies Zechariah as a priest of Aaron's division, signaling continuity with the temple cult. The name carries theological weight because it indexes the sacrificial apparatus that Christ both fulfills and supersedes.

abaddon.notes: This Hebrew loanword appears only in Revelation 9:11, where John identifies Abaddon as the angel-king of the demonic locusts from the abyss. In OT Wisdom literature, Abaddon denotes the shadowy underworld realm of the dead, parallel to Sheol. John personalizes this ancient term into a malevolent angelic figure, immediately glossing it with the Greek Apollyōn ('Destroyer') to ensure his audience grasps the destructive character. The hapax makes Abaddon theologically loaded as a symbolic embodiment of judgment and ruin.

abares.notes: Paul uses this term only once in 2 Corinthians 11:9 to insist he was not a financial burden to the Corinthian church during his ministry there. The metaphorical extension from physical weightlessness to economic non-dependency is common in Koine usage. Paul's point is pastoral and rhetorical: unlike some traveling teachers who exploited their hosts, he supported himself and accepted aid only from the Macedonians, preserving his integrity and the gospel's reputation.

abba.notes: This Aramaic vocative appears only three times in the NT, always doubled with the Greek ὁ πατήρ. In Mark 14:36, Jesus uses it in Gethsemane's anguished prayer. In Romans 8:15 and Galatians 4:6, Paul presents it as the Spirit-enabled cry of adopted children. The term carries intimate familial warmth—early Christians retained the Aramaic despite writing in Greek, preserving Jesus' own prayer language. Some scholars argue it reflects childlike address (like 'daddy'), though others note it was used by adults as well. The key theological freight is covenantal intimacy: believers address the sovereign Creator with the same vulnerable trust Jesus modeled.

abel.notes: Abel appears four times in the NT, always in loaded theological contexts. Hebrews 11:4 holds him up as the first exemplar of faith whose sacrifice was accepted by God. Matthew 23:35 and Luke 11:51 bracket him with Zechariah as bookends of martyrdom spanning the Hebrew canon—'the blood of righteous Abel' becomes shorthand for all innocent suffering. Most strikingly, Hebrews 12:24 contrasts Abel's blood that 'cried out' for vengeance (Genesis 4:10) with Christ's blood that 'speaks a better word'—mercy rather than retribution. Abel thus functions typologically: a foreshadowing of Christ's innocent death, yet inferior because his blood demands justice while Christ's offers reconciliation.

abia.notes: Ἀβιά appears in two NT contexts: Matthew 1:7 (twice) in the genealogy of Jesus as a Judean king, and Luke 1:5 identifying Zechariah's priestly division. The name derives from Hebrew אֲבִיָּה meaning 'Yahweh is father.' The priestly division of Abijah (eighth of twenty-four courses, 1 Chron 24:10) was on duty when Zechariah received the annunciation of John's birth, tying the Baptist's origins to Israel's liturgical order. Matthew's mention anchors Jesus in the Davidic royal line through this post-Solomonic king.

abiathar.notes: Abiathar appears only in Mark 2:26, where Jesus references David eating the showbread 'in the days of Abiathar the high priest.' This presents a historical puzzle since 1 Samuel 21:1-6 names Ahimelech (Abiathar's father) as the priest present at Nob. Abiathar later became David's loyal high priest after fleeing Saul's massacre at Nob (1 Sam 22:20-23). The phrase may indicate the broader period associated with Abiathar's eventual prominence rather than pinpoint chronology, or Mark uses 'in the time of' loosely to evoke the well-known priestly house.

abilene.notes: Luke 3:1 situates John's ministry with six synchronized political markers, including Lysanias as tetrarch of Abilene. This precision anchors salvation history in datable Roman administration. Abilene was a small, mountainous territory centered on Abila (modern Suk Wadi Barada), about 18 miles northwest of Damascus. Luke's reference helps modern readers see that the Gospel unfolds in real geography under real governors, not mythic space.

abioud.notes: Abiud appears only twice in the NT, both in Matthew 1:13, where he links Zerubbabel to the otherwise obscure generations leading to Joseph. The name likely derives from Hebrew אֲבִיהוּד ('my father is majesty'), but no OT figure by this name exists. Matthew's genealogy intentionally spans the silent intertestamental period, and Abiud represents one link in the legal-genealogical claim that Jesus is rightful heir to David's throne. The inclusion of unknown names like Abiud underscores Matthew's concern for historical continuity rather than celebrity.

abraam.notes: Abraham appears 73 times in the NT as the foundational covenant figure. In Romans 4 and Galatians 3, Paul redefines who counts as Abraham's true offspring—not ethnic descent but faith in Christ. The phrase 'Abraham's seed' becomes a flash point in debates over circumcision, law, and gospel. Matthew 1:1 anchors Jesus as 'son of Abraham,' validating messianic credentials. John 8:31-59 shows Jesus' opponents claiming 'Abraham is our father,' to which Jesus counters that genuine children of Abraham do his works. The indeclinable form reflects Semitic transliteration into Greek.

abussos.notes: This word carries the sense of a chaotic, unfathomable depth—originally the primordial waters of Gen 1:2 (LXX תְּהוֹם). In NT usage it shifts decisively toward the prison of demonic forces. Luke 8:31 shows demons begging Jesus not to command them into the abyss. Revelation 9:1-11 depicts the abyss as a locked shaft from which destructive locust-demons emerge, and Rev 20:1-3 shows Satan bound there for a thousand years. The term does NOT simply mean hell or Hades; it denotes a specific holding place for rebellious spiritual powers under divine restraint.

achaia.notes: In NT usage, Achaia refers to the Roman senatorial province established in 27 BC, encompassing most of southern Greece with Corinth as its administrative center. Paul's ministry there (Acts 18:12-17 under proconsul Gallio) established a network of churches, making Achaia a synecdoche for the southern Greek Christian community in his letters. The household of Stephanas is identified as 'the firstfruits of Achaia' (1 Cor 16:15), and the province's believers became models of generosity in the Jerusalem collection (2 Cor 9:2).

achaikos.notes: Achaicus appears only in 1 Cor 16:17, where Paul warmly acknowledges him alongside Stephanas and Fortunatus for refreshing his spirit. The name itself likely indicates either origin from Achaia or birth into a household with Achaian connections, a common naming practice in the Greco-Roman world. Paul's tone suggests Achaicus was part of a trusted envoy bringing the Corinthians' letter and material support to Paul during his Ephesian ministry.

acharistos.notes: This alpha-privative adjective appears only twice in the NT. In Luke 6:35, Jesus describes God as kind even to the ungrateful and wicked, modeling a radical generosity that doesn't wait for human reciprocity. In 2 Timothy 3:2, ungratefulness surfaces in the vice list of the last days, suggesting ingratitude marks broader moral collapse. The word presupposes a relational framework where grace or benefit has been extended but goes unacknowledged.

achaz.notes: This verb carries the concrete sense of physical grasping with the hand, then extends metaphorically to seizing territory or taking legal possession. Genesis 25:26 uses it when Jacob emerges from the womb grasping Esau's heel (achaz be-aqev), a wordplay on his name. The Niphal stem often describes being caught or trapped, while the Piel can denote overlaying with metal (as in tabernacle construction). The root appears in the name Ahaz (אָחָז), 'he has grasped,' reflecting typical Hebrew name theology.

acheim.notes: Ἀχείμ appears only in Matthew 1:14 within the stylized fourteen-generation structure tracing Jesus through Joseph. This name is otherwise unattested in the Old Testament and likely represents a figure from the silent centuries between the return from exile and the first century. acheiropoietos.notes: This word carries theological freight because it marks the contrast between human religious effort and divine reality. Mark 14:58 famously contrasts the handmade Jerusalem temple with the acheiropoiētos temple Jesus would raise—a saying that drove his trial. In 2 Corinthians 5:1 Paul uses it for the believer's resurrection body, a building from God not constructed by human labor. Colossians 2:11 deploys it metaphorically for the circumcision of Christ—spiritual transformation versus ritual cutting. The term always signals transcendence: God's work versus human manufacture.

The word carries a medical or phenomenological sense of visual obstruction, not abstract theological darkness. Classical usage includes both literal atmospheric mist and the clouding of vision before fainting or death, which fits Luke's precise diction in Acts.

The passive form there carries the sense that humanity has become collectively corrupt and useless for God's purposes. The word derives from the alpha-privative plus a root related to χρή (need, use), so it denotes something that has lost its utility or moral value. Context determines whether the emphasis falls on practical uselessness or moral depravity—here Paul stresses the latter.

achreios.notes: This word appears only twice in the NT, both times carrying theological weight about servants and stewardship. In Luke 17:10, Jesus tells disciples to call themselves 'unworthy servants' (δοῦλοι ἀχρεῖοι) after doing all commanded—not because their work is worthless, but because they deserve no special merit for baseline obedience. In Matthew 25:30, the 'worthless servant' who buried his talent is cast out, showing genuine unprofitability through sloth. The contrast reveals that ἀχρεῖος can denote either humble recognition of duty or actual failure, depending on context.

The alpha-privative negates χρηστός (serviceable), capturing the social and economic reality of a runaway slave who provided no labor. achuron.notes: Both NT occurrences appear in John the Baptist's eschatological warning about the Coming One who will separate wheat from chaff with His winnowing fork. The image draws on the Palestinian threshing floor where grain was tossed into the wind—useful kernels fell back while lightweight chaff blew away to be burned. In context, ἄχυρον denotes those who prove fruitless under Messiah's judgment, not merely agricultural waste. The metaphor carries OT roots (Psalm 1:4, Isaiah 17:13) but John sharpens it into a vivid picture of final division.

The Qal typically denotes inherent redness or becoming red, while causative stems indicate making something appear red or glowing. Context determines whether the redness is favorable (health, beauty) or ominous (judgment, warfare). The word does not carry heavy theological freight but provides concrete descriptive language for color and appearance throughout the Hebrew Bible.

addi.notes: Addi appears only once in Luke 3:28 as part of the genealogy tracing Jesus back through David to Adam. The name is likely a Greek rendering of a Hebrew name, possibly related to עֵד (witness) or עֲדִי (ornament). Luke's genealogy differs from Matthew's, reflecting a different theological emphasis—Luke traces through Nathan rather than Solomon and continues to Adam to underscore Jesus' universal significance. The term appears in Hellenistic papyri for uninterrupted legal obligations, which informs Paul's rhetorical force: his devotion brooks no gaps. The adverbial form ἀδιαλείπτως appears more often in the NT (five times), especially in 1 Thessalonians where 'pray without ceasing' (5:17) became a classic formulation of constant communion with God.

In Revelation 22:11 the word appears in an eschatological warning where the unjust continue their unjust acts, sealed in their moral trajectory. The term encompasses both interpersonal harm and theological rebellion against God's justice, making context essential to discern whether the emphasis is on damage done or righteousness spurned.

In Romans 1:18 Paul uses adikia as the comprehensive category for human sin that suppresses truth, while in 1 John 5:17 every sin is adikia. The term can denote active wickedness (2 Thessalonians 2:10, where it appears as the mystery of lawlessness) or specific unjust behavior (Luke 18:6, the unjust judge). It denotes not primarily an emotion but a volitional commitment—God's unconditional self-gift in Christ (John 3:16), and the character demanded of disciples (1 John 4:7–8). The word is nearly absent in secular Greek, marking it as a Christian semantic innovation. Paul uses it in 1 Cor. 11:6 and 14:35 to address conduct deemed unbecoming in worship contexts; Eph. 5:12 applies it to deeds done in darkness. The word denotes not merely ugliness but active moral turpitude or indecency—context determines whether the reference is to unseemly appearance, speech, or behavior.

The word does not primarily denote moral foreignness but rather boundary: this is *their* domain, not mine. aloao.notes: Paul uses this word to argue for the right of workers—especially apostles—to receive sustenance (1 Corinthians 9:9–13), citing the law against muzzling an ox while threshing. aloe.notes: The word denotes the fragrant resin or powdered wood of the aloe plant, used in Jewish burial practice for anointing the corpse. John 19:39 is the sole NT occurrence: Nicodemus brings approximately 100 Roman pounds of aloes to anoint Jesus' body—a gesture that signals both honor and preparation for permanent entombment. The substance was rare and expensive, imported primarily from Arabia, making its use a marker of respect and affluence.

In 2 Peter 2:12 and Jude 10, it describes false teachers as unreasoning animals driven by instinct rather than reason. amen.notes: Amen functions as a performative utterance rather than mere assent. The word denotes not mere abstract upset but concrete social destabilization—literally "unrooting" people from their normal conditions. In Paul's paraenesis and James, the word often denotes ethical living or deportment, narrowing toward 'conduct oneself' (Phil. 2:18; Eph. 2:3; 1 Pet. 1:17). Eph 4:22, 1 Pet 1:15, 1 Pet 3:1–2), it carries ethical weight as the visible outworking of faith. The word denotes the scholarly work of collecting and organizing source material rather than inventing it. Paul employs it forcefully in Rom 9:3 and 1 Cor 12:3 to denote separation from Christ and covenant blessing. Mark 14:71 shows Peter anathematizing himself; Acts 23:12 depicts a death-plot vow sealed by anathema. In Act. 25:14, Festus 'sets before' the king details about Paul's case; in Gal. 2:2, Paul declares (middle voice) the gospel to the Jerusalem pillars. Matthew's μάγοι ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν (2:2) locates the wise men geographically yet preserves an eschatological undertone. anepsios.notes: Ἀνεψιός appears only once in the NT, at Colossians 4:10, where Paul identifies Mark as a cousin of Barnabas. The word carries no theological weight in the NT; it is a straightforward kinship term. The singular occurrence makes it a rare but clear window into first-century family nomenclature and the networks within the early Christian community.

anesis.notes: In Acts 24:23, ἄνεσις denotes the relative leniency Felix grants Paul in custody—a loosening of strict confinement. The word denotes a common garden herb known in antiquity for both culinary and medicinal use. Its sole occurrence is proverbial rather than substantive to NT theology.

Paul uses it in Rom. 11:33 to describe how the depths of God's judgment and knowledge surpass human rational inquiry—the word carries theological weight precisely because it marks the boundary of human cognition. anexikakos.notes: This rare adjective appears only in 2 Timothy 2:24, where Paul instructs Timothy that the Lord's servant must be anexikakos—patient under mistreatment and not quick to anger. The heavenly sense dominates NT usage and carries theological weight: angels worship Christ (Heb 1:6), announce salvific events (Luke 1–2), and mediate divine judgment. The term's flexibility—ordinary messenger to cosmic agent—requires context to disambiguate, though supernatural markers (light, fear, worship) usually clarify the referent.

aniemi.notes: ἀνίημι appears only 4 times in the NT, most memorably in Heb 13:5 ("I will never leave thee, neither will I forsake thee"), where God's refusal to ἀνίημι reassures believers of continuous support. anileos.notes: This rare adjective appears only in James 2:13, where mercy (eleos) is contrasted with judgment toward the merciless person. The Attic variant forms (anēleēs, aneleēmōn) confirm the alpha-privative construction: a- (without) + eleos (mercy). The word denotes literal absence of ablution but carries polemical force: Jesus argues that unwashed hands do not defile a person spiritually (the heart, not external ritual observance, determines purity). anna.notes: This is a particle of supplication, not a standalone verb or noun. It carries no theological weight by itself but serves purely as a rhetorical intensifier—the Hebrew equivalent of a verbal emphatic that yanks the listener's attention to the urgency of what follows. Its most vivid use appears in the stories of Moses interceding with God (Exodus 32:31–32, Numbers 14:19) and Hannah's desperate prayer at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:11), where אָנָּא opens the petition and signals raw emotional or spiritual intensity. In Aramaic (Daniel), it performs the same function with the king.

It appears twice in the NT: 1 Timothy 6:17 warns the wealthy against trusting in riches or their enjoyment, and Hebrews 11:25 contrasts temporary apolausis of sin with identification with God's people. The passive construction in Hebrews (4:6, 10:26) shifts the sense toward 'remain' or 'be reserved,' especially in the cultic context of sabbath rest. apollonia.notes: Apollonia appears only once in the NT (Acts 17:1) as a geographical marker during Paul's second missionary journey. Luke mentions it briefly as Paul traveled westward along the Roman road, but provides no detail of apostolic activity there. The city's name derives from the god Apollo, typical of Hellenistic foundations in the region.

Luke describes him as a learned Alexandrian Christian, mighty in the scriptures, instructed in the Way, and eloquent (Acts 18:24–28). His role in Corinth becomes pivotal for Paul's treatment of factionalism in 1 Cor 1:12, 3:4–6, 4:6, where some believers claimed allegiance to him over Paul or Peter. The historical Apollos embodies no theological position hostile to Paul; rather, the Corinthians weaponized his name and rhetorical gifts as a party marker. Paul's response reframes both teachers as servants of the same gospel.

The word spans both concrete destruction (of objects, cities, persons) and spiritual ruin, making context critical: is this physical annihilation or metaphorical damnation? The famous saying at Mt 10:28—fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna—illustrates its theological charge. The passive/middle voice often hints at self-destruction or spiritual undoing (e.g., "the wicked shall perish").

apologeomai.notes: The word denotes not mere personal excuse-making but a formal defense offered in response to formal accusation. The middle voice here signals reflexive action (wash oneself clean). Not a high-frequency word, but carries sacramental weight in its single clear NT context.

apolutrosis.notes: Ἀπολύτρωσις carries the sense of redemption as a transaction—release purchased at cost. Hebrews 11:35 uses it metaphorically for the deliverance of martyrs. The word's freight lies in its fusion of juridical (ransom paid), salvific (freedom gained), and eschatological (awaiting final consummation) registers.

Mark's healing narrative (5:22–38) and Luke's healing of the bent woman (13:14) illustrate the office as one of real communal authority, sometimes wielded defensively against Jesus and the apostles.

architekton.notes: This word appears only once in the NT at 1 Corinthians 3:10, where Paul applies it metaphorically to his apostolic role in laying the foundation of the Corinthian church. The term denotes the senior craftsman responsible for blueprinting and supervising major construction work—a figure of authority and expertise. In context, Paul uses it not to boast but to acknowledge his stewardship before God.

architelones.notes: This word appears only in Luke 19:2, describing Zacchaeus. The compound emphasizes his administrative rank within the tax-farming hierarchy—not a mere tollbooth operator, but a contractor who sublet collection routes and enriched himself from the spread. The role was a fixture of Greco-Roman banquet protocol, combining aesthetic judgment with household management authority. The active voice favors the 'begin' sense (Matt 16:21, Luke 14:18), while the genitive construction emphasizes rule or authority (Mark 10:42, Rom 15:12). In Mark 10:42, Jesus contrasts ἄρχοντες with servant-leadership, making the ruling sense theologically pertinent there.

In the NT, the inceptive sense dominates—especially in Luke's narrative openings (Luk 14:18, 23:5) where ἄρχομαι + infinitive marks the start of an action. areiospagos.notes: A proper noun with dual referent: the geographic location (a rocky outcrop northwest of the Acropolis) and the venerable Athenian court that met there. argureos.notes: This rare adjective appears only three times in the NT, each in literal contexts describing objects fashioned from silver. In Acts 19:24, silversmiths craft shrines; in 2 Timothy 2:20, Paul uses household vessels (silver and gold) as an analogy for Christian usefulness; in Revelation 9:20, idols are said to be silver and gold. The term anchors a theology of mutual care and subordination to community need; it was easily abused to justify hierarchy or conversely sentimentalized as selfless devotion without structure. diarpazo.notes: διαρπάζω appears only in Matthew 12:29 and Mark 3:27, where Jesus uses it metaphorically: one cannot plunder a strong man's house without first binding him. The διά prefix intensifies the sense of ἁρπάζω, suggesting thorough, systematic despoilation. The διά- prefix intensifies the root σαφής (clear), denoting explanation that moves toward full disclosure. The Acts narratives of Paul's sea voyage (Acts 27–28) define its primary usage: the centurion ensures prisoners are brought safely through shipwreck, and all aboard come safe through to land. The διά- prefix intensifies the root σπάω, denoting separation by force applied from multiple directions or with exceptional violence rather than neat severance.

In the NT (Jas 1:1, 1 Pet 1:1), it applies to scattered believers, transferring the Jewish exile metaphor to the church's pilgrim status. diastello.notes: The word carries the sense of authoritative command with emphasis on explicit clarity—not merely instruction but forceful injunction. The διά prefix intensifies the separative or defining aspect: to command by drawing a line, marking what must be heeded. The LXX uses it for חִנָּם (free, gratuitous), anchoring it in the sense of non-reciprocal favor. dromos.notes: δρόμος denotes a course or track, but in the NT it carries figurative weight when applied to the Christian life or apostolic ministry. Paul's use at Acts 13:25 (completing his own course) and especially 2 Tim 4:7 (having finished the race) show how dromos becomes a metaphor for faithful perseverance toward eschatological completion. The word's connection to τρέχω emphasizes active striving, not passive status.

drousilla.notes: Drusilla appears once in Acts 24:24 as present when Paul defends himself before her husband Felix. Historically, she was the daughter of Agrippa I and sister of Agrippa II and Bernice. Her presence at the hearing underscores the high-ranking audience Paul faced and adds biographical texture to Luke's account of apostolic witness before Roman and Jewish nobility.

dunamoo.notes: This rare verb carries the sense of imparting or activating inner strength. Paul employs it (or its variant ἐνδυναμόω) in Eph 6:10 to exhort believers to "be strengthened in the Lord," and in Col 1:11 for empowerment unto patient endurance. The word denotes not external force but an interior fortification of capacity—theological language for spiritual maturation and resilience.

dunastes.notes: δυνάστης denotes a person invested with actual authority and influence—whether a political ruler, high official, or divine sovereign. The word emphasizes position and the power to command rather than moral quality. In Luke 1:52, Christ's reversal of social order explicitly displaces δυναστῶν from their thrones; in 1 Tim 6:15, applied to God as 'the blessed and only Potentate,' it underscores His unrivaled dominion.

dunateo.notes: Dunateō carries the sense of possessing actual power or capacity to accomplish something. In Rom. 14:4 and 2 Cor. 9:8, Paul uses it with an infinitive to affirm God's ability to sustain believers; in 2 Cor. 13:3, Paul contrasts it with astheneō (weakness) to insist that the risen Christ is not weak toward the Corinthians. The word denotes concrete, functional capability rather than abstract potentiality.

dunatos.notes: δυνατός describes what is within one's power or strength—whether physical prowess (Luke 1:49), spiritual resilience (Rom 15:1), or social standing (Acts 25:5). Context determines whether emphasis falls on capability, strength, or influence. The word does not mean magical or explosive power (cf. δύναμις), but rather the capacity to act or endure.

duno.notes: A rare Ionic and poetic variant of δύω, attested only once in Mark 1:32 (the sun setting at evening). The verb denotes physical descent or penetration into a space, narrowed in NT usage to the astronomical image of solar descent. Context determines whether 'sink into' or 'set' applies; the latter is dominant in Mark and Luke's parallel.

duo.notes: δύο appears 130 times in the NT as a straightforward numeral with no theological freight. It governs plural nouns and declines only in the dative (δυσί/δυσίν). The word is neutral across contexts: Jesus sends disciples two-by-two (Luke 10:1), the wedding jars hold two or three metretes (John 2:6), and Paul uses it for metaphorical pairing in Eph. 2:15 ('one new man' from two groups). No ambiguity attends its use.

dusbastaktos.notes: The compound δυσβάστακτος carries the sense of something too heavy or oppressive to bear, whether literal or figurative. Jesus employs it in Luke 11:46 to denounce the scribes' burdensome interpretations of the law—a polemical image of spiritual weight. The adjective is rare in NT attestation (only two passages) and does not develop the theological density of cognate burden-language elsewhere; it remains primarily descriptive of weight and grievousness.

dusenteria.notes: The word appears only once in Acts 28:8, where Paul heals Publius's father of fever and dysentery. The Greek term is a compound (dys- + enter-) reflecting medical vocabulary; this is straightforward clinical language with no theological polysemy. The condition itself illustrates the life-threatening illnesses that healers confronted in the ancient Mediterranean world.

dusermeneutos.notes: This hapax legomenon appears only in Hebrews 5:11, where the author describes certain theological truths as dusermēneutos—too intricate or obscure for his audience to grasp quickly. The adjective compounds the prefix dus- (difficult/bad) with hermēneutos (interpretable), denoting not incomprehensibility but rather the demanding labor required to parse the subject matter. Context strongly suggests Melchizedek's priesthood exemplifies such difficult-to-explain doctrine.

duskolos.notes: The word originally denoted one hard to satisfy at table (from κόλον, food), but by extension covers any reluctance or difficulty. Mark 10:24 uses it of the difficulty for the rich to enter the kingdom; the semantic shift from food-fastidiousness to moral/existential stubbornness is complete in NT usage. dusme.notes: δυσμή denotes either the sunset phenomenon or the western cardinal direction. The word appears almost always in plural (δυσμαί) in the NT, paired with ἀνατολαί (east) to denote the full expanse of earth or sky. In Luke 12:54, it refers to cloud formations rising from the western quarter. The etymological sense 'setting' (from δύνω) is synchronically visible but the word functions primarily as a spatial/directional term rather than a dynamic process.

dusnoetos.notes: This rare adjective appears only once in the NT (2 Pet 3:16), where Peter describes Paul's letters as containing things δυσνόητα—passages that the untaught and unstable distort. The compound structure (δυσ- + νοέω) emphasizes intellectual difficulty rather than moral obscurity; context matters for whether the obscurity lies in the text itself or in the reader's capacity.

dusphemia.notes: The word combines δύσ- (bad/ill) and φήμη (speech/report), denoting not merely rude speech but reputation-damaging utterance. Paul uses it in 2 Corinthians 6:8 to describe the trials apostles endure—suffering "evil report" (δυσφημία) alongside "good report" (εὐφημία)—highlighting how the gospel attracts both slander and praise. The term appears rarely in the NT but carries weight in Paul's catalogue of apostolic hardship.

eao.notes: ἐάω carries the sense of deliberate non-interference—allowing something to proceed or happen by not preventing it. It appears in contexts where restraint is actively withheld: Jesus permits demons to exit into swine (Lk 4:41), Paul is prevented from entering Asia (Acts 16:7), and God allows the heathen nations to walk in their own ways (Acts 14:16). The word does not imply approval, merely the absence of prohibition.

eber.notes: Eber appears only once in the NT (Luke 3:35) as a name-link in Jesus' genealogy tracing descent through Abraham. The figure is primarily OT and is significant in Jewish genealogical tradition as the ancestor from whom the Hebrew people (עִברִים, Hebrews) derive their ethnic identity. In Luke's context, he serves a structural role establishing historical continuity from Adam through the patriarchs.

echeo.notes: This verb appears only once in the NT, in 1 Corinthians 13:1, where Paul uses it to describe the sound of a clanging cymbal or gong—"becomes as sounding brass." The word denotes audible acoustic resonance without theological weight; context is purely physical or metaphorical (noisy faith without love).

echidna.notes: Ἔχιδνα denotes a specific venomous snake, likely the horned viper, but Jesus and John the Baptist weaponize it metaphorically to condemn the Pharisees and Sadducees as *γεννήματα ἐχιδνῶν* (offspring of vipers)—a scathing indictment of moral corruption and spiritual danger. The word carries heavy prophetic weight in Matthew 3:7, 12:34, 23:33, and Luke 3:7, embedding the image of hidden malice and deadly deception into Christological judgment.

Metaphorically, a treacherous or morally corrupt person
In eschatological or symbolic contexts, evil itself incarnate
Offspring or brood expressing hereditary wickedness

echos.notes: ἦχος denotes the physical phenomenon of sound or the auditory impression it makes. It appears rarely in the NT (4 times) but vividly in Acts 2:2 (the 'sound' of wind at Pentecost) and Hebrews 12:19 ('the sound of a trumpet'). In Luke 4:37, it shifts toward 'report' or 'rumor'—what is heard and circulates—showing that the word's range extends from the acoustic event itself to its social aftereffect.

echthros.notes: ἐχθρός carries profound theological weight, especially in Paul's redemptive logic (Rom 5:10, where even 'enemies' become reconciled to God through Christ's death). The word moves between relational hostility and eschatological opposition; note 1 Cor 15:25–26, where enemies are ultimate targets of Christ's conquest, including Death itself. Context determines whether the sense is personal enmity or cosmic opposition.

edaphizo.notes: This verb appears only once in the NT (Luke 19:44), where Jesus predicts the destruction of Jerusalem: 'they will dash you to the ground and your children within you.' The sense is overwhelmingly one of violent, complete destruction—the subjection of a city to utter devastation. Etymology from ἔδαφος (ground/floor) might suggest 'to make level,' but the attested usage in Luke and the Hebrew equivalents (notably ṣarṭ) confirm the dynamic of force and totality rather than mere leveling.

edaphos.notes: This noun appears only once in the NT (Acts 22:7, Paul's conversion account on the Damascus road) and carries the straightforward sense of the ground itself—the physical surface. In the context of Paul falling to the ground, edaphos denotes the literal earth beneath him. The word is more concrete and localized than the broader γῆ, emphasizing the immediate, solid surface rather than earth as a cosmic or theological entity.

ede.notes: ēdē marks a transition point in narrative or logical sequence, signaling that an action or state has already entered the present moment or that a threshold has been crossed. In John 4:35–37, Jesus uses ēdē to signal that the harvest is already ripe; in Romans 1:10, Paul pairs it with a future verb (ēdē pote) to express long-deferred hope finally reaching its appointed time. The word does not carry heavy theological weight but proves crucial for tracking temporal perspective in apocalyptic and eschatological contexts (1 John 2:18, 4:3).

egchrio.notes: This verb appears only once in the NT: Rev. 3:18, where the risen Christ urges the Laodicean church to buy 'eye salve to rub in your eyes.' The prefix ἐν- (en-) intensifies the simple verb χρίω, suggesting rubbing the ointment in thoroughly rather than merely applying it. In context, it carries eschatological imagery of spiritual sight restored through divine remedy.

egeiro.notes: Ἐγείρω spans everyday awakening (Mark 4:38) to the cosmic act of resurrection (1 Cor. 15:15–16, 2 Cor. 4:14). The verb's theological weight intensifies when applied to Christ's resurrection and the believer's future bodily raising; context and object determine whether the sense is literal, spiritual, or eschatological. Paul's use in Romans 13:11 exemplifies the transition from sleep-metaphor to moral urgency.

egersis.notes: This noun occurs only once in the NT (Matt 27:53), where it describes the resurrection of dead saints at Jesus's crucifixion. Though rare, it carries eschatological weight in early Christian proclamation. The term is less theologically prominent than ἀνάστασις but denotes the same reality—the rising of the dead—emphasizing the dynamic act of being raised rather than the state of having risen.

egkainia.notes: This noun occurs only once in the NT (Jn 10:22) where Jesus walks in the temple during the Festival of Dedication. The term denotes the rededication of the Second Temple by Judas Maccabeus in 164 BCE after its desecration by Antiochus IV. In Jewish custom, the eight-day feast (Hanukkah) commemorates this event, though ἐγκαίνια itself focuses on the act and anniversary of consecration rather than its duration.

The sense encompasses formal dedication with ceremonial solemnity, not mere beginning. The LXX uses it freely for temple and altar dedication, drawing on Hebrew חִנַּךְ (chinnakh).

egkaleo.notes: The word denotes accusing someone by calling them to account, often in legal or formal settings. egkataleipo.notes: ἐγκαταλείπω carries profound theological weight, especially in Christ's cry of dereliction (Mat. 27:46 par.; Mrk. 15:34), quoting Ps. 22:2. The compound prefix (ἐν + κατά + λείπω) intensifies the sense of total abandonment or rupture of relationship. In Acts 2:27 (Peter's Pentecost speech), the same verb describes God's refusal to abandon the Messiah's soul to Hades, creating a stark christological contrast.

egkatoikeo.notes: This compound appears only once in the NT (2 Pet 2:8), where it describes Lot as dwelling among the Sodomites. The ἐν- prefix adds a sense of embeddedness or deep involvement within the social matrix, not mere proximity. The verb carries no doctrinal weight but is useful for characterizing sustained residence.

egkentrizo.notes: Paul deploys ἐγκεντρίζω as the central metaphor in Romans 11:17–24 to explain how Gentile believers are grafted into the olive tree of covenant privilege originally rooted in Israel. The verb carries profound theological weight regarding election, inclusion, and the unity of Jewish and Gentile membership in Christ's body. Context is essential: Paul uses it not for botanical precision but to warn against arrogance while affirming the stability of God's promises.

egklema.notes: ἔγκλημα carries the sense of a specific accusation or legal charge laid against a defendant. It appears twice in Acts (23:29; 25:16) in contexts of Paul's defense before Jewish and Roman authorities, where it refers to formal accusations that must be substantiated. The word is forensic in register—rooted in the verb ἐγκαλέω (to accuse)—and denotes the charge itself rather than the act of accusing.

egkomboomai.notes: This verb appears only once in the NT (1 Pet 5:5), where Peter exhorts believers to 'gird yourselves with humility' toward one another. The word's etymology traces κόμβος (knot), evoking the practical gesture of tying on or binding a slave's apron; the figurative application to virtue ('gird on humility') transfers that servant-like gesture to spiritual deportment.

egkopto.notes: This verb appears primarily in Paul's letters when he describes external resistance to his ministry. In 1 Thessalonians 2:18, Paul uses it to describe Satan's hindrance of his travel plans; in Galatians 5:7, the Galatians' distraction from obedience 'cuts off' their progress. The word denotes not merely delay but active obstruction—as if breaking up a road to prevent passage.

egkrateia.notes: Egkrateia denotes not mere willpower but virtue—a fruit of the Spirit in Paul's catalogue (Gal 5:23). The term carries philosophical weight in Hellenistic ethics (temperance, sophrosyne), but Paul relocates it into eschatological renewal. Felix trembles at Paul's preaching on "self-control and judgment to come" (Acts 24:25), marking the word's tension between human effort and divine transformation.

egkrates.notes: ἐγκρατής appears only once in the NT (Titus 1:8), describing a bishop's requisite self-mastery. ekdechomai.notes: The verb denotes a patient, forward-looking stance—waiting for something whose arrival is expected but not yet realized. In James 5:7 the farmer waits for the precious fruit; in Hebrews 11:10 Abraham waits for the city whose builder is God. The metaphorical application to moral degradation is the entire point of the usage.

epaphroditos.notes: Epaphroditus appears only in Philippians (2:25; 4:18) as Paul's trusted emissary and fellow laborer. Paul honors him for his willingness to risk his health in service to the apostle, and for carrying the Philippians' generous gift. The name itself is Greek in origin (favored by Aphrodite), reflecting the cosmopolitan Philippian community. His illness and recovery (Php 2:26–27) illustrates Paul's pastoral concern and the reality of suffering in apostolic ministry.

eparchia.notes: A technical term for Roman provincial administration, used twice in Acts (23:34; 25:1) in connection with Felix and Festus governing Judea. The word denotes not merely geographical territory but specifically the jurisdictional sphere of an imperial prefect (ἔπαρχος). Its rarity in the NT reflects the evangelists' occasional need for formal Roman administrative vocabulary.

eparkeo.notes: The verb appears only three times in the NT, all in 1 Timothy 5 regarding care for widows. The middle voice (5:16) emphasizes the believing person's own capacity to sustain support rather than burden the community.

The word combines ἐπί (upon/at) with αὐλή (courtyard), denoting not merely a building but a residential estate with its attendant grounds. The prefix ἐπί- intensifies the sense of directness or immediacy. In the Gospels and Acts, it typically structures the flow of events (John 1:29 on John the Baptist's witness, Acts 10:9 on Peter's vision) without requiring deep exegetical unpacking.

epautophoros.notes: This term appears only once in the NT (John 8:4), where it describes the woman caught in adultery brought before Jesus. The word denotes literal apprehension during the act itself, not mere suspicion or hearsay. Etymology combines αὐτός (self) + φώρ (thief), literally 'self-caught thief,' though in John's usage it generalizes to any crime witnessed in progress.

The term denotes a practical outer garment—likely a fishing coat or work-cloak—distinct from formal priestly vestments, though LXX uses it to render the priestly מְעִיל. In Luke 6:28 ('bless those who curse you'), Jesus teaches disciples to pray for those who epēreazō them; in 1 Peter 3:16, believers maintain good conscience even when their good conduct is mistreated. The word denotes not mere disagreement but active, contemptuous reviling—exactly the kind of hostility Christ's followers are called to endure without retaliation.

The word appears only twice in the NT (Luke 1:5, 8) in the context of Zechariah's service as a priest in the temple. epichoregeo.notes: ἐπιχορηγέω denotes generous, abundant supply—often of divine or communal provision. The ἐπι- prefix intensifies the sense of copious giving. Appears in 2 Peter 1:5–11 (spiritual growth supplied through faith), 2 Corinthians 9:10 (God supplies seed to the sower), Galatians 3:5 (the Spirit supplied to believers), and Colossians 2:19 (the body knit together by supplied joints). The word carries no heavy theological freight, but its context often involves grace or divine enabling.

to furnish generously for a specific purpose or need
to support or sustain the growth or function of a body or community
passive: to be supplied with or equipped by

to give; broader term for transfer of goods or grace without the generosity nuance

epichoregia.notes: The word denotes generous provision or support, formed from the preposition ἐπί (upon) and χορηγέω (to supply). In Ephesians 4:16, it describes the mutual support that binds the church together; in Philippians 1:19, Paul speaks of the supply of Christ's Spirit. The term carries a sense of abundant, purposeful provision rather than bare necessity.
semanticRange: provision or supply of resources
support or aid generously given
the act of furnishing what is needed

related.note: verb form; to supply, provide, or furnish abundantly

epichrio.notes: The verb denotes the physical action of applying a substance (usually oil, salve, or mud) to skin or a surface. Both NT occurrences appear in John 9, the healing of the blind man, where Jesus rubs mud mixed with saliva onto the man's eyes as a therapeutic gesture before sending him to wash. The ἐπι- prefix emphasizes the spreading or daubing onto a surface rather than mere contact.

epidechomai.notes: ἐπιδέχομαι appears only twice in the NT and carries the sense of receiving or welcoming someone into one's presence or household. The ἐπι- prefix intensifies or marks the reception as notable. In 3 John 9–10, the verb denotes accepting or refusing to welcome traveling Christian teachers—a small but theologically weighted moment about Christian hospitality and fellowship.

epideiknumi.notes: This verb combines the preposition ἐπί (upon, toward) with δείκνυμι to intensify the sense of active showing or disclosure. In Matthew 16:1 and 24:1, the Pharisees and disciples request that Jesus ἐπιδείξῃ—display or demonstrate—signs; in Luke 17:14, Jesus tells the lepers to display themselves to the priests. The word emphasizes not mere presence but deliberate exhibition for purposes of verification or revelation.

to demonstrate or prove a point through evidence or action

epidemeo.notes: The verb carries the sense of being present in a place, whether temporarily or with some regularity, often with connotations of travel or visitor status rather than permanent settlement. In Acts 2:10 and 17:21, it describes visitors or residents at Jerusalem and Athens respectively. The ἐπι- prefix suggests presence at or upon a location, while δῆμος (people/district) grounds the word in community or territorial belonging.

epidiatassomai.notes: This rare verb appears only in Gal. 3:15, where Paul employs it to argue that even a human covenant, once ratified, cannot be invalidated or have terms added to it—a rhetorical move establishing that the Abrahamic covenant cannot be superseded by later additions (the Law). The word carries legal weight from papyrus practice, where supplementary clauses or codicils were attached to wills and contracts.
semanticRange: to add supplementary provisions to a document or covenant
to ratify or confirm by appending additional terms

epididomi.notes: The ἐπί prefix adds a sense of deliberate, often ceremonial, transfer—handing something into the possession or hands of another. Classic instances are Jesus handing bread at the table (Luke 24:30) and the scroll presented to him in the synagogue (Luke 4:17). The verb emphasizes the personal, relational act of giving rather than mere possession-transfer.
semanticRange: to hand over or deliver something to someone

epidiorthoo.notes: This hapax legomenon appears only in Titus 1:5, where Paul instructs Titus to appoint elders and complete the remaining work of church organization (ἐπιδιορθόω τὰ λείποντα). The ἐπι- prefix intensifies the simple verb διορθόω, suggesting not merely orderly arrangement but thorough correction of what had been left incomplete. The word reflects administrative and pastoral concern for proper ecclesiastical structure.

epiduo.notes: This verb occurs only once in the NT, in Ephesians 4:26 ("Let not the sun set upon your wrath"), where it carries the literal astronomical sense of sunset. The solar image grounds a temporal-ethical exhortation: anger must be resolved before nightfall, a rabbinic-influenced deadline for reconciliation. LXX attestation confirms the verb's use for solar motion and occasionally for other descents.

epieikeia.notes: Ἐπιείκεια denotes a measured, equitable quality—fairness tempered with mercy rather than rigid adherence to rule. Matthew 19:11 and Philippians 4:5 deploy it to describe Christ and Christian conduct as transcending mere justice. The word captures the idea that true reasonableness knows when to bend the letter of law for its spirit; later Christian tradition valued it as a hallmark of divine and human virtue.

epieikes.notes: Epieikēs denotes not mere softness but reasoned equity—a virtue that tempers strict justice with mercy and moderation. It appears chiefly in Pauline and Petrine household ethics (1 Tim 3:3, Tit 3:2, 1 Pet 2:18) and James's description of wisdom (Jas 3:17), where it signals generosity in interpretation and forbearance. Aristotle valued it as the capacity to apply universal law justly to particular cases; the NT adopts it to describe Christian comportment toward the weak or erring.

epigambreuo.notes: This rare verb appears once in the NT (Matt. 22:30) in Jesus' saying about resurrection and marriage. The prefix ἐπι- emphasizes the *entry into* a kinship bond through marriage. The lexical root γαμβρός (connection by marriage) distinguishes it from γαμέω, which simply denotes the act of marrying. In LXX usage, it often translates Hebrew yabam (levirate obligation), marking it as a term for marriage with legal-familial implications.

epigeios.notes: ἐπί-γειος, -ον (ἐπί, γῆ), of the earth, earthly: τὰ ἐ., Jhn.3:12 Php.2:10 3:19 (anarth.); σώματα, 1Co.15:40; οἰκία, 2Co.5:1; σοφία, Jas.3:15 (Cremer, 153).† (AS)

epiginomai.notes: The prefix ἐπι- (epi-) adds a directional or supervisory force to γίνομαι, yielding the sense that something arises *upon* or *toward* a target. In Acts 28:13, a south wind arises to aid Paul's voyage—the word denotes an environmental event that impinges on the narrative. Its rarity in the NT (hapax) and limited LXX attestation suggest it was available but not a preferred term in Koine expression.

to supervene or occur as a subsequent event
to spring up or emerge secondarily

related.note: simple form; to come into being, happen, become

epiginosko.notes: The prefix ἐπι- sharpens γινώσκω toward focused perception or attentive recognition rather than abstract knowing. In Act. 25:10 Paul insists the Sanhedrin 'recognize' (ἐπέγνω) him as a Roman citizen; in 1 Co. 13:12 the contrast between seeing dimly and seeing face-to-face hinges on the difference between partial perception and full ἐπίγνωσις. Context determines whether the sense leans toward perception, recognition, or formal acknowledgment.

to recognize or identify someone or something already known

epignosis.notes: Epignōsis carries the sense of knowledge that is relational and transformative, not mere intellectual data. In Philippians 1:9 and Colossians 3:10, Paul uses this term to denote deepening knowledge of Christ and God that shapes character and moral judgment. The ἐπί- prefix (upon/intensification) distinguishes it from simple γνῶσις: this is knowledge that comes through closer acquaintance and personal recognition rather than detached observation.

epigraphe.notes: Epigraphē denotes a visible inscription—most famously the titulus on Jesus's cross (Mark 15:26; Luke 23:38), where it publicly announces the charge. In Matthew 22:20 and Luke 20:24, it refers to the superscription and image on a Roman coin. The word is straightforward in reference, though theologically weighted when marking the crucifixion inscription.

epigrapho.notes: ἐπιγράφω carries the sense of writing or inscribing something onto a surface, most memorably the charge inscribed above Jesus at Mark 15:26. In Hebrews 8:10 and 10:16 (citing Jeremiah 31:33 LXX), the word shifts into metaphorical register: God's law is written not on stone but on the hearts and minds of the covenant people—a powerful theological image of internalized obedience.

epikaleo.notes: ἐπικαλέω carries theological weight in Acts when believers 'call upon the name of the Lord' (Acts 2:21, citing Joel 2:32), marking conversion and prayer. The ἐπί prefix signals direction toward or appeal to a higher authority. Context sharply narrows sense: Acts 7:59 (Stephen calling on Jesus) differs from Acts 10:5 (Peter being summoned by name); both are ἐπικαλέω but with distinct force.

epikalumma.notes: This rare noun appears only once in the NT (1 Peter 2:16), where Peter warns against using freedom as a cover (ἐπικάλυμμα) for malice. The word carries the straightforward sense of a physical or metaphorical veil that conceals something beneath. Its single occurrence is metaphorical and polemical, addressing hypocrisy in the early church community.

epikalupto.notes: This rare compound appears only in Rom. 4:7, where Paul quotes Psalm 32 to declare that those whose transgressions are 'covered' (ἐπικεκάλυπται) experience forgiveness. The ἐπι- prefix intensifies the root sense: sins are not merely hidden but thoroughly blotted out. The metaphorical force is theological—divine forgiveness renders sin invisible.

metaphorically, to blot out or forgive (sins)

epikataratos.notes: This word carries heavy covenantal freight in Paul's Galatians argument (3:10, 3:13), where Christ's death 'redeems us from the curse' (κατάρα) of Torah-breaking. The prefix ἐπι- intensifies the notion of a curse that *actively presses upon* the subject. Context is crucial: the word does not denote mere misfortune but the legal consequence of covenant violation in Jewish-Christian discourse.

worthy of divine condemnation or curse

epikathizo.notes: This compound verb appears only once in the NT (Mat. 21:7), where the disciples place garments on the donkey and Jesus sits upon it during his entry into Jerusalem. The ἐπι- prefix intensifies the simple verb κάθημαι, specifying not merely sitting but sitting upon a particular object, paralleling the LXX translation of Hebrew רָκַב (to ride or mount).

epikeimai.notes: ἐπίκειμαι primarily carries the sense of resting or being positioned upon something, either literally (the coal fire in John 21:9) or figuratively as an imposed obligation. The word does not denote active laying but rather the state of being laid or pressing upon. In Hebrews 9:10 and the context of ἀνάγκη, it captures the force of a regulation 'bearing down on' worshippers—useful for understanding how OT ordinances are treated in Hebraic thought.

epikoureios.notes: The term refers historically to adherents of Epicurus's school, though popular misunderstanding often caricatures them as hedonists. Acts 17:18 presents Epicurean and Stoic philosophers debating Paul in Athens, representing the full spectrum of pagan Greek wisdom. The word itself is a proper-noun adjective form derived from the philosopher's name.

One who pursues pleasure as the highest good

epikouria.notes: Paul uses this hapax legomenon in Acts 26:22 when defending himself before Agrippa: God's epikouria sustained him through hardship—the word evokes military reinforcement, lending gravitas to his claim of divine backing. The term is rare in NT but appears in Wisdom literature (LXX), suggesting a more formal, elevated register than everyday synonyms.

epikrino.notes: The ἐπι- prefix adds a sense of authority or finality to κρίνω. The sole NT occurrence is Luke 23:24, where Pilate 'decides' (ἐπέκρινεν) to grant the Jews' request to execute Jesus—a judicial pronouncement by one with executive authority. In Koine usage, the word carries administrative weight; it is not mere opinion but authoritative decree.

epilambano.notes: The ἐπι- prefix intensifies the root λαμβάνω, imparting a sense of forcible or deliberate seizure. The word appears consistently in the middle voice in both LXX and NT, suggesting a reflexive or interested engagement (the subject takes hold for oneself). Notable uses include Peter's rescue in Mat. 14:31 and the arrest of Paul in Act. 21:30—contexts where physical restraint or forceful intervention is paramount.

epilanthano.notes: ἐπιλανθάνω carries theological weight in Hebrews and Matthew contexts, where forgetting God's promises or His works is a failure of faith and covenant awareness. The preposition ἐπι- intensifies the simple λανθάνω, suggesting not momentary lapses but habitual neglect or willful inattention. In Hebrews 6:10 and 13:2, the word marks the danger of believers losing sight of God's faithfulness or failing to honor what He has done; in Matthew 16:5 and Mark 8:14, the disciples' forgetting of bread becomes a sign of spiritual dullness.

epilego.notes: ἐπιλέγω appears only twice in the NT: Jhn. 5:2 (naming the pool) and Act. 15:40 (Paul choosing Silas in the middle voice). The ἐπι- prefix emphasizes selection or designation toward a specific purpose rather than mere calling. Context determines whether the word carries the 'naming' or 'choosing' sense; the middle voice in Acts 15:40 clarifies the reflexive choosing.

epileipo.notes: A rare compound appearing only once in the NT (Hebrews 11:32), where it carries the sense of time being insufficient for the narrator to recount the deeds of the judges and other faithful. The ἐπί- prefix intensifies the simplex λείπω, suggesting a pressing or critical failure. In the LXX, it correlates with the Hiphil of שׁאר (remain), though the semantic overlap is loose.

epilesmone.notes: This noun appears only once in the NT (Jas 1:25), where it characterizes the hearer who forgets what he has heard rather than putting it into practice. The ἐπι- prefix suggests not mere absent-mindedness but a turning-away from or failure-to-retain. James contrasts such forgetfulness with the obedient doer of the law who will be blessed in his doing.

epiloipos.notes: This hapax legomenon appears in 1 Peter 4:2, where it modifies χρόνος ('the remaining time'). The prefix ἐπί- adds emphasis to the simple adjective λοιπός, suggesting what is emphatically 'still left' or 'outstanding.' In that eschatological context, it carries no special theological weight beyond its literal sense of temporal remainder.

epiluo.notes: The word denotes explaining or interpreting something opaque—typically parables (Mk 4:34) or dreams (Acts 19:39). The prefix ἐπι- intensifies the root λύω (loose), suggesting the idea of untangling or working through to a solution. Only two NT attestations; more common in the LXX for dream-interpretation.

epilusis.notes: This rare noun appears only in 2 Peter 1:20, where Peter asserts that no prophecy of Scripture admits of 'private interpretation' (ἰδία epilusis). The word carries the sense of an explanatory solution or resolution—the unpacking of what is hidden or compressed. Etymology points to ἐπί (upon) + λύω (to loose), literally 'a loosing-open,' but the synchronic usage emphasizes the interpretive act itself rather than mere mechanical release.

epimartureo.notes: This rare verb appears only once in the NT (1 Pet 5:12), where Silas testifies to the grace of God as it operates in the community. The ἐπι- prefix intensifies or adds emphasis to the simple martureō, carrying the sense of bearing witness *to* or *in support of* something with added solemnity or reinforcement. The sole occurrence limits broader theological weaponization, though it sits in a paraenetic context addressing church stability.

epimeleia.notes: ἐπιμέλεια appears only once in the NT (Acts 27:3), where the centurion Julius grants Paul ἐπιμέλειαν, allowing him kind treatment and visits from friends during the voyage to Rome. The noun denotes both the emotional posture of carefulness and the concrete actions it produces—Julius's permission and arrangement for Paul's comfort. In classical and LXX usage, it regularly carries the sense of administrative care or stewardship, not mere sentiment.

Luke 10:34–35 (the Good Samaritan tending the wounded man's injuries) and 1 Tim 3:5 (household management) both show the word in contexts of practical, hands-on responsibility. The word avoids the emotional register of ἀγάπη and carries instead the sense of diligent, attentive stewardship.

epimelos.notes: This adverb appears only once in the NT, in Luke 15:8, where the woman searches for her lost coin ἐπιμελῶς—the word underscores the painstaking, methodical nature of her search. The prefix ἐπί- (upon) + μέλη (care) suggests attention directed *onto* an object. It denotes the manner of action rather than its speed or intensity.

epimeno.notes: ἐπιμένω intensifies the simple μένω by prefixing ἐπί-, shifting focus from passive dwelling to active, sustained presence or devotion. The word appears most memorably in 1 Cor 16:8 (Paul's declaration to remain/tarry in Ephesus) and in contexts of spiritual persistence (Acts 15:34, Phil 1:24). Context determines whether the stress falls on physical location, temporal duration, or moral/spiritual steadfastness.

euphraino.notes: Euphainō carries the sense of causing or experiencing joy, often with a relational or social dimension—gladding others or celebrating together rather than isolated inner feeling. The passive usage (be happy, make merry) dominates in narrative contexts like the prodigal son (Luk 15:32), where the household's collective festivity marks reconciliation. The verb's causal force (to gladden) distinguishes it from the more neutral chairō.
semanticRange: to make glad, cheer, or gladden (someone)
to rejoice, be happy, or make merry
to celebrate or feast with joy
to delight in or find pleasure in

related.note: to rejoice or be glad; broader emotional positivity without the causal sense
Hebrew cognate in LXX; to rejoice, be glad; primary OT referent for euphrain in translation
to grieve or sadden; direct antonym in 2 Cor 2:2 (opposite emotional vector)

euphrates.notes: Euphrates carries immense symbolic weight in biblical and apocalyptic imagination. In Rev. 9:14 and 16:12, it functions as an eschatological threshold—the place where demonic armies and the kings of the east gather for final conflict. The river's historical role as Rome's eastern frontier amplifies its apocalyptic significance. John's audience would recognize it simultaneously as a geopolitical reality and as a marker of cosmic division.
semanticRange: the great river of western Asia, forming boundary between Roman and Parthian empires
in Revelation, symbolic barrier between the present age and eschatological judgment
geographical marker in apocalyptic geography and ancient Near Eastern cosmology

related.note: companion river in Mesopotamia; marks opposite boundary of Roman Near East
Hebrew name for same river; appears in OT as covenant boundary (Gen. 15:18; Deut. 11:24)
generic term for river; Euphrates is most theologically laden river in biblical literature

euphrosune.notes: Euphrosunē denotes not merely internal joy but outward, communal gladness—the kind that bubbles up in celebration. The word appears only twice in the NT (Acts 2:28 quoting Ps 16:11, and Acts 14:17), each time stressing God's provision as the source of human cheerfulness. In secular Greek it often marked festive merriment; the LXX consistently mapped it to simchah, linking it to covenantal blessing and worship.
semanticRange: Rejoicing, gladness, cheerful exultation
Joy expressed in celebration or festivity
The state of being cheerful or well-pleased

related.note: Adjective (cheerful, well-minded); etymological root of euphrosunē
Broader term for joy; euphrosunē emphasizes the festive, sociable dimension
Hebrew equivalent in LXX; denotes gladness and rejoicing, often in cultic or communal settings

eupoiia.notes: Eupoiia appears only once in the NT (Heb 13:16), where it denotes the concrete practice of beneficent works as a form of worship pleasing to God. The word carries no special theological freight beyond its straightforward ethical sense of doing good and performing acts of generosity; context treats it as a virtue accessible to Christian communities.
semanticRange: Actively doing good; beneficent action toward others
The virtue or practice of benevolence and kindness
A specific benefit or act of generosity conferred

related.note: Prefix meaning 'well'; forms the first component of eupoiia
Verb 'to do, make'; provides the root for the second component
To do good; closely related verb with similar ethical sense

euporeo.notes: This verb appears only once in the NT (Acts 11:29), where believers who are well-off decide to send relief to the church in Judea during a famine. The word denotes not mere wealth but the practical ability and capacity to help—a state of having enough to spare. In context, it emphasizes readiness and means rather than abstract prosperity.
semanticRange: to have sufficient means, be well provided for
to prosper or flourish in one's circumstances
to be in a position to afford or manage something

related.note: adjective: well-provided, prosperous; the root of euporeō
verb: to go, travel; shares the πορ- stem but distinct in meaning
noun: a journey or means of travel; cognate with different semantic focus

euporia.notes: The word appears only once in the NT (Acts 19:25), where the silversmith Demetrius warns his fellow craftsmen that Paul's preaching threatens their euporia—their economic prosperity and comfortable livelihoods. The term denotes not mere existence but the comfortable sufficiency that permits ease and security. In the LXX it translates Hebrew חַיִל (chayil, strength/wealth), marking a semantic overlap with resourcefulness.
semanticRange: abundance, plenty, sufficiency of means
ease of resources, wealth
facility, freedom from constraint

related.note: adjective: well-supplied, wealthy; the root from which euporia derives
noun: journey, course; related to the sense of facility and smooth passage
noun: abundance, surplus; comparable semantic field of material overplus

euprepeia.notes: This rare noun appears only once in the NT (Jas 1:11), where James uses it to describe the 'beauty' of a flower that withers—a metaphor for the transience of earthly glory. The word carries the sense of outward, visible comeliness rather than inner virtue. In context it denotes the perishable splendor that contrasts with the enduring word of God.
semanticRange: outward comeliness or graceful appearance
dignified beauty or stately bearing
the quality of being fitting or appropriate in form

related.note: adjective form; denotes what is comely or of goodly appearance
related term for beauty or loveliness, emphasizing seasonal freshness
broader term for beauty or comeliness in classical Greek

euprosdektos.notes: εὐπρόσδεκτος carries the sense of being acceptable or pleasing, particularly in liturgical and relational contexts. Paul uses it for offerings acceptable to God (Rom. 15:16) and for charitable giving that meets divine approval (2 Cor. 8:12), and Peter applies it to believers as a spiritual house of living stones (1 Peter 2:5). The prefix εὖ (well) intensifies the root sense of reception, marking not mere acceptance but favorable, approved reception.
semanticRange: Acceptable, pleasing to God or another authority
Favorable, meeting approval or welcome reception
Suitable for offering or presenting as a gift

related.note: Root verb meaning to receive favorably; denotes the accepting action behind the state
Related adjective meaning acceptable; εὐπρόσδεκτος is the intensified, more common form

euprosedros.notes: This rare adjective appears only in 1 Corinthians 7:35, where Paul urges undistracted devotion (ἵνα ... εὐπάρεδρος) to the Lord. The word literally conveys the notion of sitting well and close (εὖ + πρόσ + ἕδρα), emphasizing proximity and attentiveness rather than distraction. Context determines whether it stresses freedom from worry or readiness to serve.
semanticRange: devoted to; able to attend closely upon
sitting well beside; in good attendance
free from distraction; undivided in service

related.note: sitting beside; attending; related form without the εὐ- prefix

euprosopeo.notes: This verb appears only in Gal 6:12, where Paul censures those who 'want to make a fair show in the flesh'—a pointed critique of religious performativism. The word carries theological weight because it exposes the tension between inward faith and outward human impression. The prefix εὐ- (eu-) and root προσωπ- (prosōp-, face) together denote not merely appearance but the strategic *cultivation* of appearance to win social or religious standing.
semanticRange: to make a fair or impressive outward appearance
to show oneself favorably in the flesh; to present well bodily
to aim at human approval or good standing (religious context)

eupsucheo.notes: This verb carries the sense of rallying one's inner resolve—not mere emotion but steadfast courage grounded in conviction. It appears only once in Paul's letter to the Philippians (2:19), where Timothy's expected report will give Paul heart. The term reflects a Stoic-tinged vocabulary for spiritual endurance but fits Paul's pastoral tone without philosophical baggage.
semanticRange: to be of good courage or confidence
to take heart, be encouraged in spirit
to maintain cheerful resolve in adversity

related.note: adjective form; literally 'good-souled,' denoting courage or fortitude

eurokludon.notes: Eurokludōn appears only once in Acts 27:14, where it strikes Paul's ship during the voyage to Rome, creating the catastrophic storm that drives the vessel toward the African coast. The word is a hybrid Greek-Latin maritime term (combining the east wind Eurus with Latin Aquilo, the north wind), reflecting the practical navigation vocabulary of ancient sailors. Its single NT occurrence makes it a vivid meteorological detail in Luke's shipwreck narrative rather than a theologically charged term.
semanticRange: A powerful northeast wind in the Mediterranean
The tempestuous wind that struck Paul's ship near Crete
A hybrid wind between the east wind (Eurus) and north wind (Aquilo)

euruchoros.notes: Euruchōros appears only once in Matthew 7:13, where Jesus contrasts the wide gate (πλατεῖα) and spacious road (euruchōros hodos) that leads to destruction with the narrow gate and constricted path leading to life. The word emphasizes not merely width but roomy accommodation—the broad way invites and accommodates the many. The compound etymology (broad + space/room) reflects a synchronic sense of spatial ease or roominess rather than abstract breadth.
semanticRange: spacious, roomy; offering ample room or breadth
wide, broad in physical or spatial extent
expansive; permitting easy passage or movement

euschemon.notes: In 1 Cor 12:24, Paul uses εὐσχήμων to contrast the body's less honorable parts with those naturally graceful; the term bridges physical comeliness and moral propriety. In 1 Cor 7:35, the adverbial form qualifies how virgins may attend to the Lord ἀπερισπάστως—without distraction—shifting the sense toward 'proper' or 'becoming' conduct. The word carries no deep theological baggage but marks Paul's pragmatic concern for both bodily dignity and social decorum in community life.
semanticRange: Physically graceful, elegant, or comely in appearance
Morally seemly, becoming, or proper in conduct
Respectable or of high social standing
Fitting or appropriate to circumstance or decorum

Direct antonym; carries sense of unseemly, uncomely, or improper in body or conduct
Related concept of gracefulness and proper appearance; overlaps in aesthetic and moral registers

euschemonos.notes: The adverb carries the sense of conducting oneself with dignified propriety and social orderliness. It appears in Paul's ethical injunctions: 1Co 14:40 frames church order, while Rom 13:13 and 1Th 4:12 exhort believers to 'walk becomingly' in public conduct. The word does not impose a legalistic standard but appeals to the character of the gospel's public witness.
semanticRange: in a dignified, orderly, and respectable manner
with propriety and decorum appropriate to the context
in a way that reflects good judgment and social grace
decorously, becomingly (archaic sense)

related.note: adjective form; literally 'well-formed,' denotes seemly or becoming conduct

adjective meaning orderly, well-arranged; cognate semantic field of proper decorum

euschemosune.notes: This hapax carries the sense of graceful or dignified outward presentation. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 12:23 to argue that the less conspicuous members of the body deserve greater honor precisely because they merit greater care in dress and propriety—a rhetorical inversion of social convention. The word denotes not mere beauty but socially recognized decorum.
semanticRange: graceful or dignified bearing; outward comeliness
propriety or seemliness in appearance or demeanor
decorum befitting social or ceremonial context

related.note: adjective form; denotes graceful, well-formed, or of good appearance

eusebeia.notes: Εὐσέβεια is central to Pastoral theology in 1–2 Timothy and Titus, where it marks the goal of Christian instruction and the fruit of sound doctrine. The word carries both the inward posture (reverent awe) and the outward practice (obedience, moral conduct). In 1 Tim 4:7–8, Paul contrasts training in eusebeia with mere physical exercise, showing that true godliness integrates the whole person's orientation toward God. LXX and later Jewish usage (4 Maccabees) reinforce the Hebraic sense of yirah (fear of the Lord) as the root of all virtue.
semanticRange: reverent devotion toward God; fear of the Lord
godliness or piety as a moral virtue and spiritual practice
religious conduct and observance that flows from devotion
the disposition to honor and obey God in daily life

related.note: Adjective form; one who is pious or devout toward God
Verb; to act piously, to show reverence or devotion
Fear/reverence; often overlaps with eusebeia in denoting awe before God

eusebeo.notes: The verb denotes active, deliberate conduct marked by reverence—most naturally toward God or the divine, though the accusative construction allows other objects. The prefix εὖ- ('well') frames piety not as passive fear but as well-directed reverence. Attested only twice in the NT (1 Timothy 5:4 and Titus 2:12), where it characterizes familial and ethical duty within Christian households.
semanticRange: to show reverence or piety toward someone
to act dutifully in religious observance
to conduct oneself with godly respect

related.note: adjective form; devout, pious, reverent toward God
noun; piety, godliness, devout reverence—core virtue in Pastoral Epistles

eusebes.notes: εὐσεβής denotes active, observable piety—the person who fears and worships God with conduct to match. Peter's description of Cornelius (Acts 10:2) shows this word marking a Gentile exemplary in prayer and almsgiving; it bridges Jewish piety language (צַדִּיק, חָסִיד) into Greek ethical-religious vocabulary. High theological stakes: the word signals genuine godliness vs. nominal religion.
semanticRange: devout, showing reverence toward God
pious, exhibiting godly conduct and practice
righteous, characterized by fear of God and proper worship

related.note: root verb: to revere, worship, show respect toward deity

eusebos.notes: This adverb modifies verbs and clauses to characterize an entire action or lifestyle as godly and reverent. Paul uses it in 2 Timothy 3:12 to describe living piously in Christ, and in Titus 2:12 as part of exhortation toward godly conduct. The word denotes not mere outward form but internalized religious orientation expressed through behavior.
semanticRange: in a manner showing reverence toward God; piously
with religious devotion and godly conduct
in accordance with proper worship and fear of the divine

verb; to fear, revere; semantically related concept of religious reverence

eusemos.notes: This adjective appears only once in the NT (1 Corinthians 14:9), where Paul criticizes speaking in tongues without intelligibility: 'how will anyone know what is said if the speech is not intelligible (eusēmos)?' The word carries no deep theological charge but serves Paul's argument about edification through clear communication in worship.
semanticRange: Clear and distinct in meaning; intelligible to the hearer
Conspicuous or evident to perception
Easy to grasp or understand without ambiguity

To understand or perceive mentally; eusēmos describes speech that makes understanding possible

eusplagchnos.notes: This rare adjective appears only twice in the NT (Eph 4:32 and 1 Pet 3:8), both times describing the emotional posture believers should adopt toward one another. The underlying semantic range treats the σπλάγχνα (bowels) as the seat of compassion—a somatic metaphor common in Greco-Jewish thought. In Ephesians 4:32, Paul enjoins the church to be εὔσπλαγχνος in mutual forgiveness; in 1 Peter, it qualifies the συμπαθής (sympathetic) heart required for Christian community. Do not confuse the medical sense attested in Hippocrates with the NT metaphorical use; context always determines which sense is active.
semanticRange: having compassionate bowels; moved with tender mercy
emotionally responsive to another's suffering or need
merciful, kindhearted in disposition

eutheos.notes: εὐθέως carries the sense of temporal immediacy or directness of action, without connotation of urgency or emotional intensity. The word is particularly prevalent in the Synoptic Gospels and Acts to mark rapid narrative progression—see Mk 1:20 (disciples follow immediately) and Jn 13:32 (the Son is glorified directly in the Father). Unlike παραχρῆμα, which stresses the instantaneous effect of an event, εὐθέως focuses on the unbroken succession of moments.
semanticRange: Immediately, without delay or interval
Straightway, at once, in quick succession
Directly, as a prompt consequence or result

related.note: Adjective form; denotes straight, direct, or immediate in quality
Common phrase in Gospels marking sudden narrative transition or response
Near-synonym; emphasizes instant effect rather than temporal immediacy

euthetos.notes: εὔθετος denotes fitness or suitability for a specific function or role. The word appears only three times in the NT, each in a practical context: soil fit for crops (Heb 6:7), salt useful for seasoning (Lk 14:35), and a disciple fit for the kingdom (Lk 9:62). The dative construction reveals the relational nature of the fitness—something is suitable *for* a particular purpose or *to* a particular person.
semanticRange: Fit or suitable for a particular purpose or use
Ready or prepared for action or service
Usable or serviceable in a given context
Well-adapted or convenient (of persons or things)

euthudromeo.notes: This compound verb appears only in Acts, describing Paul's sea journeys: the voyage from Troas to Philippi (16:11) and from Tyre to Caesarea (21:1). The word denotes favorable sailing conditions allowing a ship to maintain a direct route without tacking or delay. In context, it signals narrative progress and divine providence enabling swift, unobstructed travel.

to make headway directly toward a destination

euthumeo.notes: The verb denotes a mental or emotional state of good cheer and courage, especially in the face of adversity. In the three NT occurrences (Acts 27:22, 25; Jas 5:13), the word carries the sense of maintaining calm resolution or encouraging oneself and others during trials—Paul's exhortation to the ship's company during the storm is the paradigmatic instance. The word is not primarily about laughter or merriment but rather composed hopefulness grounded in confidence.

to maintain an optimistic or resolute frame of mind
to encourage or comfort someone with reassurance
to make cheerful or gladden (rare transitive sense)

euthumos.notes: This rare adjective carries the sense of emotional and spiritual buoyancy—a state of hopeful resolve rather than mere happiness. Paul uses it in Acts 27:36 when reassuring the shipwrecked crew, anchoring the word firmly in contexts of crisis resilience. The compound structure (εὖ + θυμός) denotes literally a "well-spirited" condition, though context (not etymology alone) determines whether emphasis falls on cheer, courage, or kindness.
semanticRange: of good cheer, cheerful in spirit
encouraged, emboldened in disposition

euthuno.notes: This rare verb (2× in NT) operates at the intersection of literal and figurative senses. In Jas.3:4 it denotes the pilot's steering of a ship; in Jhn.1:23 (quoting Isa.40:3 LXX) it carries the prophetic sense of preparing or making straight the Lord's way. The word does not signify moral straightening in the modern pietistic sense, but rather the practical work of clearing and directing a path.

euthus.notes: In the NT, εὐθύς most often describes literal straightness—especially of roads and paths in OT prophecy citations (Isa 40:3 in Matt 3:3, Mark 1:3, Luke 3:4). The word carries a secondary figurative sense of moral rectitude or directness of purpose (Acts 13:10, 2 Peter 2:15), but lacks the dense theological weight of terms like λόγος or χάρις. Context determines whether the referent is spatial or ethical.

euthutes.notes: This noun appears only once in the NT (Heb 1:8, quoting Ps 45:7 LXX), where it characterizes the scepter of God's kingdom. The word carries the sense of moral uprightness or integrity grounded in its root εὐθύς (straight). Though semantically related to δικαιοσύνη, εὐθύτης emphasizes the quality of being aligned or undeviating rather than forensic justice.
