eutonos.notes: This adverb denotes forceful, intense action or speech. In Luke 23:10, the chief priests and scribes accuse Jesus εὐτόνως (with vehemence), and in Acts 18:28 Apollos disputes εὐτόνως (vigorously) using Scripture. The word emphasizes not mere volume but concentrated, sustained effort—etymologically from eu (well) + teinō (to stretch), but synchronically it simply marks earnest, vigorous execution.

eutrapelia.notes: In classical Greek, eutrapelia denoted admirable wit and social grace (Plato, Aristotle). By the NT period, the term had narrowed to mean vulgar or licentious joking. Eph 5:4 condemns it alongside foolish talk and obscenity as incompatible with thanksgiving, marking a sharp ethical pivot from earlier panegyric use.

eutuchos.notes: Eutychus appears only in Acts 20:9–12, the account of a young man who fell asleep during Paul's lengthy sermon in Troas, tumbled three stories from a window, and was pronounced dead—only to be restored to life through Paul's intervention. His name, etymologically 'fortunate' (eu + tyche), carries ironic weight given the near-fatal accident, though the narrative outcome vindicates the sense of the name. This is purely a narrative character with no theological loading beyond the miracle itself.

exago.notes: ἐξάγω primarily denotes a purposeful leading out—physical removal from a space, condition, or custody. The word is heavily freighted in exodus narratives (Acts 7:36, Heb. 8:9) and scenes of liberation or rescue (Acts 5:19, 16:37–39), where it carries connotations of divine agency and deliverance. Context determines whether the emphasis falls on the leader, the journey, or the destination; the ἐξ- prefix consistently signals the directionality of movement away from an origin point.

exagorazo.notes: Exagorazō carries rich soteriological weight in Paul's letters, especially Galatians 3:13 and 4:5, where Christ's redemptive work is framed as buying believers back from the curse of the Law and slavery to bondage. The ἐξ- prefix intensifies the notion of extraction or removal. When applied to time (Eph. 5:16, 'redeeming the time'), the word denotes seizing an opportunity with decisive purpose—not merely spending but reclaiming what would otherwise be wasted.

exaiphnes.notes: ἐξαίφνης denotes not merely speed but the aspect of surprise or lack of forewarning. Luke 2:13 (sudden appearance of the heavenly host) and Acts 9:3 (Philip's abrupt encounter with the risen Lord's light) exemplify the word's force in marking divine or narrative turning-points. The prefix ἐξ- intensifies the root notion of the sudden.

exaireo.notes: ἐξαιρέω appears 8 times in the NT, concentrated in Matthew (eye-plucking, 5:29, 18:9) and Acts (Paul's rescue narratives, 26:17). The verb denotes forceful or purposeful extraction—not gentle removal. The middle voice (especially in Acts 26:17) shifts focus to personal agency: God choosing or delivering Paul from hostile circumstances. The LXX background confirms rescue semantics; context determines whether the sense is physical (removing an eye) or metaphorical (deliverance from peril).

The ἐξ- prefix intensifies the basic request (αἰτέω), carrying the sense of demanding with particular force or urgency. The middle voice form ἐξῃτήσατο emphasizes the agent requesting something for himself or his own benefit.

By the first century, it had already crystallized as a technical term for the sacred writings—not mere human documents but the oracles of God. The plural αἱ γραφαί (the Scriptures) became standard for the entire scriptural canon. Controversy arises when modern readers conflate this formal term with modern concepts of textual inerrancy; the ancient sense emphasizes divine authority and interpretive force, not mechanical inspiration.

graptos.notes: Graptos appears only once in the NT (Rom 2:15), where Paul describes God's law as 'written' upon human hearts—denoting not mere inscription but the permanent, divinely impressed character of moral law. The term denotes concrete military gear in John 18:3 (arresting party's weapons) but carries Paul's ethical force in 2 Cor 10:4 regarding spiritual warfare. Without knowledge of its Hebrew root and temple context, modern readers easily miss the depth: early crowds were not merely cheering but invoking salvific expectation. The phrase 'hosanna to the Son of David' (Matthew 21:9, 15) crystallizes this fusion of praise and petition.

huperogkos.notes: This rare adjective denotes speech or character that swells beyond due bounds—arrogant and grandiloquent. It appears in warnings against false teachers in 2 Peter 2:18 and Jude 16, where those who speak 'great swelling words' (hypérogka) exploit unstable believers. Etymology connects to εἶδον (to see), but synchronic usage simply denotes 'what appears to the eye.'

In the NT it appears frequently to distinguish private property, personal relationships, or the domestic household from public or communal spheres; see Jn 1:41 (εὑρίσκει τὸν ἴδιον ἀδελφόν, 'finds his own brother') and 1 Tim 3:4 (τοῦ ἰδίου οἴκου καλῶς προϊστάμενος, 'managing his own household well'). The word carries no deep theological loading; it is a straightforward ownership and particularity marker.

The single occurrence is geographical background rather than theological freight.

Early patristic sources predominantly understood the figure as female, though post-medieval exegesis often masculinized the name. The theological significance lies in the verse's implication of women in authoritative apostolic roles.

ioustos.notes: Ioustos is a Latin cognomen (meaning 'just' or 'righteous') adopted as a Greek proper name in the NT. kataloipos.notes: This adjective appears only once in the NT, in Acts 15:17 (LXX citation), where it refers to the remnant of humankind sought by the Lord. The κατά- prefix emphasizes what is left in reserve or set apart rather than simply 'rest.' The term carries OT resonance through its Hebrew equivalents (שְׁאֵרִית, יָתַר), where 'remnant' theology is theologically significant, but the Greek adjective itself is primarily descriptive rather than loaded with Pauline or Johannine freight.
semanticRange: left behind, remaining after others depart
surviving remnant (of people or things)
what is left over or reserved

kataluma.notes: The word appears only three times in the NT, most famously in Luke 2:7 where Mary and Joseph find no kataluma in Bethlehem—often rendered "inn" in English, though the term can denote either a public lodging house or a private guest room. Context alone determines whether it means a commercial establishment or household hospitality space; the Lukan usage does not settle the question definitively.
semanticRange: a lodging place or inn for travelers
a guest room or room for hospitality

related.note: verb root: to lodge, stay temporarily, or dissolve
noun: inn or caravanserai, semantic near-synonym in Lk 10:34
Hebrew: chamber or guest room, used in LXX parallels for kataluma

kataluo.notes: This verb carries a significant semantic split: the physical/structural sense (destroying the temple, Matt. 26:61) and the legal/covenantal sense (nullifying law or justice, Gal. 2:18; Rom. 3:31). The lodging sense (Acts 10:48 context) appears less frequently but is attested. The temple-destruction accusation against Jesus is one of the most charged uses; context is crucial to avoid conflating metaphorical dissolution (of covenants) with literal demolition.
semanticRange: to destroy, tear down, demolish a structure
to overthrow, nullify, or render void (a law, covenant, claim)
to lodge, stay temporarily as a guest
to dissolve or break up (a gathering, assembly)

Build up, construct; kataluō stands as its direct antonym in Gal. 2:18

katamanthano.notes: This rare verb (NT hapax, Mat.6:28) carries the sense of sustained, deliberate observation that issues in understanding. The κατα- prefix intensifies the base μανθάνω, sharpening the focus from mere learning to meticulous attention and careful consideration. Jesus uses it when directing disciples to observe the lilies—not casual glancing, but penetrating study of how God provides.

to learn or understand thoroughly through careful observation
to consider deliberately; to contemplate or reflect upon

related.note: base verb: to learn or understand; κατα- adds intensive force
similar intensive compound; to perceive fully or pay close attention to
related semantic field: to observe or gaze upon with understanding

katamartureo.notes: This compound carries the force of judicial testimony that works *against* the defendant. The κατα- prefix intensifies the adversarial character. The word appears only three times in the NT, all in the passion narrative (Matthew 26:62, 27:13; Mark 14:60), where false or hostile witnesses testify against Jesus at his trial. The construction takes both the accusative (the charge or thing testified) and genitive (the person accused).

to provide damaging evidence or accusation that incriminates another person
to stand as a witness whose testimony works to someone's detriment

related.note: base verb: to testify or bear witness generally, without the adversarial sense
noun: a witness; one who gives testimony in judicial or religious contexts

katameno.notes: This rare compound verb (only once in the NT) denotes physical or temporal permanence in a location. The κατα- prefix intensifies the sense of stability or settled remaining, though the semantic distinction from simple μένω is subtle. Acts 1:13 uses it of the apostles staying in Jerusalem after the Ascension.

to abide or dwell permanently

katanalisko.notes: This hapax legomenon appears only in Heb 12:29, where it describes God as a consuming fire (πῦρ κατανάλισκον). The perfective κατά- prefix intensifies the simplex ἀναλίσκω, emphasizing thorough or complete consumption. The word echoes the LXX rendering of divine judgment imagery without carrying the theological density of more frequent terms.

katanarkaomai.notes: The word denotes a figurative paralyzing or exhausting burden. Paul uses it in 2 Corinthians 11:9 and 12:13-14 to describe refusing financial support lest he become a drain on the church's resources. The etymology (κατα- + ναρκάω, 'to numb') roots it in the physical sensation of numbness, but in Pauline usage it carries the sense of becoming an impediment or weight rather than literal paralysis.

katanathema.notes: This rare word appears only in Romans 9:3, where Paul declares his willingness to be ἀνάθεμα (anathema) ἀπὸ τοῦ Χριστοῦ for the sake of his kinsmen. The κατα- prefix intensifies the sense of being under divine judgment and separation. The word carries deep theological weight regarding covenant exclusion and divine judgment.

katanathematizo.notes: The κατα- prefix intensifies the sense of cursing. The word occurs only once in the NT, at Matthew 26:74, where Peter curses and swears while denying Jesus—a moment of bitter self-imprecation. The compound emphasizes vehement, emphatic cursing rather than mere ill-wishing.

kataneuo.notes: κατανεύω occurs only once in the NT (Luke 5:7), where James and John respond to Simon Peter's overflowing catch of fish by nodding to their partners in the other boat to come help. The κατα- prefix may suggest 'down toward' (reinforcing the physical gesture) or simply add emphasis. This is straightforward gestural communication with no theological baggage; context alone determines whether the nod signals assent, summons, or acknowledgment.

to nod in assent or agreement
to beckon or gesture toward someone

katangeleus.notes: This noun appears only once in Acts 17:18, where Paul is called a κατανγελεύς of foreign deities by Athenian philosophers. The term denotes not merely private speech but public declaration or heralding—a professional function. In the inscriptional evidence cited (κ. ἀγώνων, 'herald of contests'), the word carries dignity and official standing. Context determines whether the proclamation is approved or mocked.

A herald or messenger of a particular doctrine or philosophy

katangello.notes: Katangellō carries the sense of solemn proclamation, often of Christian witness or doctrine. The kata- prefix intensifies the notion of announcing throughout or before an audience. It appears frequently in Acts as the verb for apostolic preaching (Acts 3:24, 4:2, 13:5), where early believers 'proclaim' the resurrection and the word of God.

To declare (especially news, doctrine, or a message) to an audience

katanoeo.notes: The κατα- prefix intensifies νοέω, signaling a deliberate, sustained act of attention and reflection rather than mere looking. In Mat. 7:3 and Luk. 6:41 (the mote and beam passage), Jesus uses it to spotlight the hypocrisy of noticing another's fault while ignoring one's own—the word carries moral force through context, not inherent theology. The verb often involves a moment where awareness crystallizes into understanding.
semanticRange: to observe carefully, take deliberate note of
to perceive or become aware of something
to consider or contemplate with understanding
to look at and comprehend the significance of

katantao.notes: In Acts, κατανταω typically refers to physical arrival at a port or city (Acts 16:1, 18:19, 27:12). The κατα- prefix intensifies the sense of directional completion; the word denotes not merely coming, but coming *to* a specific, fixed point. Context determines whether the emphasis falls on the journey itself or on the terminus reached.

to come down to, descend upon (of condition or state)
to attain or achieve (a goal or status)
to end up, result in (with sense of completion)

katanusso.notes: κατανύσσω appears only once in the NT (Acts 2:37), where it denotes the crowd being 'pierced' in heart at Peter's accusation of crucifying Jesus—a vivid image of conscience struck by prophetic word. The LXX uses it for both literal piercing and the stunning/silencing of the heart by divine truth. This word carries weighty theological cargo: the internal wounding of awareness that precedes repentance.

to stun or strike with overwhelming force
to pierce the heart or conscience with deep emotion

katanuxis.notes: This rare noun appears only once in the NT (Rom 11:8), where Paul quotes Isaiah 29:10 to describe the hardened spiritual condition of Israel—a divinely-sent insensibility to God's truth. The word denotes not mere drowsiness but a judicial blindness of mind, making it theologically weighted in discussions of divine hardening and election. The connection to κατανύσσω (to pierce) is etymological but secondary to the torpor sense in actual usage.

Torpor or stupefaction of the mind

katapateo.notes: Katapateō occurs primarily in synoptic narrative and Hebrews. The literal sense (trampling pearls, Lk 8:5) shades into strong figurative usage in Heb 10:29, where trampling the Son of God denotes apostatic rejection of redemptive grace—a high-stakes theological moment. The prefix kata- carries the force of 'down' and intensification.

to crush or press under foot, often of animals or crowds
metaphorically, to treat with contempt or reject

katapauo.notes: In Hebrews 3–4, κατα­παύω carries immense theological weight: it denotes both God's ceasing from work (Heb 4:4, citing Gen 2:2–3) and the believer's entering into eschatological Sabbath rest through faith in Christ. The verb bridges OT Sabbath observance with NT fulfillment theology. Acts 14:18 uses it more plainly to mean 'restrain' (preventing a crowd from offering sacrifice).

to bring to rest; to make cease from labor

katapausis.notes: Katapausis carries significant theological weight in Hebrews, where it refers not merely to physical rest but to the eschatological rest of God into which believers enter through faith (Heb 3:11, 4:1). The term evokes the Old Testament promise of rest in the land (Psalm 95:11 LXX) and God's own rest after creation, making it a key term for Christian soteriology and perseverance.
semanticRange: cessation from labor; state of rest or repose
the eschatological rest promised to God's people
a resting place or settlement

katapetasma.notes: The term carries significant theological weight in the NT, especially in Hebrews and the passion narratives. Its tearing at Jesus' death (Matt 27:51, Mark 15:38, Luke 23:45) symbolizes the removal of the barrier between God and humanity. In Hebrews 6:19 and 10:20, it represents the separation the old covenant maintained, now rendered obsolete by Christ's intercession.

the inner veil of the Jewish temple (the veil of the Holy of Holies)

kataphero.notes: The word carries a spatial or directional sense (downward motion via the κατα- prefix) that narrows in Acts to legal voting—either casting a ballot against an accused (Acts 26:10) or presenting charges (Acts 25:7). The passive sense of being overcome by sleep (Acts 20:9, Eutychus drowning at Troas) extends the 'brought down' sense metaphorically to physical exhaustion. Context alone determines whether the action is literal, juridical, or metaphorical.

katapheugo.notes: Katapheugō appears only twice in the NT, each with distinct force. In Acts 14:6, Paul and Barnabas flee physically to Lystra and Derbe when threatened; in Hebrews 6:18, the verb shifts to metaphor—believers 'flee for refuge' by grasping the hope set before them in God's promises. The preposition κατά- intensifies pheugō, marking not mere escape but deliberate, purposeful flight toward a safe haven.

kataphileo.notes: This verb denotes a kiss characterized by intensity or emotion—whether tender affection (the father embracing the prodigal son in Luke 15:20) or, notoriously, Judas's betrayal (Matthew 26:49). The κατα- prefix suggests either repeated action or emphatic force. Context alone determines whether the gesture is genuine or performative.

kataphroneo.notes: Kataphroneō denotes a mental stance of dismissal or contempt toward a person or thing, expressed through the prefix κατά- (down) + φρονέω (to think). The word appears most distinctly in warnings against despising the vulnerable (Mat. 18:10, 1 Ti. 4:12) and in Paul's contrast between serving God and despising Him through greed (Mat. 6:24, Luk. 16:13). The contempt is not mere passive dislike but an active thought-pattern that shapes behavior.

kataphronetes.notes: This rare term appears only once in Acts 13:41 (Paul's synagogue speech quoting Hab. 1:5 LXX) to describe those who reject the divine message. The κατα- prefix intensifies the contempt, marking a settled disposition to scorn rather than a momentary dismissal. Context in Acts emphasizes willful resistance to God's work.

kataphtheiro.notes: The single NT occurrence (2 Tim 3:8, passive perfect participle κατεφθαρμένοι) describes minds morally corrupted in the context of false teachers resisting truth. The perfective κατα- intensifies the base verb φθείρω, marking complete, thoroughgoing depravation. LXX usage tilts heavily moral rather than merely physical destruction.

katapino.notes: κατα­πίνω ranges from the mundane (swallowing food or drink) to the dramatic metaphorical—especially in apocalyptic contexts where it denotes being overwhelmed or annihilated. The prefix κατα- intensifies the verbal action toward completion or downward direction. Paul's use in 1 Corinthians 15:54 ("death is swallowed up in victory") and the image of the earth swallowing the serpent's flood in Revelation 12:16 showcase its theological force.

katapipto.notes: The kata- prefix intensifies the notion of falling downward or collapsing. In Acts 26:14, Paul falls to the ground in the vision; in Luke 8:6, seeds fall upon rocky soil and fail to germinate—a figurative use of the same verb. The word carries no special theological weight beyond its literal or semi-literal narrative function.

katapleo.notes: This compound appears only once in the NT (Luke 8:26), where Jesus and the disciples sail across the lake to the region of the Gerasenes. The kata- prefix emphasizes downward or directional motion toward land; the word is purely navigational with no theological freight, though the voyage itself frames the demoniac's healing.

kataponeo.notes: This rare compound carries the sense of systematic oppression or maltreatment that gradually wears down the victim. Both NT instances appear in passive voice: Stephen's account of Pharaoh's harsh treatment of Israel (Acts 7:24) and Lot's distress among the wicked Sodomites (2 Pet 2:7). The κατα- prefix intensifies the simple verb πονέω (to labor or suffer) into an image of cumulative, relentless burden. Not heavily theological, but dramatically human in depicting unjust suffering.

katapontizo.notes: The verb appears only twice in Matthew's Gospel, both in dramatic moments: Peter sinking in the sea (14:30) and the rebuke against causing a child to stumble (18:6, where drowning in the sea carries judgment language). The prefix κατα- intensifies the sense of downward motion into water. In the LXX it renders Hebrew verbs of drowning and overwhelm (ṭābaʿ, bālaʿ, šāṭap), anchoring it firmly in the semantic field of aquatic destruction.

katapsucho.notes: This hapax legomenon appears only in Luke 16:24, the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, where the tormented rich man begs for his tongue to be cooled with water. The prefix κατα- intensifies the sense of thorough or complete cooling. The word's singular appearance makes it contextually straightforward without significant theological overload, though its use in an eschatological setting gives it narrative weight.

kataraomai.notes: This word carries significant theological weight because cursing in Scripture invokes divine judgment and exclusion from blessing—matters central to covenant theology and NT ethics. The verb appears most pointedly in James 3:9–10, where the tongue that blesses God yet curses humans is exposed as contradictory; and in Romans 12:14, where believers are commanded not to curse persecutors, reversing the Old Testament permission for imprecatory speech. The passive perfect participle (ἐπικατάρατος) denotes those under the law's curse in Galatians 3:10.

katargeo.notes: Κατάργέω carries heavy theological freight in Paul's letters, particularly Romans 3–7 and 1 Corinthians 15, where it denotes the eschatological invalidation of the Law and the final defeat of death and hostile powers. The word does not mean simple cessation but rather the stripping away of active force or authority. In Luke 13:7, the fruitless fig-tree's claim on the soil is κατηργημένη—no longer operative. Modern readers often flatten this to mere 'ending,' but Paul's usage stresses the exposure of functional obsolescence or the reversal of an incumbent power-structure.

katarithmeo.notes: The kata- prefix intensifies the sense of counting into or among a particular group. Acts 1:26 provides the sole NT occurrence, where the apostles count Matthias among the twelve—the verb marks formal inclusion by enumeration. katartisis.notes: Paul uses κατάρτισις only in 2Co.13:9 to describe his apostolic aim: the spiritual strengthening and restoration of the Corinthian church. The term carries ethical weight, denoting not abstract perfection but the concrete process of bringing believers into proper alignment with Christ. It shares conceptual space with τέλειος (mature) and σωτηρία (wholeness), making it theologically charged in discussions of sanctification.

The word denotes the outcome or state of being thoroughly prepared and fitted for ministry—not a moment but a condition. Its rarity and single occurrence mean it carries no extended theological burden, though the context of Ephesians' ecclesiology gives it pastoral weight.

kataschesis.notes: κατάσχεσις carries the sense of active seizure or holding, not mere passive ownership. In Acts 7:5 and 45, it refers to Abraham's and the Hebrews' inherited territorial claims—the land 'given' as a holding they would occupy. The prefix κατά- intensifies the notion of firm control. keleuo.notes: κελεύω denotes authoritative verbal command, typically by someone of higher status directing action or movement. It appears frequently in narrative contexts where Jesus or officials summon crowds, disciples, or servants (e.g., Mat. 14:19 feeding, 27:64 guard the tomb). The word emphasizes the act of ordering by word, not coercion; context determines whether compliance is expected or guaranteed.

keleusma.notes: Hapax legomenon in the NT, appearing only in 1Thess 4:16 in the phrase "with a shout of command" (ἐν κελεύσματι), where it describes the Lord's authoritative summons at the parousia. The word denotes not mere speech but a forceful, piercing call—the kind that compels immediate obedience. In the broader Greek world, it carries military or nautical overtones: the cry of a centurion marshaling troops or a helmsman commanding crew.

kenodoxia.notes: This hapax legomenon appears only in Phil 2:3, where Paul exhorts the Philippians to do nothing ἐκ κενοδοξίας—"out of vainglory." The term denotes not mere pride but a particularly hollow, baseless conceit: self-esteem untethered from actual virtue or achievement. In the context of Paul's call to humility and mutual regard, κενοδοξία represents the spiritual posture opposed to the mind of Christ exemplified in verses 5–11.

kenodoxos.notes: Paul uses this word uniquely in Gal 5:26 (the only NT occurrence) within the vice list of the flesh, warning against the folly of seeking esteem through self-promotion. The compound structure (kenos + doxa) captures a distinctly Pauline theological concern: pride divorced from genuine virtue or divine recognition is spiritually empty. The word echoes Hellenistic moral critique of vainglory but receives its force in Paul's contrast between flesh-driven boasting and Spirit-enabled humility.

kenoo.notes: Kenoō appears only five times in NT, but Philippians 2:7 (Christ emptying Himself) has generated centuries of christological debate. The verb denotes not literal evacuation but deprivation of power, status, or validity—it strips something of its force or meaning. In 1 Corinthians 9:15, Paul warns against letting his boast become hollow; in Philippians, the semantic weight shifts to Christ's voluntary self-limitation in the Incarnation.

kenos.notes: κενός operates on two registers: literal (an empty vessel) and metaphorical (vain talk, faith without substance). Paul weaponizes it in 1 Corinthians 15:14 to warn that without resurrection, kerygma and faith collapse into vacuity. The word carries polemical weight in warnings against false teaching (Colossians 2:8), where ideas are exposed as hollow rather than merely disagreeable.

kensos.notes: κῆνσος is a Latin loanword (census) denoting the poll tax imposed on conquered territories. It appears only in the Synoptic accounts of Jesus's confrontation with the Pharisees about paying tribute to Caesar (Matt. 17:25; 22:17; Mark 12:14). The word itself is politically charged—submission to κῆνσος signified acceptance of Roman occupation—but the theological weight lies in Jesus's response, not the term itself.

kentron.notes: κέντρον carries the sense of a literal sting (Rev 9:10, locusts) and extends metaphorically to the wounding power of death itself (1 Cor 15:55, where Paul echoes Hos 13:14). The word denotes not death abstractly, but the sharp, piercing agent by which death inflicts its injury—a rhetorical image of mortality's cruelty.

kenturion.notes: Mark alone uses this Latin loanword (κεντυρίων), while Matthew and Luke employ the hybrid Greek form ἑκατοντάρχης. The centurion at the cross (Mk 15:39) becomes a paradigm of faith recognizing Christ's identity—a gentile outsider whose confession mirrors the reader's own confession of faith. The word is a straightforward military designation without theological freight.

kephalaioo.notes: This verb occurs only once in the NT (Mark 12:4), where servants sent to collect vineyard rent are beaten on the head. The word carries the sense of striking or wounding the head, but in broader Greek usage (Thucydides, Sirach) it denotes summarizing or recapitulating. kephalis.notes: Κεφαλίς appears only once in the NT (Heb 10:7), quoting Psalm 40:8, where it denotes the rolled scroll containing the divine law or will. The name carries christological weight: the rock-name parallels OT foundation imagery and secures Peter's role in Matthew 16:18, though Paul treats Kēphas as a historical authority figure rather than a doctrinal pillar. kepos.notes: κῆπος denotes a walled or enclosed garden—a space deliberately planted and tended, not wilderness. In the NT it appears in Luke 13:19 (mustard seed in a garden), John 18:1 (garden across the Kidron), and John 19:41 (garden tomb of Joseph). The word carries connotations of cultivation, privacy, and care. No special theological weight attaches to it beyond its literal sense and occasional symbolic use for fruitfulness or sanctuary.

The compound κηπ-ουρός literally pairs κῆπος (garden) with οὖρος (watcher/guardian), emphasizing the custodial role. keraia.notes: The word carries the sense of a small distinguishing mark—literally a horn-like projection—visible in Hebrew script where fine strokes differentiate letters (ד vs. ר). The pairing with iota underscores that nothing in Scripture, down to its tiniest marks, will pass away.

Matthew's reference to the potter's field (27:7) is a narrative detail with eschatological resonance in Christian tradition, though the word itself remains concrete.

The term carries no special theological freight beyond its literal reference to material composition.

In Revelation 14:10 and 18:6, the term carries judicial weight—the 'mixing' of God's wrath becomes an oxymoronic image of undiluted judgment poured into a cup. The word appears only twice in the NT but gains symbolic force through its wine-mixing associations in Hellenistic culture.

keration.notes: This word appears only in Luke 15:16, the parable of the prodigal son, where the famished younger son longs to eat the carob pods that the swine consumed. kerdaino.notes: κερδαίνω carries sharp theological weight in the Gospels, especially Matthew 16:26 and parallels, where gaining the whole world is juxtaposed against losing one's life—a paradox exposing the emptiness of mere material profit. The word's range spans mundane commercial gain (servants investing talents, Mat. 25) to the spiritual calculus of discipleship. Without context, 'gain' misses the moral weight: in Jesus's teaching, κερδαίνω often marks what is ultimately *disadvantageous* when weighed against the kingdom.

The word denotes small coins—likely representing the loose change of temple commerce. The kermatistēs denotes a person whose trade was currency exchange—converting pilgrims' foreign coinage or large denominations into the small change needed for Temple sacrifices and vows. kopazo.notes: In the NT, κοπάζω appears only in the storm-stilling narratives (Matt. 14:32; Mark 4:39, 6:51), where the word denotes the wind ceasing to rage rather than human weariness. The semantic development from 'grow weary' to 'abate' reflects how exhaustion naturally leads to cessation of activity; context determines which sense operates. The LXX uses it for both divine calming (the flood subsiding) and human fatigue, showing the root's flexibility across domains.
semanticRange: to cease raging or blowing (of wind, storm)
to grow weary, become exhausted
to abate, die down, become calm
to stop, come to an end

related.note: noun: weariness, toil; etymological root of κοπάζω
verb: to grow weary, labor to exhaustion; overlapping semantic field
Hebrew: to abate, subside; LXX equivalent in Gen. 8:1 (flood narrative)

kope.notes: κοπή occurs only once in the NT (Heb. 7:1), where Melchizedek meets Abraham after the king's decisive slaughter of the enemies. The word carries military force—not mere injury but defeat in battle. In the LXX, it consistently translates Hebrew words for smiting and military defeat (נָכָה, נָגַף), anchoring it firmly in the register of war.
semanticRange: A blow or stroke delivered in battle; slaughter
A smiting or decisive defeat in warfare
A pounding or striking action (classical sense)

kopetos.notes: This word appears only in Acts 8:2, where devout men make great κοπετός over Stephen's death. It denotes the audible, physical expression of grief in Jewish mourning practice—beating one's chest, tearing garments, wailing. The term is not theologically freighted but culturally specific to Mediterranean funeral customs.
semanticRange: audible lamentation or wailing, especially at funerals
ritual beating of head and breast as sign of mourning
public expression of grief or sorrow for the dead

Hebrew equivalent in LXX; denotes lamentation and funeral dirge

kophinos.notes: Κόφινος denotes a practical household basket, likely of wicker construction. In the Synoptic feeding narratives (Mark 6:43, 8:19; Matthew 14:20, 16:9; John 6:13), the twelve baskets of leftover fragments carry symbolic weight—abundance and provision—but the word itself is semantically straightforward. The near-synonymy with σφυρίς in parallel accounts suggests no theological distinction between basket types.
semanticRange: A wicker or woven basket for carrying food
Container used in the feeding miracles (loaves and fishes)
By extension, a receptacle or vessel for provisions

kophos.notes: κωφός denotes both literal deafness and muteness but carries significant theological weight in the Gospels, especially in healing narratives where Jesus restores speech to the mute (Mat. 9:32–33; 12:22; 15:30–31; Luke 11:14). The word often appears in contexts of spiritual insensitivity—the inability to perceive divine truth—making it emblematic of resistance to the kingdom. In Matthew 15:30–31, the healing of κωφοί functions as a sign that the messianic age has arrived.

Unable to speak; mute or dumb
Spiritually insensitive or unresponsive to truth

kopiao.notes: The verb denotes not mere activity but effort-laden work, often implying physical or spiritual fatigue. Jesus uses it at Mat.11:28 to invite the weary to rest, while Paul applies it to apostolic labor in 1 Cor.15:10. The sense combines striving and exhaustion; context determines whether emphasis falls on the toil itself or its wearying effect.

kopos.notes: Κόπος denotes strenuous, costly exertion—not mere activity but work that exhausts. Paul uses it to measure apostolic ministry (1 Th 1:3, "labor of love") and to validate the Corinthian workers' effort in building the church (1 Co 3:8, 15:58). The word carries moral weight when paired with ἀγάπη, suggesting love expressed through sacrifice and weariness.

kopria.notes: κοπρία carries the literal sense of a dunghill or manure pile—a place of waste and refuse. In Luke 14:35, salt that has lost its flavor is fit only to be cast on the κοπρία, employing it as a symbol of uselessness. The word's low-register status makes it rare in NT (2 occurrences) and reserved for vivid pastoral or metaphorical contexts where worthlessness requires graphic expression.

kopto.notes: The middle voice (κόπτομαι) is crucial: it shifts from active cutting to ritual mourning—beating the breast in grief, as in Matthew 21:8 (Triumphal Entry) and Revelation 18:9 (lamentation over Babylon). The verb bridges violent action and emotional display; context determines which sense governs.

korasion.notes: Κοράσιον is a diminutive, colloquial form that carries a note of affection or tenderness while denoting a girl typically younger or more vulnerable than a grown woman. In the Gospels it appears most memorably in the raising of Jairus's daughter (Mark 5:41–42, Matt. 9:24–25) and Herod's stepdaughter (Matt. 14:11), contexts where the girl's youth and dependence on adult male figures structure the narrative.

korax.notes: The word appears uniquely in Luke 12:24, where Jesus invokes ravens as a lesson in trusting divine provision—they neither sow nor reap yet God feeds them. In OT law, ravens were classified as unclean (Lev 11:15; Deut 14:14), yet this negative cultic status contrasts sharply with the NT use as an emblem of God's care. The natural history is straightforward; the theological weight derives entirely from context.

korban.notes: This Semitic loanword carries the full weight of Jewish sacrificial piety. In Mark 7:11, Jesus invokes it as a cautionary example of how a pious-sounding dedication (Korban—'it is an offering') could be weaponized to exempt adult children from supporting aging parents, exposing the gap between external religious form and commandment-keeping. The word denotes not just any gift but a consecrated one, withdrawn from ordinary use.

kore.notes: Κορέ appears only in Jude 11 as a historical-typological warning: 'they perished in the rebellion of Korah' (τῇ ἀντιλογίᾳ τοῦ Κορέ). The reference invokes Num 16, where Korah and 250 Levites challenge Moses' mediation, claiming all Israel is holy and needs no priestly intermediary. Their destruction by divine fire becomes a standard OT example of presumption and sedition against God's appointed order.

korennumi.notes: The word denotes satiation or complete satisfaction, whether of hunger (Acts 27:38, where the ship's company ate to fullness after the storm) or of spiritual longing (1 Cor 4:8, where Paul uses it ironically of the Corinthians' presumed spiritual self-satisfaction). The passive voice marks the recipient as being filled; the imagery is culinary but carries metaphorical weight in Paul's rhetoric.

korinthios.notes: Κορίνθιος appears twice in Acts (18:8; 27:1) to identify persons associated with Corinth, and forms the implicit addressee group of 1 and 2 Corinthians. The adjective denotes geographic and social identity; Paul's letters to the Corinthian church are his longest and most theologically dense, though the word itself carries no inherent freight—it is the theological context of those letters that matters.

korinthos.notes: Corinth was a strategic commercial and political center where Paul labored (Acts 18:1–18) and subsequently addressed serious theological and ethical issues in his letters. The city's notorious reputation for sexual immorality and idolatry informs the content of 1 Corinthians. A proper noun carries no inherent semantic ambiguity, though the cultural context of Corinth shapes interpretation of Paul's correspondence.

kornelios.notes: Cornelius appears only in Acts 10, the hinge-point narrative for Gentile inclusion in the early church. His household baptism (Acts 10:24–48) marks the moment when Peter recognizes that God shows no partiality and grants repentance unto life to non-Jews. He is consistently portrayed as pious, God-fearing, and generous—qualities that make him the ideal narrative vehicle for demonstrating that ethnic identity no longer determines covenant membership.
semanticRange: Roman centurion in Caesarea, convert to Christianity
Gentile recipient of Peter's vision and gospel inclusion

koros.notes: Koros appears only once in the NT (Luke 16:7, parable of the unrighteous steward), where it quantifies oil and wheat in a commercial debt scenario. The word is a direct transliteration of the Hebrew kor, which Luke uses without explanation—assuming his audience's familiarity with Jewish metrology. Not theologically freighted; purely a unit of measure.

Unit for grain and similar bulk commodities
Commercial standard in ancient Mediterranean trade

kos.notes: Kos denotes both a literal drinking vessel and, crucially, the metaphorical contents of one's divinely appointed fate or suffering. In Psalm 23:5 ('my cup overflows') and Isaiah 51:17 ('the cup of his wrath'), the word carries heavy theological weight. In the NT, Jesus' anguished prayer in Gethsemane ('let this cup pass from me') pivots on kos/potērion as the symbol of sacrificial suffering and divine will.
semanticRange: A drinking vessel; any cup or goblet
A cup as metonym for its contents (wine, poison, or blessing)

kosam.notes: Cosam appears only once in the NT, in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (3:28), where he occupies a position in the post-exilic ancestral chain. The name is otherwise unattested in surviving Jewish sources, making its historical identity uncertain. Luke's genealogical list differs from Matthew's, and Cosam's placement here reflects the evangelist's particular reconstruction of messianic descent.

Son of Elmadam in the descent line from David

kosmeo.notes: The verb denotes practical arrangement or beautification of space and objects. In Mat.12:44 and Luk.11:25, it carries the sense of furnishing a house; in Mat.25:7, trimming lamps. The sense is always concrete—making something orderly or attractive—never abstract or metaphorical in NT usage.

to adorn, decorate, or furnish (a house, lamp, grave)

kosmikos.notes: The adjective κοσμικός carries weight in Hebrews 9:1 (the 'worldly sanctuary') and Titus 2:12 ('worldly desires'), where it signals the tension between temporal, created, or ethically compromised reality and the transcendent or holy. It does not denote 'universal' or 'cosmic' in the modern sense, but rather 'of this world'—often with a pejorative undertone in ethical contexts. The word is rare in the NT but theologically significant wherever the author contrasts earthly institutions or values with heavenly or divine ones.

of this present age, earthly as opposed to heavenly

adjective; eternal, heavenly; semantic opposite in Pauline contrast between worldly and divine

kosmios.notes: κόσμιος carries the sense of orderly or properly arranged behavior and appearance, grounded in the notion of κόσμος as ordered arrangement. It appears only in 1 Timothy (2:9, 3:2) where Paul prescribes modest dress and conduct for women and church leaders, respectively. The word is civic rather than strictly theological—it denotes what is culturally appropriate and decorous.

kosmokrator.notes: The term appears only in Ephesians 6:12, where Paul identifies kosmokratores as the primary category of hostile spiritual forces believers wrestle against. The word carries significant theological weight precisely because it bridges earthly and heavenly dominions—suggesting demonic powers that exercise actual control over worldly systems and institutions. Context makes clear these are not neutral cosmic administrators but actively opposing agents of darkness.

kouartos.notes: Quartus appears only in Romans 16:23, where Paul includes him in greetings alongside Gaius (whose house hosted the assembly) and Erastus (the city treasurer). His name is Latin, reflecting the cosmopolitan character of Corinthian Christianity; he is likely a freedman or slave in Gaius's household. The single mention tells us nothing beyond his presence in the Corinthian community and Paul's apostolic knowledge of him.

koumi.notes: This is an Aramaic interjection preserved untranslated in Mark 5:41, where Jesus speaks it to Jairus's dead daughter (Talitha koum). The word is a direct command form, not a Greek construction, which Matthew and Luke later render into Greek equivalents. Its retention in the original Aramaic suggests the evangelists valued the ipsissima vox (the very voice) of Jesus in this miraculous moment.

kouphizo.notes: The verb occurs only once in the NT (Acts 27:38), where Paul's shipmates lighten the vessel by jettisoning cargo during the storm. The word denotes straightforward physical reduction of weight. No theological loading; it is a practical maritime term.

koustodia.notes: A Latin loanword (custodia) appearing only three times in Matthew's resurrection account (27:65–66; 28:11), where it refers to the Roman guard detail posted at Jesus' tomb. The word carries a military administrative sense: the κουστωδία is both the armed unit and their protective function. Context alone determines whether emphasis falls on the soldiers themselves or their duty of surveillance.

krabbatos.notes: A Macedonian loanword (cognate with Latin grabatus) denoting humble, portable bedding rather than furniture of status. The word lights up in Mark 2:4–12 (paralytic's descent through roof) and John 5:8–11 (healing at Bethesda), where it marks both the sufferer's condition and the physical sign of restoration. Its ordinariness reinforces the irony of miraculous healing.

kraipale.notes: This rare word denotes the nausea and physical distress that follows heavy drinking—a hangover state—rather than intoxication itself. It appears uniquely in Luke 21:34 where Jesus warns against being caught in κραιπάλη on the day of judgment, linking it to the moral carelessness of excessive eating and drinking. The word carries a vivid, almost visceral sense of bodily deterioration from vice.

kranion.notes: Kranion denotes the literal skull bone or bone-structure of the head. The word appears exclusively in the Passion accounts (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) to identify the execution site called Golgotha—'place of a skull'—suggesting either the topography or a traditional burial ground. The anatomy is concrete; the theological weight attaches to the location, not the word itself.

kraspedon.notes: Kraspedon denotes the edge or fringe of a Jewish ritual garment, particularly the tassels (tzitzit) worn on the four corners of the robe according to Torah law. In the Gospels, it appears in healing narratives where the afflicted reach out to touch the edge of Jesus' cloak—a gesture that recalls both physical contact and symbolic respect for his authority (Matt 9:20, Mark 6:56, Luke 8:44). Matthew 23:5 critiques the Pharisees for enlarging their kraspedon to display piety.

krataioo.notes: The verb carries the sense of becoming or being made strong—whether physical robustness (Luke 2:40: the child Jesus grew strong) or spiritual/moral fortitude (1 Corinthians 16:13: "be strong in the faith"). The passive voice predominates in NT usage. Luke 1:80 and Ephesians 3:16 emphasize Spirit-enabled strengthening, where human growth is undergirded by divine power rather than mere physical development.

It appears only once in the NT (1 Peter 5:6), where God is described as mighty in the context of believers humbling themselves before His strength. kratistos.notes: κράτιστος appears only 4 times in the NT, all in formal contexts addressing officials (Acts 23:26; 24:3; 26:25; Theophilus in Luke 1:3). In Eph 1:19 and 6:10, Paul invokes God's kratos as the supreme force undergirding Christian confidence. The term carries eschatological weight: it frames divine dominion over all creation and opposing powers (Heb 2:14, where Jesus strips death of its kratos). Etymology from κύω (to swell) reflects the synchronic sense well.

kumbalon.notes: Κύμβαλον appears once in the NT at 1 Corinthians 13:1, where Paul uses it proverbially: even the loudest cymbal becomes a clanging noise (χαλκὸς ἠχῶν) when divorced from love. The word denotes the actual bronze percussion instrument familiar in both Jewish temple worship and Greco-Roman musical practice, but in Paul's argument it functions as a symbol of meaningless noise—technique without substance.

kuminon.notes: Κύμινον appears only once in the NT (Matt 23:23), where Jesus rebukes the Pharisees for tithing cumin—a minor herb—while neglecting weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faith. The word itself is not theologically loaded, but its appearance carries Jesus' critique of legalistic minutiae divorced from moral substance. The spice was well-known in ancient Mediterranean and Near Eastern cuisine.

kunarion.notes: The word appears only in Matthew 15:25–27 and Mark 7:27–28, in Jesus' encounter with the Syrophoenician woman. Though κυνάριον is literally a diminutive (small dog), the context is densely theological: the woman reframes the term as a humble acceptance of dependent status, turning a potential insult into a plea for mercy. The diminutive does not soften the reproach but rather underscores the rhetorical reversal—she claims the position of a household pet beneath the table, entitled to crumbs. This moment hinges on semantic and social negotiation of the word itself.

The word appears prominently in the Simon of Cyrene pericope (Matt 27:32; Mark 15:21; Luke 23:26), establishing his origin before identifying him as the man pressed into service to bear Jesus' cross. Acts 6:9 and 11:20 show Cyrenaic Jews active in Jerusalem and Antioch, underscoring the diaspora community's missionary reach in early Christianity.

kuriotes.notes: κυριότης carries significant theological weight in Pauline cosmology. In Colossians 1:16 and Ephesians 1:21, it denotes one of several ranks of heavenly powers or dominions (alongside θρόνοι, ἐξουσίαι, δυνάμεις); Christ's supremacy is measured partly by his exaltation above such powers. In 2 Peter 2:10 and Jude 8, false teachers are condemned for despising δόξα and reviling κυριότης, likely referring to angelic authorities. Context is crucial: dominion can mean either the abstract authority or a class of celestial beings who wield it.

lachanon.notes: Lachanon carries the sense of domesticated garden produce—herbs and vegetables rather than wild plants. The word appears mostly in plural forms discussing dietary practices (Romans 14:2) and in Jesus's parable of the mustard seed (Mark 4:32, Luke 11:42), where a single seed grows into a bush large enough to shelter birds. The word does not imply randomness alone but rather submission to a divinely-guided or ceremonially-recognized process.

lamech.notes: Lamech appears in Luke's genealogy (3:36) as the tenth generation from Adam through the line leading to Jesus. In the Genesis account, he is notable as Noah's father and for his speech about vengeance (Gen. 4:23–24); the single NT mention is genealogical only, establishing continuity between Adam and Christ.

The term appears most memorably in Matthew 25:1–13 (the ten virgins with their lamps awaiting the bridegroom) and John 18:3 (the torches carried by the arresting party). In Revelation's visionary language, it carries symbolic weight for celestial or divine fire, though the primary referent remains a physical flame-bearing object.

In Revelation 3:14–22, the angel of the church receives Jesus's most severe rebuke: spiritual lukewarmth, self-sufficiency despite poverty, and blindness to their actual condition. The church's wealth (historically rooted in Laodicea's banking and textile industries) becomes a metaphor for false security.

Lysanias held tetrarchy over Abilene, a region northwest of Damascus. Ancient historians (including Josephus) confirm a ruler by this name in the first century, though chronological details remain debated among scholars. The reference underscores Luke's historiographical claims.

He is the officer who rescued Paul from a Jewish mob and later sent him under guard to the governor Felix in Caesarea, suspecting a plot against Paul's life. In the Greco-Roman world, mageia could refer neutrally to the wisdom of Persian Magi, but in early Christian usage it denotes practices viewed as demonic deception. Matthew's Magi (2:1–12) exemplify the positive trajectory, while Acts 13:6–8 (Bar-Jesus/Elymas) shows the pejorative sense. mallon.notes: μᾶλλον is the comparative form of μάλα and appears frequently in Pauline epistles to intensify arguments or mark preference (Phil 1:12, Rom 3:8). The word typically requires close attention to its syntactic frame—whether it introduces a comparison (with ἤ), reinforces intensity, or marks a shift in logical emphasis. In 1 Cor 12:22 and 14:1, it signals theological priority without ambiguity.

To a greater degree, more intensely or significantly

mamme.notes: μάμμη is a diminutive-like onomatopoetic term (children's speech) that carries warmth and familiarity. In 2 Timothy 1:5, Paul celebrates Timothy's genuine faith as inherited through his mother Eunice and grandmother Lois—one of the rare NT glimpses of intergenerational Christian formation. The word's informality makes it perfect for that intimate, domestic setting.

mammonas.notes: Mammōnas is a Semitic loan word (Aramaic מָמוֹנָא) that Jesus personifies as a rival master in the antithetical sayings of Mt. 6:24 and Lk. 16:13. The term carries theological weight because it does not denote mere possession but rather wealth as an active, enslaving power—a false god competing for allegiance. In Lk. 16:9–11, the "mammon of unrighteousness" suggests that wealth gained dishonestly or hoarded selfishly stands under judgment, making the word freighted with ethical and eschatological tension.

manaen.notes: Manaen appears only once, in Acts 13:1, as one of five prophets and teachers in the Antioch church. The name derives from Hebrew מְנַחֵם (menaḥem), 'comforter,' reflecting Aramaic-speaking Jewish Christian circles. His identification as having been raised with Herod Antipas suggests possible court connections or proximity to Herodian circles before conversion—a rare biographical detail Luke preserves.

manasses.notes: Manasseh appears in Matthew's genealogy (1:10) as a link between Hezekiah and Amon, and in Revelation's tribal census (7:6). The name carries no theological abstraction—it is a purely historical and genealogical marker. The 2 Kings account (21:1–18) presents the king's reign as theologically significant for apostasy and subsequent repentance, though the NT references are merely genealogical.

mania.notes: μανία denotes wild, violent madness—not mere confusion but aggressive frenzy. Paul's single use at Acts 26:24 (Festus accuses him of μανία) carries the sting of appearing dangerously unstable, not merely forgetful. The word sits at the intersection of mental derangement and demonically-inflamed ecstasy in Hellenistic thought, which explains why it surfaces in contexts of possession and prophetic excess.

manna.notes: Manna appears primarily in Jn 6:31–58, where Jesus reinterprets it christologically: the bread from heaven typifies himself as the living bread from heaven. In Hebrews 9:4, the golden jar of manna becomes a type of heavenly provision within the covenant structure. In Revelation 2:17, the promise of hidden manna symbolizes future communion with Christ. The word carries tremendous typological freight in Christian reading and should never be reduced to mere historical detail about ancient food.

manthano.notes: Μανθάνω denotes active acquisition of knowledge—whether through formal instruction, observation, or direct encounter—rather than passive reception. The learner is the agent of the process. In 1 Corinthians 14:31 and Philippians 4:9, the emphasis falls on learning doctrine or behavior by example; in John 7:15, on learning through formal study. The word appears frequently in contexts where moral or theological formation matters.

maraino.notes: This verb appears only once in the NT (Jas 1:11), where it describes the fading of a rich person's wealth and status. The classical sense ranges from quenching fire to causing anything to wither or waste away. In James, the word carries metaphorical force—riches do not merely disappear; they fade like a flower scorched by the sun, emphasizing transience and the futility of earthly prosperity.

maranatha.notes: This Aramaic phrase appears untranslated in 1 Corinthians 16:22, marking it as a fixed liturgical formula from the earliest Jewish-Christian communities. The preservation of the Aramaic form rather than Greek translation suggests it held special weight in apostolic prayer practice, anchoring Christian eschatology in Aramaic-speaking Palestinian roots. Early patristic sources (Didache 10:6) parallel its use as a maranatha cry in the eucharistic setting.

margarites.notes: In Matthew 13:45–46, the pearl functions as a parable image for the kingdom of heaven itself—a treasure of incomparable worth. Matthew 7:6 employs pearls proverbially as something sacred that should not be cast before swine, establishing the word's association with preciousness and reverence. In Revelation and 1 Timothy, pearls appear as luxury goods in descriptions of wealth and adornment, grounding the term in its literal, commercial sense.

maria.notes: Μαρία is a proper name denoting several women in the NT; the most theologically significant is Jesus' mother (Luke 1–2, John 2, Acts 1:14), whose role as bearer and witness shapes early Christian devotion. The name itself is Hellenized Aramaic, marking the text's bilingual Jewish-Greek world. No single unified 'theology of Mary' emerges from the canonical gospels; later tradition substantially developed Marian doctrine beyond the NT data.

markos.notes: Mark appears eight times in the NT as a historical figure in Acts (12:12, 15:37, 15:39) and Paul's letters (Col 4:10, 2 Tim 4:11, Philm 24), identified as Barnabas's cousin and a companion in missionary work. Early church tradition, attested by Papias and others, identifies him as author of the second Gospel, though the Gospel itself names no author. His youthful flight in Gethsemane (Mark 14:51–52) and later reconciliation with Paul (2 Tim 4:11) hint at a biographical arc in early Christian memory.

marmaros.notes: The word denotes a lustrous, crystalline stone—likely marble—prized in antiquity for temples, statuary, and grand structures. In Rev. 18:12, marmaros appears in John's list of luxury goods, signaling Babylon's wealth and material excess. The hapax legomenon status in the NT reflects the term's specialized architectural and economic register rather than theological centrality.

martha.notes: Martha appears primarily in Luke 10:38–41 (the Bethany scene) and John 11 (Lazarus's resurrection). In Luke, she represents the tension between anxious service and contemplative devotion; in John, she demonstrates faith and dialogue with Jesus about resurrection. Her name derives from Aramaic מָרְתָּא (marta), meaning 'lady' or 'mistress.' She is not a theological term but a historically situated character whose portrait illuminates different aspects of discipleship.

Figure of worry and distraction from devotion

martureo.notes: μαρτυρέω bridges forensic witness-bearing (John 1:7–8, John's testimony to Jesus) and faithful confession under persecution (Rev 2:13). In the Fourth Gospel especially, the word crystallizes Johannine theology: the Spirit, the works, and the law all 'testify' to Jesus. The slippage from legal testimony to martyrological witness (Greek martys → English martyr) reflects the high stakes of early Christian confession.

marturia.notes: Μαρτυρία carries weight across legal, epistemic, and theological domains. In the Gospels it denotes courtroom testimony (Mark 14:56; Luke 22:71), but in John and 1 John it becomes freighted with the sense of divine authentication—Christ's witness to himself as sent by the Father. The word also bridges to later martyrdom theology: the martyr's death becomes the ultimate μαρτυρία of faith. Context sharply narrows whether the sense is juridical evidence, eyewitness account, or confession.

marturion.notes: μαρτύριον carries weight in early Christian discourse as both eyewitness testimony (Acts 4:33) and God's own attestation of the gospel (2 Thess 1:10). In 2 Corinthians 1:12, Paul appeals to his *testimony*—his conduct—as proof of apostolic integrity. The word also denotes the sanctuary furnishings or covenant tablets as divine witness (Heb 9:4), a usage rooted in LXX rendering of עֵדוּת. Context determines whether emphasis falls on human witness, divine proof, or institutional sign.

Paul uses it in Acts 20:26 (protesting his innocence before Ephesian elders) and Gal. 5:3 (affirming the obligation of the law with gravity). The verb emphasizes the act of calling witness and the weight of the declaration, not mere reporting of facts.

martus.notes: μάρτυς carries forensic weight throughout the NT: in courtroom scenes (Matt 26:65, Acts 6:13), Paul's martyrdom becomes the supreme attestation (Acts 22:20), and by the late patristic period the word narrows to mean 'martyr' exclusively. Context is everything—Acts 10:41 emphasizes eyewitness testimony; Hebrews 12:1 deploys it metaphorically as a 'cloud of witnesses.' The semantic bridge from 'one who testifies' to 'one who dies for the faith' occurs in Revelation and post-canonical literature, not yet complete in the NT itself.

In Hebrews 12:6, the verb shifts to paternal discipline, drawing on Proverbs 3:12 theology: God's loving correction of his children. mastix.notes: Mastix carries both literal and theological weight in the NT. This metaphorical sense echoes OT wisdom tradition (Proverbs 3:12) where affliction disciplines the righteous. Without context, readers may miss that the term implies not mere suffering but divinely purposed chastisement.

mataiotes.notes: Ματαιότης carries profound theological weight in Paul's argument about creation's subjection to futility (Rom 8:20), where it becomes cosmic rather than merely psychological. The word denotes not mere foolishness but the structural emptiness that results from human disconnection from God's purpose—a condition Ecclesiastes explores relentlessly. In Eph 4:17 it describes the futility of pagan reasoning; in 2 Pet 2:18 it names the empty boasts of false teachers. The word does not simply mean "useless" but rather points to the hollowness of endeavor untethered to divine purpose.

Paul treats it not as mere excess but as incompatible with Christian soberness of mind.

methermeneuo.notes: This verb appears chiefly in narrative contexts where the Gospel writers pause to translate Aramaic or Hebrew words for Greek-speaking audiences. Mark uses it most (5:41 'Talitha koum'; 15:22, 34 'Eloi Eloi lama sabachthani'); John does so for Hebrew names (1:38, 42 'Rabbi,' 'Cephas'). The prefix μετα- does not denote 'meta-translation' but rather serves to intensify or mark the action as systematic rendering. Always carries the sense of making foreign or opaque language intelligible to the reader.

methistemi.notes: μεθίστημι carries the sense of removing or displacing something from its current position, with the preposition μετά- marking the shift or change involved. The word surfaces memorably in 1 Corinthians 13:2, where Paul speaks of faith that could remove mountains—a vivid image of transformative power. In the five NT occurrences, it denotes physical or spatial change rather than metaphysical transformation; context determines whether the action is literal relocation or figurative displacement.

In Heb 12:15 it appears in the warning against bitterness that 'defiles many'; in Jude 8 it denotes the corruption of the flesh through sexual immorality. The verb straddles physical, ritual, and moral registers—what starts as a concrete image of staining becomes a metaphor for spiritual corruption. The conscience itself can be 'stained' (Tit 1:15), showing how thoroughly the word has been metaphorized in early Christian ethics.

The word appears only once in the NT (2 Pet 2:20 in plural form), where it refers to the defilements of the world from which converts initially escape. In LXX usage, it translates several Hebrew terms (פִּגּוּל, שִׁקּוּץ, בֶּצַע) related to ritual taboo and ethical corruption. The metaphorical extension from physical stain to spiritual corruption is characteristic of Koine moral discourse.

In broader Greek thought, miasma suggested a kind of infectious pollution; here it functions theologically to mark spiritual degradation.

In Jude 9, Michael disputes with Satan over Moses' body; in Revelation 12:7, he leads God's army against the dragon. The figure bridges Jewish apocalyptic tradition and Christian eschatology.

neoterikos.notes: This adjective denotes qualities characteristic of youth, especially impulsive desires and passions. In its sole NT occurrence (2 Timothy 2:22), Paul counsels Timothy to flee youthful lusts (neōterikai epithymiai), marking the word as part of early Christian moral instruction about self-restraint. The term carries no theological baggage but signals a developmental contrast between maturity and youth.

neotes.notes: νεότης denotes the period or state of youth as a life stage, not merely chronological age. In the NT it appears primarily in biographical or autobiographical contexts: Mark 10:20 and Luke 18:21 (the rich ruler's claim to have kept commandments since νεότης), Acts 26:4 (Paul's way of life from νεότης in Jerusalem), and 1 Timothy 4:12 (Timothy's instruction not to let anyone despise his νεότης). The word carries a sense of formative years and the vigor associated with them.

nephaleos.notes: The word denotes sobriety as both literal abstinence from wine and metaphorical mental clarity. In Pastoral epistles (1Tim 3:2, 3:11; Tit 2:2), it characterizes required temperament in church officers—a practical virtue rather than a theological construct. The variant νηφάλιος appears in some manuscripts; both forms are equivalent.

At the Transfiguration (Mat. 17:5; Mrk. 9:7), the cloud shelters the divine presence; at the Parousia (Mat. 24:30; 26:64), Jesus comes 'with' or 'on' clouds, echoing Dan. 7:13. The word denotes a discrete, visible phenomenon distinct from abstract vapor, and in eschatological contexts signals God's active intervention in history.

In 1Th 5:6–8 and 1Pe 5:8, sobriety becomes a metaphor for spiritual watchfulness in the face of cosmic struggle; without context, the word can be flattened to mere temperance. nephos.notes: Nephos appears only once in the NT (Heb. 12:1), where it denotes the 'cloud of witnesses'—a metaphorical throng rather than literal meteorological phenomenon. The term carries OT resonance (LXX uses it for עָנַן), evoking divine presence and concealment, but the author's choice here emphasizes sheer numerical density rather than theological weight. Nephelē, its near-synonym, proves far more common in apocalyptic contexts.

nephros.notes: Nephros appears only once in the NT (Rev. 2:23, where Christ claims to search the kidneys and hearts), but it carries enormous theological weight as the OT metaphor for the innermost seat of will, desire, and moral consciousness. The kidneys were thought by both Hebrews and Greeks to be the seat of deepest emotion and divine scrutiny—what we might call the conscience. Without the OT context, modern readers miss the profound claim that Christ penetrates the hidden recesses of human intention.

The metaphorical range (childish reasoning, naïveté) is strong in Paul but less dominant than literal childhood. Context is essential: Jesus' declaration about νήπιοι in Matthew 21:16 invokes blessing of innocence, whereas Paul's νήπιος reasoning signals incompleteness in faith.

The name here almost certainly refers to a Christian convert, not the mythological sea-god; using a pagan deity's name for a human was not uncommon in the Greco-Roman world. The single NT occurrence offers no theological weight—it is simply a personal name embedded in Paul's salutations.

neri.notes: Neri appears only once in the NT, in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (3:27), where he is identified as the son of Melchi and father of Salathiel. nesion.notes: This diminutive appears only once in the NT (Acts 27:16), where Paul's ship takes shelter under the lee of a small island called Clauda during the Mediterranean storm. The word carries no theological weight; it is purely geographical terminology used in narrative context to specify a minor island as a navigation landmark.

nesteia.notes: Fasting in early Christian practice carried symbolic weight: self-denial, repentance, and intensified prayer (Acts 14:23; Luke 2:37). Jesus himself fasts in Matthew 4:2 as preparation before temptation, yet Matthew 6:16–18 warns against performative fasting for human approval. The controversy narratives (Mark 2:18–20 pars.) position fasting as a marker of Jewish piety that Jesus reinterprets—his disciples do not fast while the bridegroom is present. The etymology (νη- privative + ἐσθίω 'to eat') is transparent and synchronically accurate. In context, it denotes physical depletion rather than ritual fasting; the word focuses on the concrete state of not having eaten, though early Christian tradition would develop νηστεία into a formal spiritual discipline.

Christ conquers (Rev 3:21; 5:5), and believers are called to 'overcome' through faith—a victory that is simultaneously present and future (Rev 2:7–3:21; 1 John 5:4–5). The word denotes not mere military triumph but spiritual dominion and perseverance through trials.

Its single NT occurrence (1Jn 5:4) carries theological weight—the faithful's victory over the world through faith in Christ—but the word itself remains a straightforward victory-term without the semantic complexity of more polysemous theological vocabulary. The LXX connection to נֶצַח and its presence in the Maccabees suggests strong connotations of divinely-enabled triumph.

nikodemos.notes: Nicodemus appears uniquely in John's Gospel (5 occurrences) as a foil for exploring the tension between Jewish learning and Christian rebirth. His night visit (3:1–2) initiates the famous dialogue on being born ἄνωθεν, his cautious defense in 7:50 marks growing alignment with Jesus, and his burial assistance (19:39) signals full discipleship. He embodies the Johannine theme that intellectual assent must yield to spiritual transformation.

Ancient sources (Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria) connect them to Nicolas of Antioch, a proselyte deacon in Acts 6:5, though the historical link remains debated. The specific nature of their error—whether antinomian license, participation in pagan worship, or sexual immorality—is inferred from condemnation of eating food sacrificed to idols and 'fornication,' making Nicolaitans a touchstone for discerning false teaching in apocalyptic Christianity.

nomizo.notes: νομίζω carries the sense of opinion or assumption, often tinged with customary or conventional thinking rather than certain knowledge. The word frequently appears where a character's or community's habitual view is at stake—notably Matt 5:17 where Christ addresses what people *suppose* about his relation to Torah, and Acts 16:13 where Lydia and others *assume* a prayer-place exists. Context determines whether the supposition is correct or mistaken.

nomodidaskalos.notes: The term appears only three times in the NT and carries no pejorative weight by itself, though Luke records Jesus' interaction with a nomodidaskalos at 5:17, and Acts 5:34 refers to Gamaliel as one. The compound structure (nomos + didaskalos) is transparent: a teacher whose domain is Torah and its halakic exposition. In 1 Timothy 1:7, the reference is ironic—those 'wanting to be teachers of the law' are rebuked for speaking without knowledge.

nomothesia.notes: This rare term appears only once in the NT (Rom 9:4), where Paul lists nomothesia among Israel's covenantal privileges—not mere jurisprudence, but the privileged reception of God's authoritative legislation. In 7:11, it refers to the people being furnished with the law under the Levitical priesthood; in 8:6, Christ mediates a better covenant, enacted with superior promises. The word carries no inherent theological freight outside its syntactic context; its weight derives from the argument structure of Hebrews itself.

The term carries theological weight by distinguishing the transcendent legislative authority from human judicial power—a key assertion in debates over religious authority and conscience. The word appears rarely in the NT (Acts 5:2–3 of Ananias and Sapphira, Titus 2:10 of dishonest slaves), where it functions as a marker of hidden fraud or embezzlement. Luke 13:34 (the lament over Jerusalem) uses it metaphorically: 'How often I longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her brood (νοσσιά) under her wings.' The word carries literal legal weight in Greco-Roman and Jewish contexts—a bastard child had no inheritance rights and stood outside the family covenant. Here it functions metaphorically to describe those outside God's paternal care. The term is rare in NT Greek but appears in Wisdom literature (LXX) with similar force regarding legitimacy before God.

In Hebrews 5:11 and 6:12, the term carries a spiritual edge—the readers are sluggish in hearing and understanding the deeper things of faith, not merely slow but negligent in spiritual growth. nouthesia.notes: Nouthesia carries the sense of admonition that blends warning with constructive counsel—not mere scolding but redemptive correction. The word appears rarely in the NT (1 Corinthians 10:11, Ephesians 6:4, Titus 3:10), each time in pastoral or familial contexts where the goal is behavioral reformation, not punishment. Paul pairs it with encouragement (1 Thess. 5:12), signaling that nouthesia operates within a relational framework of care.

noutheteo.notes: Noutheteō carries the sense of wise, reasoned correction directed toward a person's conscience or judgment rather than mere emotional rebuke. The etymology (νοῦς + τίθημι, 'to place in mind') reflects the word's force: admonition aims to instruct and redirect, not punish. Paul uses it prominently in Acts 20:31 (weeping warnings to Ephesian elders) and Rom. 15:14 (mutual exhortation in the church), where the corrective tone serves pastoral care.

The word denotes a complete twenty-four-hour cycle and emphasizes the full ordeal of a night-and-day shipwreck experience. No theological freight; purely temporal and physical.

numphas.notes: Nympha appears once in Col. 4:15, where Paul greets 'the church in her/his house.' The textual tradition preserves ambiguity about gender (Νυμφᾶς masculine vs. Νύμφα feminine), reflecting uncertainty in early manuscripts. This person exemplifies the household church model central to early Christian assembly practice.

However, in Revelation 21:2, 9 and 22:17, the term carries enormous theological weight as the Church's identity as Christ's bride—a metaphor that shapes medieval and Reformation ecclesiology. The LXX also uses it for daughter-in-law (following כַּלָּה), a semantic extension absent from most NT usage. Context is crucial: literal bridal references versus eschatological identity.

numphios.notes: Νυμφίος carries significant christological and ecclesiological freight in the NT. Jesus applies it to himself in the Synoptic pericope of fasting (Mark 2:19–20 par.), where his presence as bridegroom reframes fasting practice. The parable of the ten virgins (Matt. 25:1–13) and especially John 3:29 (John the Baptist's testimony) establish the bridegroom as a messianic type. Revelation 18:23 invokes it eschatologically. Early Christian theology developed the bridal imagery of Eph. 5:25–32 and 2 Cor. 11:2, making this term theologically dense.

The image becomes theologically freighted in later Pauline and Johannine thought (Ephesians 5, Revelation 19–21) where Christ and the church are bride and bridegroom, though the noun νυμφών itself does not appear there.

ourbanos.notes: Urbanus appears only in Rom. 16:9, where Paul extends greetings to him as a fellow worker in Christ. The name is Latin in origin (from urbanus, 'urban' or 'civilized') and reflects the cosmopolitan character of the Roman church. The name carries no theological weight in Greek per se but serves as a historical and moral anchor to Israel's kingship. Matthew's inclusion of Bathsheba (via Uriah) among Jesus's ancestors underscores redemption across human failure.

ous.notes: In the NT, οὖς functions both literally (Lk 22:50, cutting off the servant's ear) and idiomatically for spiritual hearing (Mt 13:16, 'ears to hear'). The formula 'having ears to hear' (ἔχω ὦτα ἀκούειν) becomes a test of true discipleship, especially in the synoptic parables and Revelation.

ousia.notes: In the NT, οὐσία appears only in Luke 15:12-13 (the Prodigal Son), where it denotes the younger son's material inheritance or estate. Philosophically and patristically, the word carries immense theological weight as a technical term for substance or essential nature—especially crucial in Nicene trinitarian discourse (one ousia, three hypostases). Context is everything: in Luke's parable it is plainly about property; in doctrinal texts it concerns metaphysical being.

oxos.notes: Ὄξος denotes cheap sour wine (posca), the standard beverage of Roman soldiers and agricultural laborers. In the NT, it appears almost exclusively in the Passion narratives (Mat 27:48, Mrk 15:36, Luk 23:36), where soldiers offer it to Jesus on the cross—a gesture oscillating between mockery and practical comfort, since the acidic drink could dull pain. The word carries no theological weight in itself, but its context saturates it with Christological resonance.

oxus.notes: In the Apocalypse, ὀξύς primarily denotes the sharpness of Christ's sword-like utterance (Rev. 1:16, 2:12, 19:15), carrying symbolic weight as divine judgment. In Romans 3:15, it describes feet swift to shed blood, rendering the Hebrew שָׁנַן (sharp) through speed metaphor. ozias.notes: Ozias appears only in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Mat. 1:8–9), establishing royal Davidic lineage. He was a historically significant king of Judah whose reign saw military expansion but ended in divine judgment (leprosy) for temple transgression. The name denotes 'Yahweh is my strength' in Hebrew etymology, though Matthew's usage is straightforwardly genealogical.

ozo.notes: ὄζω appears only once in the NT at John 11:39, where Martha protests that Lazarus's tomb will stink because he has been dead four days. pachuno.notes: Though rare (2 NT occurrences), pachunō carries significant theological weight. In Matthew 13:15 and Acts 28:27, Jesus and Paul invoke Isaiah 6:10, where the verb denotes the hardening of hearts against God's word—a condition of spiritual dulling or moral insensitivity rather than mere physical thickening. The metaphorical pivot from physical fatness to spiritual callousness reflects OT idiom (Deuteronomy 32:15) where prosperity breeds spiritual obesity.

pagideuo.notes: This verb appears only once in Matthew 22:15, where the Pharisees attempt to ensnare Jesus ἐν λόγῳ (by his words). The word denotes the action of catching someone through cunning or deception, not merely physical entrapment. Its Hebrew parallels (נָקַשׁ, יָקֹשׁ) confirm the sense of deliberate, malicious snaring.

pagis.notes: Παγίς carries theological weight when applied to moral and spiritual dangers. Paul uses it to warn against the snares of greed (1 Tim 6:9) and the devil's schemes (2 Tim 2:26), while in Romans 11:9 it echoes Psalm 69:22 to describe Israel's stumbling. The word's metaphorical range—from literal hunting traps to invisible spiritual pitfalls—makes context crucial for interpreting the severity of the danger intended.

paidagogos.notes: In 1 Corinthians 4:15, Paul uses paidagōgos to denote the stern guardian of the Law—necessary but temporary—before Christological maturity. The term carries institutional and disciplinary weight: a slave entrusted with moral formation, not intellectual instruction (hence the distinction from didaskalos). In Galatians 3:24–25, the pedagogical role of the Law itself—restrictive, preparatory, pointing toward Christ—crystallizes the metaphor's theological freight.

paidarion.notes: This diminutive form of παῖς appears only once in the NT (Jn 6:9, the boy with loaves and fishes). The suffix -άριον originally marked smallness or endearment, but in Hellenistic Greek the diminutive force weakens considerably, and the word functions much like its parent. Context alone determines whether the referent is genuinely small, young, or merely styled informally as a 'lad.'

paideia.notes: Paideia carries profound theological weight in Hebrews and Ephesians, denoting not mere schooling but formative discipline rooted in love. In Heb. 12:5–11, the term encompasses God's corrective work that produces righteousness; in Eph. 6:4, it describes the father's responsibility to nurture children. The word bridges education, moral formation, and divine correction—contexts that must be distinguished carefully.
