paideuo.notes: In the NT, paideuō carries dual force: education and correction intertwined. Acts 7:22 highlights Moses trained in Egyptian wisdom; 2 Timothy 2:25 implies patient instruction of opponents. The word echoes LXX usage for divine discipline (Heb 12:6–7 applies it to God's chastening), where suffering itself becomes formative. Context determines whether the accent falls on instruction or rebuke.

In Rom. 2:20, Paul applies it to the law as an instructor; in Heb. 12:9, the contrast with physical fathers emphasizes spiritual discipline and formation. The term appears frequently in nativity and healing narratives—the infants in Matthew 2, the child John the Baptist, the daughter of Jairus—where the emphasis falls on helplessness, innocence, or the miraculous. Jesus' use of παιδίον in Mark 10:15 as a model for kingdom entry carries symbolic weight about receptivity, though the word itself denotes literal childhood rather than a loaded theological concept.

The verb denotes festive, often musical entertainment in a communal setting, not mere recreation. In the LXX it translates both צָחַק (tsāḥaq, 'to laugh/play') and שָׂחַק (śāḥaq, 'to play/sport'), anchoring its sense in physical merriment and dance rather than solitary amusement.

palai.notes: πάλαι carries the sense of absolute temporal remoteness—'way back when'—rather than relative sequence. It anchors narrative or theological claims in the distant past, as when Jesus invokes judgment on Tyre and Sidon (Mat. 11:21, Luk. 10:13: they would have repented long ago if granted such deeds), or when Hebrews frames God's ancient revelation to the patriarchs (Heb. 1:1). The LXX frequently uses it for יָשֵׁן (worn, stale) and בָּלֶה (worn out), anchoring it firmly in the sense of deterioration as well as mere age.

The word carries significant theological weight in Pauline soteriology, signifying the obsolescence of the Mosaic covenant regime in relation to Christ's fulfillment. palin.notes: Palin is the workhorse temporal adverb for iteration and return in NT narrative. Its frequency (117 times) reflects the Gospels' and Paul's habit of marking repeated actions or sequential thought: Jesus heals, then palin heals again; Peter denies palin. While usually straightforward, in passages like Gal 1:9 (palin lego) it marks rhetorical emphasis or insistence. Spatial uses ('back, backwards') are rarer but appear in directional clauses. pante.notes: This adverb appears only once in Acts 24:3, where Tertullus flatters Felix by acknowledging his benefactions 'in every way.' The dative form πάντῃ intensifies the sense of totality and universal scope, emphasizing complete coverage rather than a single aspect. In Luke 13:11, the woman was bent over and unable to raise herself ἐπὶ τὸ παντελές ('completely, utterly'). pantokrator.notes: Pantokratōr appears 10 times in the NT, predominantly in Revelation (9 occurrences), where it punctuates eschatological visions of God's absolute dominion. The term combines πᾶς (all) and κρατέω (to rule), denoting not mere power but sovereign kingship over all forces. In apocalyptic literature especially, it carries weight as a declaration that no earthly or demonic authority rivals God's ultimate control.

pantos.notes: Πάντως carries the sense of emphatic affirmation or certainty, strengthening a speaker's resolve or commitment. In 1 Corinthians 16:12, Paul uses it to signal his firm intention ("I will come to you"); in Luke 4:23, it frames a proverb with authoritative weight. The word does not primarily mean "all" but rather appeals to the totality or inevitability of a claim—hence the renderings "surely" or "by all means" capture its pragmatic force as an adverbial marker of certainty.

pantote.notes: Πάντοτε denotes temporal completeness—every moment or occasion without interruption. The word denotes a method of indirection—not mere illustration but a device that simultaneously conceals (for outsiders) and reveals (for disciples; cf. Mk 4:11–12). The preposition παρα- and the root sense of 'throwing' suggest one moves from safety into exposure. Context shows it as a virtue—willing endangerment for another's welfare—rather than recklessness. paracheimasia.notes: This rare nautical term appears only in Acts 27:12, where Luke describes the search for a suitable harbor on Crete to 'winter' the ship during Paul's voyage to Rome. The word denotes both the practical activity of overwintering and the physical location or facilities that enable it—a harbor with good anchorage and shelter from winter storms. Context makes clear the urgency: ships in antiquity could not safely navigate during winter months, so finding secure paracheimasia was essential for survival.

parachrema.notes: Παραχρῆμα carries the sense of swift, immediate action or state-change. It appears frequently in healing narratives (Luke 4:39, 8:44–55) and miraculous events where transformation occurs without interval. The word denotes not mere future imminence but present, actualized instantaneity—the fever left her παραχρῆμα; the woman hemorrhaged for twelve years, then was healed παραχρῆμα. Paul uses it positively (1 Cor. 11:2, 15:3) to denote authoritative apostolic teaching he himself 'received and delivered,' yet negatively in Colossians 2:8 when tradition becomes mere 'human tradition' divorced from Christ. The word denotes not mere politeness but active, warm kindness—a deliberate generosity of spirit. It builds on the φιλ- (friend/affection) root and -φρον (mind/disposition), so etymologically it captures "friendly-minded," though in context it refers to the practical hospitality extended to a shipwrecked apostle.

Unlike ἀγάπη, which can denote divine self-giving love, philia stresses mutual fondness and companionship. In Acts 19:31, the Ephesian 'friends' of Paul are civic allies. The word itself is neutral—the pursuit of wisdom is not inherently wrong—but in that pericope it denotes human systems of thought that lack Christ and draw believers away from truth. Care must be taken not to dismiss all rational inquiry, but rather to mark what Paul targets: hollow doctrines divorced from Christ's sufficiency.

In that Hellenistic setting, philosophos denotes adherents of organized schools of thought, not the generic pursuit of wisdom. The term is notably absent from most NT epistolary discourse, reflecting early Christian suspicion of pagan philosophical authority as a rival source of truth claims.

phulake.notes: The word denotes both the active function of guarding and the physical or temporal space/place where that guarding occurs. In the NT, φυλακή appears frequently in narrative contexts of imprisonment (e.g., Acts 5:18–19; 12:4–10) but retains its original sense of "guard" or "watch" in other contexts. The semantic range spans from military/security duty to penal confinement, depending on context.
semanticRange: A guard or watchpost; the act of guarding or keeping watch
Imprisonment or place of confinement; a prison or jail
A period of time during which guard duty is performed; a watch or shift
Figuratively, spiritual protection or safekeeping under divine care

related.note: Verb: to guard, keep watch, preserve; parent verb of φυλακή
Noun: a guard or sentinel; agent noun from same root
Hebrew equivalent; to guard, keep, preserve; LXX often renders with φυλάσσω family

phulakizo.notes: This verb appears only once in the NT (Acts 22:19), where Paul recalls imprisoning believers in synagogues. It is a denominative formation from φυλακή (prison) and carries the sense of placing someone under custodial confinement, typically for judicial or punitive purposes. The context in Acts highlights the word's use in early Christian persecution.
semanticRange: to place or hold in custody or confinement
to imprison as judicial or punitive action
to guard or keep under lock (rare)

related.note: prison or guard-post; the noun from which this verb denominatively derives
to guard or watch; shares root but emphasizes protective custody rather than punitive confinement
prisoner; describes the state that φυλακίζω produces

phulakterion.notes: In Matthew 23:5, Jesus criticizes Pharisees for enlarging their phylacteries for display—the word denotes the small leather boxes with Torah strips Jews wore during prayer, especially morning prayer. The term itself carries no inherent theological judgment; the loading comes from Jesus's use of it to illustrate hypocritical piety. The practice itself was legitimate Jewish observance (Exodus 13:9, Deuteronomy 6:8), but externalism without inner righteousness was Jesus's target.
semanticRange: Small parchment strip containing Torah passages, worn on forehead or arm as religious observance
Amulet or protective charm (broader Greek usage)
Safeguard or fortification (classical usage)

related.note: Verbal root meaning 'to guard'; phylactērion is that which guards or protects
Hebrew source term; rabbinic prayer fillets containing Deuteronomy passages
Sign or mark; phylacteries functioned as visible markers of devotion

phulakterios.notes: This word denotes a military or civic guard responsible for maintaining security or custody. All three NT instances (Acts 5:23, 12:6, 19) place guards at the apostolic prison, where the term carries its straightforward occupational sense. The word is relatively rare in the NT and carries no theological weight beyond its literal referent.
semanticRange: One who stands guard; a sentry or watchman
A keeper or custodian responsible for security
One appointed to protect or defend a place or person

related.note: Root verb: to guard, keep watch, protect; agent noun derives from this
Synonym: a guard or keeper; alternate form with same semantic range
Cognate noun: a guard-post, prison, or place of confinement

phulasso.notes: φυλάσσω carries both protective and observational senses: physical guarding (Acts 12:4, the angel guards Peter in prison) and moral/legal observance (Gal 6:13, keeping the Law). The word's theological weight lies in the tension between external vigilance and inward faithfulness—one 'guards' commandments by obeying them, not merely by protecting them. In 2 Tim 1:14, Timothy is called to φυλάσσω the deposit of faith entrusted to him, suggesting stewardship of doctrine.
semanticRange: to guard or watch over; protect from harm or escape
to keep, maintain, or preserve in a specified condition
to observe, obey, or adhere to (law, command, teaching)
to be on one's guard; remain cautious or vigilant

related.note: noun: guard, watch, custody; derived from same root
noun: guard, watchman; one who performs the action of φυλάσσω
Hebrew cognate (LXX frequent equivalent); to keep, guard, observe covenant

phule.notes: Φυλή carries the sense of a kinship-based social or political unit, most commonly applied to the twelve tribes of Israel in both OT and NT contexts. In Matthew 19:28 and Luke 22:30, Jesus promises the apostles authority over the twelve tribes, invoking the tribal restoration tradition. The word denotes genealogical and geographic cohesion, though by the NT period the historical reality of distinct tribal units had largely dissolved.
semanticRange: A social group united by kinship, descent, or shared ancestry
One of the twelve divisions of Israel; a tribe
A clan or family subdivision within a larger ethnic group
Metaphorically, any distinct people or nation

related.note: To guard or keep; shares root sense of protecting/maintaining a group
Family or clan; narrower kinship term often overlapping with phulē
OT term for tribe; primary LXX equivalent of phulē

phullon.notes: Phullon is a concrete botanical term with minimal theological weight in the NT. It appears chiefly in the fig-tree passages (Matthew and Mark) where Jesus observes its leafing to illustrate readiness and seasonal signs, and in Revelation's vision of the tree of life whose leaves bring healing to nations (22:2). The word simply denotes the literal foliage without metaphorical freight.
semanticRange: A leaf of a tree or plant
Foliage collectively; leafy covering
In eschatological vision, healing or sustenance symbolized by leaves

related.note: Adjective: shedding leaves; botanical term for deciduous character
Hebrew cognate; LXX typically renders as phyllon; leaf or foliage
Noun: tree (the plant of which leaves are part); broader botanical reference

phuo.notes: The word primarily denotes organic growth, especially the sprouting and development of vegetation. In Luke 8:6–8 (the Parable of the Sower), φύω captures the action of seed germinating and plants rising from the soil. The verb spans both transitive (producing offspring, bringing forth) and intransitive (naturally growing) senses, reflecting its use across classical and biblical contexts without distinctive theological weight.
semanticRange: to spring up, grow (of plants)
to bring forth, produce, beget (transitive)
to cause to grow or flourish
to be naturally born or generated

related.note: a plant; cognate noun denoting what is grown or planted
nature, natural disposition; noun from same root emphasizing intrinsic character
to increase, grow; near-synonym but emphasizes expansion rather than sprouting

phurama.notes: Phurama denotes a lump of kneaded dough, but Paul employs it with sustained theological weight in 1 Corinthians 5:6–7 and Romans 11:16 as a metaphor for the church as a unified body. The "firstfruit" consecrates the whole lump; conversely, a little leaven corrupts it. The word draws on Exodus 12 (unleavened dough at Passover) and Numbers 15 (the dough offering), making it a loaded term for corporate holiness and the danger of complacency.
semanticRange: a lump of dough or batter that has been kneaded
the mass of dough destined for baking or offering
figuratively, a community or group viewed as a unified whole

related.note: verb: to mix or knead; etymological root of phurama
noun: leaven; often paired with phurama in metaphorical corruption imagery
verb: to sanctify; contrasts with the defiled lump in 1 Corinthians 5

phusikos.notes: The term φυσικός denotes what belongs to or flows from the natural order of creation. In Rom 1:26–27, Paul uses it to contrast homosexual behavior (contra physin, 'against nature') with what the natural order reveals about divine design. The word carries no inherent moral judgment but serves a descriptive function: it marks the boundary between what accords with created order and what violates it.
semanticRange: Produced or governed by nature; innate rather than acquired
According to the natural order or constitution of things
Operating by natural instinct without rational deliberation
Contrasted with supernatural, spiritual, or divine intervention

related.note: Root noun; carries sense of essential nature, natural constitution
Antonymic phrase; denotes what is contrary to or unnatural
Related adjective; describes the soulish or natural human realm as distinct from spiritual

phusioo.notes: Phusioō is almost exclusively metaphorical in Paul, denoting spiritual arrogance or self-inflation detached from love and truth. It appears in 1 Corinthians 8:1 (knowledge puffs up) and repeatedly in chs. 4, 5, and 13, where it contrasts sharply with the humility and charity required in the body of Christ. The word carries diagnostic force: being 'puffed up' signals a failure to love and a misuse of spiritual gifts.
semanticRange: to puff up, inflate with air or breath
to make proud, cause arrogance or conceit
to be swollen with pride or self-importance
to boast or behave arrogantly toward others

related.note: noun, bellows; root of phusioō, literal sense of inflating
vain, conceited; describes one puffed up by false estimate of self
to blind with pride, obscure judgment; similar metaphorical sense of spiritual inflation

phusiosis.notes: Phusiōsis appears only in 2 Corinthians 12:20, where Paul lists it among the vices he fears finding in the Corinthian community. The word's root imagery (swelling, puffing up) captures the Pauline critique of pride as an inflated self-perception divorced from reality before God. It denotes not mere confidence but pathological arrogance that corrupts community.
semanticRange: Inflated self-regard; a state of being puffed up with pride
Arrogance or conceit that manifests in boastful behavior
Spiritual inflation—pride that opposes humility before God

related.note: Verb: to puff up, inflate with pride; the root verbal form
Direct semantic opposite: humility, lowliness of mind
Related vice: vain conceit; empty glory-seeking paired with pride

phusis.notes: In Paul's anthropological and ethical reasoning, φύσις carries weight: Rom 1:26–27 condemns passions contrary to nature; Rom 2:14–15 appeals to the gentile conscience inscribed by nature; Rom 11:24 exploits the paradox of grace grafting contrary to natural horticultural law. The term bridges Stoic natural philosophy and Torah-rooted ethics, making it theologically fraught where creation order and divine will intersect.
semanticRange: The innate constitution or essential character of a thing or person
Natural powers, capacities, or inclinations inherent to something
The natural world or created order; the realm of physical reality
By extension, one's temperament or disposition (esp. in plural usage)

related.note: Root verb meaning to grow or produce; φύσις denotes the result of natural growth
Prepositional phrase: 'according to nature'; marks conformity to natural order or inclination
Prepositional phrase: 'contrary to nature'; denotes violation of natural law or expectation

phuteia.notes: Phuteia occurs only once in the NT (Matt 15:13), where Jesus declares that every plant (phuteia) his Father has not planted will be uprooted—a metaphor for false teaching and those who mislead. The word denotes both the activity of planting and its concrete result, though context determines which sense applies. In Matt 15:13, it clearly refers to the planted thing itself.
semanticRange: the act or process of planting
that which has been planted; a plant or plantation
vegetation or growth resulting from cultivation

related.note: verb: to plant, transplant; root of phuteia
noun: planted thing, plant; synonymous with phuteia in Matt 15:13
noun: plant, herb; broader botanical term

phuteuo.notes: φυτεύω carries the literal sense of planting vineyards, fig trees, or seeds (Matt 21:33, 1 Cor 9:7), but frequently moves into metaphorical register for establishing or founding churches and faith (1 Cor 3:6–8). The verb's semantic trajectory from horticultural labour to spiritual institution-building makes it rich in Pauline ecclesiology, though the word itself is not theologically overloaded the way λόγος or δικαιοσύνη are.
semanticRange: to plant (seeds, vines, trees) in the ground
to establish or found (a community, church, faith)
to set in place for growth or development

related.note: noun: a plant or cutting; the root noun from which φυτεύω derives
verb: to bring forth, grow, produce; the etymological parent verb
verb: to grow out, sprout forth; cognate denoting emergence or fruiting

piazo.notes: πιάζω denotes physical seizure or forceful apprehension, often in contexts of arrest (Acts 3:7; John 7:30, 32) or capture. The verb is primarily somatic—the subject grabs or restrains the object. In Acts 12:4, Herod πιάζει Peter for imprisonment, grounding the word firmly in the custody register rather than mere touching.
semanticRange: to seize or lay hold of physically
to arrest or take into custody
to catch or capture (in hunting or conflict)
to grasp or apprehend (literal or figurative)

related.note: earlier form; πιάζω is Doric/late Attic variant with broadened sense
to hold fast, seize; overlaps in arrest/custody contexts
to take, receive; related in sense of physical apprehension but broader

piezo.notes: Πιέζω appears only once in the NT at Luke 6:38, where it denotes the pressing down of grain measure in the steward's hands—a vivid image of generous overflowing. The verb's rarity and concrete sense make it straightforward; no theological weight attaches to it. Note the distinct but overlapping πιάζω (to seize), which some later sources conflate with piezō.
semanticRange: to press down or compress physically
to press together, crowd or squeeze
to seize or take hold of (later sense)

related.note: cognate verb meaning to seize or capture; distinct in classical usage but semantically drifts toward piezō in later Greek
Hebrew דָּרַךְ (darak, to tread) rendered by piezō in LXX Mic 6:15; indicates pressure through motion

pikraino.notes: The verb operates on two planes: literal (Revelation 10:9–10, where John's scroll becomes bitter to the stomach) and metaphorical (Colossians 3:19, where husbands are warned against becoming embittered toward wives). The passive voice in Rev. 8:11 personifies a star making waters bitter. Context determines whether physical taste or emotional/relational sourness is at stake.
semanticRange: to make bitter in taste or quality
to embitter emotionally; to cause resentment or bitterness
to turn sour or unpleasant (of circumstances or relationships)

related.note: adjective; bitter in taste or character; parent of pikrainō
noun; bitterness, resentment, gall; abstract form of the same root
to wither, waste away; cognate concept of decay and deterioration

pikria.notes: In Paul's ethical lists (Eph. 4:31), πικρία denotes the internal state of acrimony that erupts in harsh speech and fractured community—not mere lip bitterness but a rooted hostility of heart. Heb. 12:15's phrase ῥίζα πικρίας ('root of bitterness') warns that unaddressed resentment spreads corruption through the body of believers, making this word carry significant pastoral weight in NT paraenesis.
semanticRange: Bitter taste or quality (literal, physical sensation)
Harsh or acrimonious disposition; bitterness of spirit
Animosity, resentment, or malice in character
Root of bitterness; deep-seated grievance or corruption

related.note: Adjective form; carries sense of bitter in taste, harsh in manner
Antonym; sweetness, pleasantness (opposite emotional/relational quality)
Hebrew cognate; bitterness in taste and metaphorically in experience and spirit

pikros.notes: The word operates primarily in its literal sense (bitter taste) but readily extends to emotional and relational contexts. In Jas 3:11-14, πικρός describes both literal brackish water and metaphorically the bitter jealousy and strife that poison the speech of an unstable person—illustrating how bitterness contaminates the whole person. The adjective denotes a sharp, penetrating quality whether physical or spiritual.
semanticRange: bitter to taste; sharp and unpleasant flavor
harsh or severe in manner or speech
characterized by anger, resentment, or painful emotion
cutting or penetrating in effect or sensation

related.note: causative verb: to make bitter, embitter, provoke to anger
abstract noun: bitterness, severity, acrimonious spirit
Hebrew cognate: bitter; often carries metaphorical sense of grief or rebellion

pilatos.notes: Pilate appears 55 times in NT, almost exclusively in passion narratives (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John) and Acts 3:13, 1 Timothy 6:13. He is a historical figure—prefect under Tiberius—whose role shifts narratively: Matthew and Mark emphasize his attempt to release Jesus; Luke stresses his declaration of innocence; John portrays theological confrontation with Pilate as the reluctant instrument of kingship. His name became proverbial in Christian thought for political expediency overriding justice (cf. the Nicene Creed's "suffered under Pontius Pilate"), though the Gospels depict him as pressured by Jewish authorities and the crowd.
semanticRange: Roman prefect (procurator) of Judea, 26–36 CE
The judge who authorized Jesus's crucifixion
A figure emblematic of political expediency and moral compromise
In later theology, a type of judicial abdication before injustice

related.note: Adjective denoting Pontius (his praenomen); rarely used independently
Another Judean ruler-figure; contemporary political authority in Gospels
Generic term for judge; Pilate exemplifies a judge who evades responsibility

pimpremi.notes: This verb appears only once in the NT (Acts 28:6), where Paul's hand swells after a viper bite but he suffers no harm—a sign of divine protection. The classical sense denotes burning or inflaming; the medical sense (swelling of body parts) dominates the LXX and NT usage. Context determines whether physical inflammation or divine judgment is in view.
semanticRange: to swell up, become inflamed (of body parts)
to cause swelling or inflammation
to burn or inflame (rare classical sense)

related.note: related verb; to fill or swell; shares root with pimprēmi
fire; etymologically related; classical sense of pimprēmi involved burning

pinakidion.notes: This diminutive appears uniquely in Luke 1:63, where Zechariah calls for a pinakidion to write the name 'John' after his muteness. The word denotes a small wooden or wax tablet, the standard writing instrument for brief records in antiquity. The diminutive form underscores its portability and domestic context rather than any pejorative force.
semanticRange: A small writing tablet or wax-coated board for temporary notation
A portable surface for recording names, messages, or brief records
Specifically a writing implement used to signify or confirm an action

related.note: The parent noun; a writing tablet or wooden board, broader in scale
To write or inscribe; the primary action performed with such tablets
A tablet for writing; a cognate term for writing surface in Hellenistic Greek

pinax.notes: The word denotes a flat, typically wooden object whose specific sense depends on context: structural (plank), functional (tablet), or culinary (platter). It appears memorably in the beheading accounts (Matthew 14:8–11, Mark 6:25–28), where John's head is brought on a πίναξ—a detail that emphasizes the gruesome presentation. Luke 11:39 uses it of a dish that is unclean on the inside.
semanticRange: A wooden board, plank, or flat surface
A tablet or writing surface
A dish or platter for serving food

related.note: Diminutive form; a small tablet or writing surface
Related term for a disc or platter; more typically round

pino.notes: Πίνω is straightforward physical action with minimal theological freight in isolation, though context matters enormously in eucharistic passages (1 Cor 10:21, 11:25–26) and sayings about abstinence (Rom 14:21). The verb often takes the accusative of the liquid itself (wine, water) or metonymically the cup (ποτήριον). Luke and John use it frequently in narrative and dialogue settings.

to drink habitually or as a practice; to be a drinker
to drink from a cup or vessel (often with metonymic sense of the cup's contents)
to partake of or consume something by drinking (figurative or sacramental sense)

related.note: drinking; a drink or drinking bout; related noun form
cup; vessel from which one drinks; frequently object of pinō in NT
to intoxicate; semantic opposite denoting excess or drunkenness from drinking

piotes.notes: This rare noun appears only once in the NT (Rom 11:17), where Paul uses it metaphorically of the spiritual richness of the olive root into which Gentiles are grafted. The word denotes literal fatness or the productive abundance of fertile ground; the figurative application capitalizes on agricultural abundance as an image of divine blessing. No theological controversy attends the term itself.
semanticRange: fatness, richness of soil or substance
abundance, fertility (agricultural context)
figurative: spiritual richness or abundance

related.note: adjective 'fat, fertile'; etymological root of πιότης
LXX equivalent for דֶּשֶׁן; also denotes fatness or ashes of sacrifice
related notion of abundance or overflowing fullness in NT

piprasko.notes: πιπράσκω is a straightforward commercial verb denoting the act of selling goods or property. It appears most prominently in Acts 2:45 and 4:34 (early church liquidating possessions) and Matthew 13:46 (the merchant selling all to buy the pearl). The word carries no intrinsic theological weight; its force depends entirely on context.
semanticRange: to sell or dispose of something for money
to vend or retail goods in commerce
to betray or hand over (figurative extension)

related.note: Near-synonym; more common verb for selling; often used interchangeably
Antonym; to buy or purchase; opposite commercial transaction
Hebrew cognate in LXX; primary OT term for selling or dealing in commerce

pipto.notes: πίπτω spans literal descent (sparrows falling, Mat. 10:29) through moral collapse (1 Cor. 10:12) and eschatological judgment (Rev. 6:13). The verb carries weight in Pauline anthropology and Johannine cosmology where "falling" signals spiritual defection or divine judgment. Context determines whether the fall is accidental, catastrophic, or morally culpable.
semanticRange: To fall, descend from a position or surface
To fall down, collapse, or be overthrown
To fall away morally or spiritually; to stumble
To fall in battle; to die or perish

Noun: a stumbling-block; related to moral/spiritual falling

pisidia.notes: Pisidia appears twice in Acts, both times marking Paul's itinerary (14:24 and implicitly 13:14 with Antioch). It denotes a real geographical and administrative region of the Roman Empire, not a theological concept. The term's significance lies in its role as a waypoint in apostolic missionary geography.
semanticRange: A region in south-central Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey)
Territory traversed by Paul and Barnabas during the first missionary journey
Geographical marker in early Christian missionary expansion

related.note: Major city in Pisidia; Paul's notable synagogue discourse (Acts 13:14–52)
Broader Roman province containing Pisidia as a subregion

pisteuo.notes: πιστεύω, [in LXX chiefly for אמן hi. ;] __1. intrans., to have faith (in), to believe; in cl., with accusative, dative, in NT also with prep, (on the significance of the various constructions, see M, Pr., 67f.; Vau.…

pistikos.notes: This rare adjective appears twice in the NT, both times to describe νάρδος (nard/spikenard) as 'pure' or 'genuine' in the anointing narrative (Mark 14:3, John 12:3). The word denotes quality and authenticity rather than moral virtue. The adjectival form πιστικός bridges the classical sense of 'persuasive' with the NT emphasis on genuineness and trustworthiness, though the latter senses are primary in our texts.

trustworthy, reliable, or worthy of trust (of persons or things)
faithful or loyal in character
persuasive or carrying conviction (rare, classical usage)

verb: to persuade or convince; shares semantic field of trust and credibility

pistis.notes: πίστις, -εως, ἡ (πείθω), [in LXX chiefly for אֱמוּנָה ;] __1. in active sense, faith, belief, trust, confidence, in NT always of religious faith in God or Christ or spiritual things: Mat.8:10, Luk.5:20, Act.14:9,…

pistoo.notes: This verb appears only once in the NT (2 Timothy 3:14), where Paul urges Timothy to remain convinced of the things he has learned. The term denotes not mere subjective feeling but a solid assurance grounded in what is objectively reliable. In the LXX, pistoō regularly renders the Niphal of āmēn, which carries the sense of being established or confirmed.
semanticRange: to establish or confirm as reliable or firm
to make trustworthy or credible (active voice)
to be assured or convinced of something (passive/middle voice)

pistos.notes: Πιστός bridges two senses that English 'faithful' must carry together: (1) active trustworthiness in the agent, and (2) passive belief or commitment in the believer. Paul uses it of servants (1 Cor 4:2), of Timothy as a co-worker (2 Tim 2:2), and—crucially—of God and Christ as reliable (1 Thess 5:24; 2 Tim 2:13). The word does not primarily denote emotional intensity but rather dependable character. In Matt 24:45–25:23, the 'faithful servant' is one who performs his duties without wavering, making it a cornerstone of NT ethics and christology.

believing, one who has faith or trusts in God or Christ
sure, certain, dependable in character or promise

pithanologia.notes: This word appears only in Col 2:4, where Paul warns against deceptive persuasive speech—speech that sounds convincing but lacks truth. The classical distinction between pithanologia and apódeixis (proof) is crucial: Paul is not condemning rhetoric per se, but the kind of clever argumentation that substitutes plausibility for genuine doctrine. The theological freight here concerns the conflict between human eloquence and apostolic truth.
semanticRange: Persuasive or plausible speech; rhetoric based on probability rather than proof
Argumentation that appeals to likelihood or seeming credibility without logical demonstration
Deceptive eloquence; speech designed to sway through charm rather than truth

related.note: Adjective: persuasive, plausible; root sense of the noun
Noun: logical proof or demonstration; classical antonym to pithanologia
Noun: word, speech; broader term for utterance that pithanologia specifies as rhetorical

planao.notes: πλανάω, -ῶ (πλάνη), [in LXX chiefly for תָּעָה ;] to cause to wander, lead astray. Pass., to go astray, wander: Mat.18:12-13 Heb.11:38, 1Pe.2:25 (cf. Isa.53:6). Metaphorical, to lead astray, deceive: with accusative…

plane.notes: In the NT, πλάνη denotes not mere intellectual mistake but moral and spiritual error—especially the deceptive leading-astray by false doctrine or Satan's influence. The word emphasizes both the wandering itself and the deception that causes it. Paul uses it in 2 Th. 2:11 for the 'strong delusion' God sends; in Eph. 4:14, it describes the destabilizing effect of false teaching on believers. Etymology traces to 'wandering' (cognate with πλάνος, 'wanderer'), but in NT usage the sense sharpens to religiously culpable error rather than innocent mistake.

Error, mistake, or false belief in religious or moral judgment
Deliberate deception or deceitfulness leading others astray

planetes.notes: This adjective occurs only once in the NT (Jude 13), where it describes ἀστέρες πλανήται—'wandering stars'—an image of false teachers. The term borrows from astronomical language: ancient Greeks used it of planets (whose apparent motion differs from fixed stars), but in Jude it carries ethical resonance, implying unpredictability and spiritual instability. No root-fallacy trap here; the 'wandering' sense is synchronically primary.

one who wanders or roams
vagrant, unstable in position or trajectory

planos.notes: πλάνος denotes both the action of deceiving and the character of the deceiver. It appears substantively as 'deceiver' or 'impostor' in Matthew 27:63 (where Jesus's enemies call him a πλάνος) and 2 John 7 (Antichrist as deceiver). The phrase πνεύματα πλάνα in 1 Timothy 4:1 is theologically weighted—deceiving spirits that promote false doctrine. The word's semantic range includes genuine wandering (cf. LXX), but in NT usage leans heavily toward willful or supernatural deception.

wandering, straying from the path or truth
fraudulent, deceptive (as attribute)

plasma.notes: Paul uses this hapax in Romans 9:20 to denote the vessel or artifact shaped by the potter—a metaphor for human creaturehood before God. The word denotes the result of the potter's craft, emphasizing humanity's status as formed, not self-originating. The theological weight lies not in the term itself but in its function within Paul's argument about divine sovereignty and human objection.

A formed object; a creation or artifact
Human nature as divinely formed or fashioned

plasso.notes: πλάσσω carries the sense of deliberate shaping or molding, often with attention to intentional design. In Rom. 9:26 (LXX quotation) and 1 Tim. 2:13, Paul applies the image to God's forming of humanity, drawing on Genesis creation language where the potter's work becomes theological metaphor for divine sovereignty and human nature.

to create or fashion (in divine or human action)
to mold character or nature; to form intentionally

plastos.notes: In 2 Peter 2:3, πλαστός carries the sense of fabricated or feigned when describing false teachers who exploit believers with made-up words. poreia.notes: Πορεία carries the sense of literal travel or passage in Luk 13:22 (Jesus on his way to Jerusalem). In Jas 1:11, it denotes the transient movement or progress through life—the rich fade even while 'in motion,' suggesting the futility of earthly pursuits. The word spans both literal physical movement (Acts 8:39, Lk 1:39) and metaphorical conduct or manner of life (1 Pet 1:18, Eph 2:2). The metaphorical application in Revelation 17–19 is theological and polemical, not descriptive of actual women. porneia.notes: Porneia appears 24 times across the NT in vice catalogs (Gal. 5:19; Col. 3:5; Rev. 9:21) and disciplinary contexts (1 Cor. 5:1; 6:18), consistently denoting sexual conduct outside the covenant bond of marriage. The word carries theological weight in early church sexual ethics and boundaries; modern English 'pornography' derives from this root but misses the relational and covenantal significance of the original term. In Revelation's prophetic discourse, porneia also indexes idolatry (syncretism with pagan worship), extending the semantic range from bodily to spiritual unfaithfulness.

The term is not primarily clinical but moral-theological; it lumps together the prostitute, the fornicator, and the sexually immoral man under a single condemnation. The word moves from physical callusing (medical imagery) to metaphorical spiritual insensitivity. Critical: this is not mere weakness but active resistance—a condition God permits as judgment. The passive form (especially Rom 11:7) raises the question of divine agency versus human responsibility.

porphura.notes: Porphura denotes the costly purple dye produced from the murex snail, highly prized in antiquity and associated with royalty and wealth. The word shifts from the substance itself to the fabric dyed with it, and by extension to garments made from purple cloth—a marker of status that becomes literal in the mockery of Jesus (Mark 15:17, 20) and the description of the rich man (Luke 16:19).

In John 19:2–5, the soldiers dress the mocked Jesus in purple to parody his claim to kingship; in Revelation 17:4 and 18:6, the harlot Babylon adorns herself in purple and scarlet, symbolizing both her luxury and her idolatrous power. porphuropolis.notes: Lydia at Acts 16:14 is the sole NT instance. The term denotes not merely a vendor but a businesswoman of means—purple was one of antiquity's most expensive dyes, extracted from murex shells and controlled largely by Tyrian producers. porro.notes: The word denotes spatial remoteness in the NT, appearing only three times. In Mark 7:6 and Matthew 15:8 (citing Isaiah 29:13), the phrase "this people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far away" uses πόρρω to express spiritual distance rather than mere geography. In Luke 17:12, the ten lepers stand afar off when they cry to Jesus; in Hebrews 11:13, Abraham sees the promises only from a distance (πόρρωθεν), marking the gap between earthly pilgrimage and eschatological fulfillment. portheo.notes: The word denotes violent destruction—originally of cities or fortifications, then extended figuratively to the persecution of Christians. Paul uses it retrospectively to describe his pre-conversion campaign against the church (Acts 9:21; Gal 1:13, 23), where it carries the force of systematic devastation rather than mere harassment. The collateral form πορθέω appears chiefly in poetry and the LXX, making it somewhat elevated in register.

posakis.notes: The word denotes an interrogative inquiry into frequency or repetition. All three NT occurrences (Matthew 18:21, 23:37; Luke 13:34) appear in passages heavy with pathos: Peter asking about forgiveness, Jesus lamenting Jerusalem's rejection. The emotional weight lies not in the word itself but in its context—the speakers pose the question with exasperation or yearning, not mere curiosity about numbers.

In Rom 14:17 and Col 2:16 it denotes the practice or custom of drinking in relation to dietary law; in Jhn 6:55 it refers to Christ's blood as something to drink. The image is of violent displacement by floodwaters rather than mere wetting. The word combines ποταμός (river) with a passive participle sense of φέρω (to carry), denoting something overwhelmed and carried off by torrential force.

The word carries both literal sense (vessel for wine) and metaphorical freight: Christ's 'cup' in Gethsemane (Mk 14:36) denotes the portion of suffering ordained by the Father. Revelation 17:4 weaponizes the image—the harlot's cup holds abomination. Context determines whether the referent is domestic table ware, ritual symbol, or divine appointment.

pothen.notes: πόθεν is an interrogative adverb that asks about origin, source, or point of departure. In John's Gospel it recurs notably (3:8, 6:5, 8:14, 9:29-30, 19:9) where Jesus's interrogators demand to know his source or credentials; the rhetorical force often implies 'how could you possibly?' when combined with negative presuppositions. The word denotes physical location (Mat. 15:33: 'whence shall we get loaves?') and metaphysical origin (Jhn. 2:9: the headwaiter asks whence the wine came).

In Paul (Rom.8:29, 11:2) it denotes God's prior knowledge and election of believers; in 1Pe.1:20 it refers to Christ's predetermined purpose. Luke uses it to identify the oracular spirit driving the girl's divination. While condemned by Atticist purists as post-classical, it is well-attested in Hellenistic prose and the LXX for military or covenant signals.

a prearranged gesture or token used for identification
a covenant sign or authenticating mark

sussomos.notes: This hapax legomenon appears only in Ephesians 3:6, where Paul uses it to describe Gentiles as συσσωμος—co-embodied members of Christ. The term carries significant theological freight: it moves beyond mere fellowship to assert organic, bodily union in the church. The compound structure (σύν + σῶμα) emphasizes that believers are not merely associated but are literally incorporated into one living body, making it a crucial Pauline assertion of ecclesial unity across ethnic boundaries.

members of a single corporate entity or fellowship

sustasiastes.notes: This rare noun appears only once in the NT (Mark 15:7), where Barabbas is described alongside sustasiastai—rioters who had committed murder during an insurrection. The σύν- prefix emphasizes collective participation in sedition rather than solitary rebellion. Context is crucial: the word denotes political/military insurgents, not moral or theological categories.

sustatikos.notes: This adjective appears only once in the NT (2 Corinthians 3:1) in the phrase ἐπιστολαὶ συστατικαί, 'letters of commendation.' Paul uses it to distinguish external credentials from his apostolic authority grounded in the Spirit. The word denotes something designed to introduce or commend the bearer, not inherent merit.

sustauroomai.notes: This word carries enormous weight in Pauline soteriology. At the literal level (Matthew 27:44, Mark 15:32, John 19:32), it describes the two bandits executed alongside Jesus. But in Romans 6:6 and Galatians 2:20, Paul deploys sustauroomai metaphorically to articulate Christian participation in Christ's death—a foundational claim about baptismal and mystical union that has shaped Christian theology of sanctification. Context is everything: the same verb shifts from historical narrative to theological claim.
semanticRange: to be crucified together with someone (literal co-crucifixion)
to undergo mystical or spiritual death alongside Christ (Paul's theology)

sustello.notes: Sustellō appears only twice in the NT (1Cor 7:29 and Acts 5:6). In 1Cor 7:29, Paul uses it metaphorically—"the time has been drawn together" (i.e., shortened or compressed)—to emphasize eschatological urgency. The burial sense (wrapping a corpse) appears in Acts 5:6 with Ananias. The word denotes a literal or figurative drawing-in, without the theological weight of more central terms.

sustenazo.notes: Attested only once in the NT, Romans 8:22, where Paul writes that 'the whole creation groans together (συστενάζει) and travails in pain together' as part of his theology of redemptive suffering. The prefix συν- emphasizes not individual sighing but collective, shared groaning—the cosmos in unified anguish. Though rare, the word carries eschatological weight in that context.

sustoicheo.notes: This hapax legomenon appears only in Gal 4:25, where Paul uses it to argue that the earthly Jerusalem corresponds to or aligns with the present age of bondage, while the heavenly Jerusalem aligns with freedom. The word carries both a concrete sense (lining up in rank) and metaphorical sense (matching or paralleling). Context is crucial: without Galatians 4:21–31, the correspondence Paul intends could be missed.

sustratiotes.notes: Paul employs this term only twice in the NT (Phil 2:25 for Epaphroditus; Phlm 2 for Archippus), deliberately activating military imagery to honor those who labor alongside him in gospel proclamation. sustrepho.notes: The word denotes a gathering or assembling, often with the implication of coming together in response to something. In Acts 28:3, it refers literally to the viper twisting itself around Paul's hand; in Matthew 17:22, the passive form describes the disciples gathering together during Jesus's ministry. The LXX connection to קָשַׁר suggests overtones of binding or uniting, though the NT usage emphasizes the physical act of assembly rather than conspiracy.

sustrophe.notes: Συστροφή carries the sense of an assembled crowd marked by disorder, agitation, or potential violence. In Acts 19:40, Paul urges calm after the Ephesian silversmith riot, warning the town clerk that they risk being charged with συστροφή—a riotous gathering. The word implies not merely proximity but tumultuous, coordinated (hence the prefix συν-) commotion. LXX usage connects it to conspiracy and coordinated wrongdoing (קָשַׁר, qachar).

suzao.notes: Paul uses suzaō exclusively to express mystical union with Christ—both the present reality of shared life in Him and the future resurrection hope. In Rom. 6:8 and 2 Tim. 2:11, it denotes participation in Christ's risen life; in 2 Cor. 7:3, it describes Paul's affectionate solidarity with the Corinthian community. The verb's theological weight lies in its refusal to separate present discipleship from eschatological destiny.

suzeteo.notes: The word carries the sense of joint inquiry with an undertone of contention. In the NT it often appears in scenes of public dispute or Pharisaic challenge—particularly in Mark's Gospel (e.g., Mark 1:27; 8:11) where disciples or opponents interrogate Jesus. The prefix συν- emphasizes the participatory nature: multiple parties are engaged in the questioning.

suzetetes.notes: Paul deploys this term in 1 Corinthians 1:20 ('Where is the debater of this age?') as part of his polemic against human wisdom and rhetorical skill. The word carries no inherent theological weight beyond its cultural backdrop—Paul is simply dismissing the value of mere disputatious cleverness in light of divine wisdom. It appears nowhere else in the NT.

suzeugnumi.notes: This verb appears only twice in the NT, both in Jesus's logion on divorce (Matt. 19:6; Mark 10:9), where he declares what God has "joined together" in marriage. The metaphorical extension from literal yoking (as in agriculture) to marital union is transparent and culturally rooted: two oxen bound by a yoke cannot be separated without breaking the bond. No theological overloading occurs; the word simply denotes the binding act itself.

suzoopoieo.notes: This compound verb appears only twice in Paul (Eph 2:5; Col 2:13) and carries dense soteriological weight: believers are made alive together with Christ in his resurrection. The σύν- prefix is crucial—the vivification is not individual but corporate union with Christ. Not mere physical restoration of life, but the Spirit's work of spiritual quickening in baptismal and covenantal framework.

suzugos.notes: σύζυγος appears only in Phil 4:3, where Paul addresses a faithful coworker—possibly by proper name (Synzygus) or as an honorific title—urging unity with Euodia and Syntyche. The term draws its force from the agricultural metaphor of oxen yoked for labor, transferring it to human partnership in gospel ministry. Context, not etymology alone, determines whether it emphasizes marital, collegial, or apostolic partnership.

tabernai.notes: Τρεῖς Ταβέρναι appears only once in Acts 28:15, marking Paul's arrival near Rome. The site was a well-known mercantile stop on the Via Appia, some 33 miles south of the capital, where Roman Christians met him. This proper noun preserves a Latin institutional term (taberna) embedded in Greek, reflecting the bilingual reality of the Roman empire and the practical geography of early Christian travel networks.

tabitha.notes: Tabitha appears only in Acts 9:36–40, where Peter raises her from the dead in Joppa. The narrative gives both her Aramaic name (Ταβιθά) and its Greek translation (Δορκάς), emphasizing her dual cultural identity in the early Jewish-Christian community. Luke's mention of her as a beloved disciple (μαθήτρια) and her reputation for acts of mercy (ἔργα ἀγαθά) highlight her as a model of practical charity in the apostolic church.

tacha.notes: In the NT, τάχα appears only twice (Rom 5:7; Phlm 15) and carries the sense of 'perhaps' or 'possibly,' introducing a tentative, hypothetical scenario. The adverb bridges two semantic domains: the poetic/classical sense of 'quickly' (rare by Hellenistic standards) and the more developed sense of 'by chance' or 'perchance.' Its infrequency in the NT suggests it belongs to higher register discourse; note Paul's careful use at Rom 5:7 ('one would scarcely die for a righteous person—though perhaps for a good person') to mark a logical concession.

tacheos.notes: The adverb carries a straightforward sense of temporal or physical quickness, but context determines whether the speed is prudent (Phil. 2:19—Timothy sent promptly) or ill-advised (Gal. 1:6—the Galatians turned away from the gospel hastily). In 2 Thess. 2:2 and 1 Tim. 5:22, ταχέως signals rash action that carries spiritual risk, so English translation must balance "quickly" with tonal cues about propriety.

In 1 Corinthians 15:23, Paul employs it figuratively for the order of resurrection: Christ as firstfruits, then those belonging to Christ at his parousia, then the end—each group appointed to its proper sequence. talantiaios.notes: This adjective appears only once in the NT (Rev 16:21), describing hailstones of talent-weight falling on humanity. The term carries the sense of extreme, crushing weight—a talent weighed roughly 75–125 pounds depending on the standard. Paul uses it of himself in 2 Cor. 11:7 and 12:21 to signal self-abasement and acknowledgment of weakness. tapeinosis.notes: Tapeinōsis denotes the concrete state or condition of being humbled—whether through circumstance, persecution, or spiritual discipline—rather than the emotional experience. In Luke 1:48, Mary speaks of God's regard for her low estate; in Acts 8:33 (quoting Isa 53:8 LXX), it describes the Servant's judicial degradation; in Philippians 3:21, it refers to the body's present weakness before glorification. The word carries theological weight precisely because early Christian theology inverted its normal valuation: humiliation becomes a mode of identification with Christ's suffering.

taphe.notes: The word occurs only once in Matthew 27:7, where the chief priests and elders purchase a potter's field as a taphē for strangers—a burial place associated with shame and rejection. The concept carries weight in ancient Mediterranean custom and Jewish piety (proper burial was sacred duty), but the term itself is not a high-theological marker like logos or pneuma. Context determines whether taphē emphasizes the physical act, the location, or the moral/religious quality of the burial.

bavel.notes: Babylon carries immense theological weight throughout the OT and into NT apocalyptic. The folk etymology in Genesis 11:9 (Babel from balal, 'to confuse') cements the association with human rebellion. By Revelation 17–18, Babylon becomes a cipher for Rome itself—any worldly power arrayed against God's people. Context is decisive: historical Babylon ≠ theological symbol.

In Gen 49:3–4 (Reuben) and elsewhere, the term carries honor tied to birthright, which makes Jacob's blessing of Judah over Reuben (Gen 37, 49) theologically charged. By NT times, the term became a title of supremacy—applied to Christ in Colossians 1:15 (firstborn of all creation) and Romans 8:29 (firstborn among many brethren).

bekhorah.notes: Bekhorah carries substantial covenant weight in Israelite theology. The term denotes not merely a legal mechanism but a divinely ordered hierarchy: the firstborn inherited twice the portion of other sons and led the household (Deut 21:15–17). Esau's sale of his bekhorah to Jacob (Gen 25:29–34) dramatizes how disposable this privilege could become through folly, while Reuben's loss of it (Gen 49:3–4) shows divine prerogative to strip it away. In later theology, Israel itself is called God's firstborn (Exod 4:22), making bekhorah a metaphor for elect status.

Her genealogical function—bearing Cain, Abel, and Seth—anchors the primordial lineage leading to Noah.

chayah.notes: חָיָה anchors OT theology at the creation account (Gen 1:30, 2:7) where life is God's gift. The word carries covenantal weight: covenant renewal and obedience promise life (Deut 30:15–16), while disobedience brings death. In prophetic literature, restoration formulae invoke חָיָה to signal resurrection or national revival (Ezekiel's dry bones, Hosea 6:2). Context determines whether the sense is merely biological survival or covenant-bound flourishing.

chazaq.notes: חָזַק denotes strength that is active, dynamic, and often relational—prevailing *over* something or *for* a cause. In Exodus 4:21 and 7:13 the verb carries the problematic sense of God hardening Pharaoh's heart, which theology must reconcile with human agency. The word appears across narratives of Israel's courage (Josh 1:6–7), God's strengthening of judges and kings, and the intensification of plagues, so context is crucial for discerning whether the sense is moral courage, physical might, or divine hardening.

Its single occurrence limits interpretive weight; the verse serves primarily to document family lineage rather than to narrate Hazo's own actions or significance.

cheder.notes: The word denotes primarily a room or chamber, with emphasis on privacy and enclosure. It appears frequently in descriptions of the temple (1 Kings 6:5–6), palaces, and domestic interiors. chelev.notes: In the sacrificial system, chelev denotes the fatty portions the priest burned on the altar as the most desirable offering to the Lord (Lev 3:14–16, 7:23–25). The word acquires theological weight: fat symbolizes abundance, fertility, and the choicest gift. When Israel turns from God, the prophets accuse them of eating the fat while neglecting justice (Isa 43:24). The dietary prohibition against chelev (Lev 3:17) marks Israel's covenant distinctiveness.

The word appears only twice in the OT (Isa. 63:9; Jer. 50:42), and its rarity makes each occurrence linguistically weighted. It denotes not mere sentiment but compassion that moves to action, distinct from the more frequent rachamim (mercy from the womb) in that chemla emphasizes the emotional movement toward sparing or relieving.

chen.notes: Chen denotes favor that flows from a superior's will rather than obligation—what a subject enjoys in the eyes of a king, or humanity in the eyes of God. The term bridges aesthetic charm (1 Sam 25:3 of Abigail) and relational grace (Gen 6:8 of Noah). It is foundational to OT theodicy: survival and blessing depend on finding chen. Do not conflate with hesed (covenant fidelity); chen is discretionary and unearned, though once extended it shapes ongoing relationship.

The etymology traditionally connects to the sense of 'rapid' or 'swift,' reflecting the river's character, though the name is ultimately a Semitic adaptation of the Akkadian Idiglat. Beyond metaphor, gepen also denotes the literal plant used in viticulture across the Levant, grounding the figure in agricultural reality.

By Second Temple Judaism, ger begins to shift toward 'proselyte' (religious convert), though the sociological sense persists. The word carries the tension between legal exclusion and moral inclusion.

The word carries no special theological weight, though its precision is essential in genealogical and chronological contexts.

sheloshim.notes: שְׁלֹשִׁים denotes the cardinal number thirty and appears frequently in historical narratives, chronologies, and monetary reckoning (e.g., the thirty pieces of silver paid to Judas; the thirty years of Jesus' ministry before baptism). The word follows the standard Hebrew pattern for tens (20, 30, 40, etc.) and requires no special theological loading—it functions as a straightforward numeral whose significance depends entirely on its referent in context.

shem.notes: Shem is theologically dense: it denotes not mere label but identity, honor, and divine presence. The phrase 'in the Name of YHWH' (בְשֵׁם יְהוָה) invokes God's active character and covenantal authority. In Exodus 3:15 and Psalm 20:1, the Name encodes YHWH's self-revelation; in Deuteronomy 12:5, worship centers on 'the place where He causes His Name to dwell.' This semantic freight—name as character, power, and presence—makes shem inseparable from identity theology in the OT.

shemen.notes: Shemen denotes primarily olive oil, essential in ancient Near Eastern economy, diet, medicine, and ritual. In cultic contexts it carries sacramental weight—anointing with oil marks consecration of priests (Exod 29:7) and kings (1 Sam 10:1). The word also carries metaphorical force for divine blessing and prosperity, as in Psalm 23:5 (cup overflowing) or the 'fat of the land' in Genesis 45:18. Context distinguishes utilitarian from sacred use.

shemesh.notes: Shemesh appears 108 times and functions both as literal celestial body and theological marker. In Judges 5:31 and Psalm 84:11, the sun imagery frames divine blessing; by contrast, 2 Kings 23:5 and Jeremiah 8:2 expose sun-worship as idolatry Israel must renounce. The word also anchors spatial orientation (east/west) and public visibility, so phrases like 'under the sun' (Ecclesiastes) exploit both literal and philosophical registers.

shemever.notes: Shemeber appears only once in the biblical record (Gen 14:2) as a minor Canaanite king who joined a coalition against Abraham. The name may derive from a root suggesting 'lofty flight,' but he is preserved in Scripture primarily as a narrative participant in the war of the kings rather than for theological significance. His presence illustrates the political landscape of Canaan in the patriarchal age.

shemoneh.notes: A straightforward cardinal and ordinal numeral with high frequency in genealogies, temple measurements, and ritual prescriptions (e.g., circumcision on the eighth day, Levitical age requirements). No significant theological overloading, though eight carries some symbolic resonance in eschatological and renewal contexts (e.g., the eighth day as a new creation motif in later Jewish thought). Context determines whether it functions as pure enumeration or carries symbolic weight.

shemonim.notes: A straightforward cardinal and ordinal numeral with no theological freight. Appears chiefly in genealogies and chronological passages (e.g., Gen 35:28 for Isaac's age at death; 1 Kings 6:1 for the interval between the exodus and temple construction). shen.notes: Shen primarily denotes the physical tooth in everyday usage (human or animal). In legal contexts it anchors the principle of retaliation (Exodus 21:24, 'tooth for tooth'), though the phrase itself emphasizes proportional justice rather than dental theology. The secondary sense of ivory reflects the commercial and material reality of tusks in the ancient Near East; this usage is lexically distinct but semantically continuous—ivory as the tooth-substance of larger animals. Rare metaphorical extension to 'sharp rock' appears in topographical language.

shenah.notes: שְׁנָה denotes physical sleep and rest but also carries symbolic weight in biblical narrative, especially when God sends sleep (Gen 28:11 Jacob's ladder; 1 Sam 26:12 David and Saul). The word is neutral in itself; theological significance emerges from context—sleep as protection, as divine intervention, or occasionally as spiritual negligence (Prov 6:9–11).

shenayim.notes: שְׁנַיִם is the standard dual/plural cardinal numeral throughout the Hebrew Bible, appearing 663 times. Beyond simple counting, it carries force in formulaic pairs—'two tablets' (Exod 32:15), 'two cherubim' (1 Kgs 6:24)—and in the distributive sense 'both.' The word grounds biblical narrative and law in concrete duality; context determines whether emphasis falls on the pair's unity or their separateness.

sheni.notes: שֵׁנִי functions primarily as an ordinal adjective (second day, second son) and adverbial marker of recurrence or difference. The semantic range naturally spans from strict numerical position (Gen 1:8) through temporal repetition ("a second time") to the sense of "other" or "another" where emphasis falls on distinction rather than sequence. sheol.notes: Sheol in OT thought denotes the shadowy underworld realm where all the dead—righteous and wicked alike—dwell in a diminished state, not a place of conscious torment (that theology develops later in Second Temple Judaism). The word carries profound theological weight: it represents the horizon of death itself, the silence where God's praise ceases (Ps 6:5), yet righteous texts affirm that even Sheol cannot separate the faithful from divine care (Ps 139:8). Later Christian tradition conflates Sheol with Hades and Gehenna, importing NT dualism backward into OT texts—a reading anachronism to avoid.

shepher.notes: Shepher appears only 3 times in the OT (Psalm 96:6; 1 Chronicles 16:27; and one other instance), always in poetic contexts celebrating divine splendor. The word denotes beauty as observable comeliness or magnificence, not abstract moral goodness—though the raw definition's mention of 'goodness' likely reflects the aesthetic and evaluative overlap in Hebrew thought. In Psalm 96:6, it stands parallel to honor and majesty in Yahweh's sanctuary, anchoring it firmly in the realm of visible, impressive form.

shephiphon.notes: Šĕphîphôn denotes a particular venomous serpent, attested only once in the Hebrew Bible (Psalm 91:13), where the faithful tread upon it as a sign of divine protection. The identity of the specific species remains debated—ancient and modern sources suggest either a horned viper (Cerastes) or an asp. The metaphorical association with danger and treachery is implicit but not developed theologically in the single occurrence.

shepho.notes: Shepho appears only in the genealogical register of Edomite clans at Gen. 36:23 and 1 Chr. 1:40. The name may carry the sense 'bold' or 'bare,' but its primary function here is genealogical: he marks a branch within Shobal's household in the Edomite genealogy. sheqel.notes: The shekel was the primary unit of weight and value in ancient Israel and the Near East, functioning as both a measure of metal and a medium of exchange long before coined currency. Different materials (gold, silver, copper) had different ratios to the talent, reflecting their relative worth. The word appears frequently in legal, commercial, and priestly contexts (e.g., Exodus 30:11–16 on the temple tax, 1 Samuel 9:8 on purchase prices).

sherets.notes: Sheretz appears predominantly in Levitical purity laws (Lev 11:20–23, 41–42; Deut 14:19). The word denotes small, prolific creatures—insects, reptiles, small quadrupeds—that swarm or multiply. In the ritual context, sheretz creatures were classified as unclean and forbidden for consumption. The emphasis is on their mode of locomotion (crawling, swarming) and reproductive abundance rather than size alone.

shesh.notes: Shesh denotes a luxury stone material—typically alabaster—prominent in OT descriptions of royal and temple furnishings (1 Kings 10:18 alabaster throne; Esther 1:6 marble pavement). The word does not carry theological freight but marks material wealth and divine honor through architectural splendor.

shet.notes: The semantic field of שׁאת remains contested in scholarship; it appears primarily in poetic and prophetic texts denoting either physical ruin (Ps 35:8) or abstract calamity. Context determines whether the term refers to literal desolation of land or figurative collapse of social standing. Its low frequency and infrequent pairing with clear grammatical parallels have left its precise nuance uncertain.

sheva.notes: Sheba appears 368 times in the OT, primarily as a geographical and ethnic designation for the wealthy, spice-trading kingdom of southwestern Arabia. The name first occurs in the genealogical table (Gen 10:7) but gains prominence in narratives of trade (1 Kgs 10:1–13, Job 1:15, 6:19) and prophetic oracles (Isa 60:6, Jer 6:20, Ezek 27:22–23). Though the lemma carries an etymological tag meaning 'seven' or 'oath,' synchronic biblical usage treats it as a proper ethnonym without active semantic overlay.

shever.notes: שֶׁבֶר denotes the concrete result or act of breaking—whether the fracture of bone (Ps. 51:8), a gap in a wall (Judg. 21:15), or societal collapse. The metaphorical sense of dream-breaking (Dan. 2:41) extends the term to interpretation or dissolution of meaning. Context determines whether the sense is violent rupture, structural damage, or dissolution.

shevet.notes: Shevet carries rich symbolic weight in Israel's self-understanding. It moves from the concrete (a shepherd's rod, Gen 30:37–39) to the political-spiritual (the twelve tribes of Jacob/Israel, e.g., Gen 49; Num 1). The metaphorical link is patriarchal authority: a father's staff becomes a tribe's genealogical line. In royal contexts (esp. Psalms, 1 Samuel), shevet denotes the monarch's scepter—the visible emblem of divine appointment and justice (Ps 45:6; 110:2). The phrase "shevet of his tribe" underscores both blood kinship and hierarchical order.

shevii.notes: שְׁבִיעִי carries deep theological weight in OT covenant and ritual law. The seventh day, seventh year (Jubilee), and seventh month structure Israel's sacred calendar and mark boundaries of divine rest and restoration. In Genesis 2:3, God blesses the seventh day; Exodus 20:10 and Deuteronomy 5:14 enshrine it as mandatory rest. Context determines whether the word denotes simple ordinal sequence (e.g., "the seventh son") or carries symbolic significance tied to completion and holiness.

shevuah.notes: שְׁבוּעָה carries significant theological weight: it marks a legally binding speech-act that invokes God as witness and enforcer. The word encompasses both positive oaths (swearing innocence, making vows) and curses (self-imprecations that call down judgment). In Deuteronomy and the legal corpus, oaths settle disputes and consecrate covenants; Psalm 15:4 praises one who swears even to his own hurt, marking oath-fidelity as a cardinal virtue.

shillem.notes: The noun שִׁלֵּם denotes recompense or requital—payment rendered in return for service, loss, or transgression. It appears only three times in the OT (Proverbs 11:31; Job 15:31; Isaiah 34:8), and in each case the context emphasizes either just recompense for conduct or divine repayment. The word's force rests on the root שׁלם (to complete, make whole), so recompense carries the nuance of balancing or settling accounts. Not a high-frequency term, but semantically straightforward.

shillesh.notes: This adjective marks position or generation in a series. It appears sparingly in the OT (5 occurrences) and denotes either ordinal rank—'the third'—or generational distance, as in 'third generation.' The meaning of 'Shiloh' in that verse remains philologically uncertain—proposed interpretations range from a personal/dynastic name to a place-name (Shiloh), to a common noun meaning 'rest,' 'tribute,' or 'he to whom it belongs.' Rabbinic and patristic sources diverge sharply on whether the verse refers to the historic son or to a future deliverer.

shimon.notes: Shimon appears exclusively in 1 Chronicles 4:20 within the genealogy of Judah, identified as father of four sons. shinar.notes: Shinar appears primarily in Genesis (Tower of Babel, 11:2; Abraham's origins, 11:31) and Daniel (Nebuchadnezzar's realm). The name derives from Akkadian Šin'āru, likely "plain of two rivers." While not inherently a loaded term theologically, Shinar gains symbolic weight in narrative contexts involving human rebellion and imperial power. Its eight OT occurrences cluster in foundational and prophetic moments rather than appearing as a mere geographical reference.

tan.notes: Tan denotes a large serpentine creature—sea-monster, dragon, or whale—occupying the boundary between natural history and myth. The word appears chiefly in poetry and apocalyptic contexts (Jer. 51:34; Isa. 27:1; Ps. 74:13), where it often symbolizes chaos, divine opposition, or Egypt itself. Modern speculation about dinosaurs or plesiosaurus is fanciful; the Hebrew imagination drew on Near Eastern dragon-lore (Ugarit, Mesopotamia) and genuine aquatic megafauna. The word appears chiefly in Levitical legislation (Lev 25:6, 23, 40, 45) to define the legal status of non-Israelite residents in the land, distinguishing them from mere transients (ger can overlap but is broader). Context determines whether the emphasis falls on emotional satisfaction, practical utility, or ethical rightness; failure to account for this range produces flat translations. The rarity of this particular form suggests the writer chose a forceful, memorable term for ethical corruption.

hor.notes: Mount Hor appears exclusively in Numbers (20:22, 20:23, 20:25, 20:27; 21:4; 33:37, 33:41, 33:42; Deut 32:50) and functions chiefly as the burial site of Aaron and the locus of his priestly succession by Eleazar. The toponym anchors Israel's wilderness itinerary and marks the southwestern boundary of Edom. While geographically significant, the name itself carries no theological freight independent of its narrative frame.

horam.notes: Horam appears in the conquest narrative (Josh 10:33) as king of Gezer, defeated by Joshua in the southern campaign. His name likely carries the sense of 'exalted' (from ram, 'high'), a typical royal epithet. The reference is incidental to the broader account of Canaanite resistance and provides no theological elaboration beyond the factual record of conquest.

hoshama.notes: Hoshama appears only in 1 Chronicles 3:18 as a member of Shealtiel's family within the Davidic genealogy. The Chronicler preserved this name to document continuity of the royal line through the Babylonian exile, a theologically significant moment for Jewish identity. His presence in this list affirms that the promise to David's house survived national catastrophe.

hoshayah.notes: Hoshaiah appears only three times in the OT, all in Neh. 12:32, where he leads a thanksgiving procession at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt walls. The theophoric name carries the sense 'Yahweh has saved,' reflecting post-exilic hope in divine restoration. As a proper noun designating a specific historical figure, the word itself carries no theological freight—though the context of his appearance embodies the broader narrative of return and rebuilding.
semanticRange: A Jewish leader during the post-exilic restoration under Nehemiah
Prince of Judah who participated in the wall dedication ceremony

hoshea.notes: Hoshea (reigned ca. 732–722 BCE) was the 19th and final king of Israel, son of Elah. His reign witnessed the Assyrian siege of Samaria and the deportation of Israel's population—marking the end of the northern kingdom. Though his name carries the root שׁוּע (deliverance), his political failure could not avert the kingdom's doom. The prophet Hosea is a different figure entirely, though both names share the sense of salvation.

hotir.notes: Hothir is a minor genealogical figure in 1 Chronicles 25, part of the extensive list of David's musical appointees. His name appears only twice in the OT (1 Chr 25:4, 28) as a member of the guild of prophetic musicians. No theological weight attaches to the name itself; it functions purely as a patronymic marker in the genealogy of Levitical singers.

hotsen.notes: This rare noun appears only once in the OT (2 Sam. 12:33), where David's mighty men are described in connection with war-making. The exact referent—whether defensive armor, offensive weapon, or general equipment—remains uncertain due to the hapax legomenon status and limited context. Ancient versions offer little help, and the word may reflect a specialized or archaic military term.

The word's limited frequency and narrow semantic focus make it a specialized term for calamity rather than a polyvalent theological concept. Its connection to the root חוה (to fall upon) suggests the sense of something that crashes down rather than a gradual decline.

hoven.notes: Ebony appears only in 1 Kings 10:18, where Solomon's great throne is inlaid with it—a hallmark of his legendary wealth and cosmopolitan trade reach. The word denotes an actual imported hardwood, not a metaphor, though its rarity and value in the text underscore royal splendor. Egyptian and Nubian ebony was highly coveted in the ancient Near East.

hoy.notes: הוֹי is a high-impact interjection that anchors both lament and prophetic denunciation. In wisdom and prophetic literature (especially Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the woe-oracles), it signals divine judgment and human suffering. The same word can express sympathy or grab attention depending on context; prophets weaponize it to open judgment speeches (Isa 5:8–23; Jer 23:1). Do not flatten it to mere exclamation—its force depends entirely on the speaker's role and the cosmic stakes.

hu.notes: Hu is the standard masculine singular pronoun for third person, used both as a simple referent and with emphatic force—especially when placed after a predicate or verb to foreground or resume the subject (common in narrative resumption). In biblical prose it often marks a topic shift or lends weight to predication, as in Gen 2:23 (wə-hu yiqra-ēh iššāh) where the pronoun underscores the naming act. Context determines whether emphasis is operative; isolated occurrence carries no inherent stress.

hukh.notes: This Aramaic verb appears only twice in the OT (Dan 2:24, 3:24) and carries the straightforward sense of physical movement or locomotion. It is the Aramaic equivalent of the much more frequent Hebrew halakh (הָלַךְ), which dominates biblical narrative for both literal travel and metaphorical 'walking' in obedience or divine relationship.

hum.notes: The verb הוּם carries the sense of producing an audible disturbance—whether literal (the roaring of animals or waters) or social (murmuring crowds, civil commotion). The Niphal stem signals the subject being thrown into disarray; the Hiphil, causing murmurs or unrest. In 1 Samuel 4:5, the people's shout (הָרִנָּה) causes the Philistines to be discomfited, though הוּם itself appears more with internal tumult or complaint (cf. Psalm 83:3, where enemies murmur).

hun.notes: This hapax legomenon (1 Sam 4:9) carries the sense of ease and readiness in preparation. The Hiphil causative allows for the interpretation of dismissing or treating something as trivial, which the Philistines do when facing Israel ('be men... don't become slaves'). Despite its rarity, the word points to a semantic domain shared with other verbs denoting facility and light burden.

huyydah.notes: This rare feminine plural noun appears only in 2 Chronicles 29:30, where King Hezekiah's scribes provide הֻיְּדוֹת (hymnic praises) from David and Asaph for congregational singing. iddah.notes: This word appears only once in the OT (Isa. 64:6, rendered 'filthy rags' or 'menstrual cloths') as a metaphor for the worthlessness of human righteousness before God. The term carries complex theological weight: it invokes both ritual impurity laws and profound moral-spiritual degradation. Context is essential to avoid conflating menstrual taboo with the prophetic indictment of sin.

iddan.notes: עִדָּן appears primarily in Daniel and Aramaic contexts (often in the form עִדַּן) and carries the sense of a marked or bounded period. The word emphasizes time as a measurable duration rather than a fleeting moment. In Daniel 3:5, 7, 15, the phrase "when you hear the sound of the horn, pipe, etc." uses עִדָּן to denote the appointed moment; in Daniel 2:16, it refers to a time interval within which Daniel seeks wisdom.

iddar.notes: This term appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (Hosea 13:3) as a simile for something that disperses like chaff from a threshing floor. The threshing floor was a vital agricultural fixture in ancient Israel—an open, hard-packed area where workers separated grain from chaff. Though rare, the word carries the concrete imagery of separation and loss that prophets exploited for judgment rhetoric.

iddo.notes: Iddo appears eleven times in the OT, primarily in Ezra and Nehemiah as a priest, scribe, or prophet during the post-Exilic restoration under Zerubbabel and Nehemiah. Multiple individuals bear this name across different periods, creating some interpretive complexity in genealogical reconstruction. The theophoric dimension—'he will praise'—fits the restoration community's emphasis on renewed worship.

iezer.notes: Iezer is a minor patriarchal figure appearing only in the census list at Numbers 26:30, where he is identified as a son of Gilead within the Manassite genealogy. His name became a clan designation (the Iezerites), following the typical pattern of eponymous ancestors in tribal records. No theological weight attaches to this name itself; its significance lies in preserving tribal lineage and land inheritance memory.

iggeret.notes: Iggeret denotes a written communication, typically formal or official in character. It appears prominently in 2 Kings 19:14 (Sennacherib's letter to Hezekiah) and Ezra 4:11 (adversaries' letter to the king), contexts where the letter carries political or authoritative weight. ikhavod.notes: Ichabod appears three times in 1 Samuel (4:21; 14:3; 22:20), each time marking the aftermath of priestly failure and national calamity. His name is a prophetic utterance rather than a conventional patronymic—born at the moment his grandfather Eli died and the Ark was captured, he embodies the theology of judgment. The etymology 'no glory' (אִי + כָּבוֹד) operates as both personal identifier and spiritual indictment.

The etymology 'exalted' is plausible but cannot be verified from usage since only the proper noun survives.

The semantic drift from 'something that rises up' (via etymology) to 'pretext or false reason' is pragmatic rather than inherent to the root; context determines whether עִלָּה refers to a genuine circumstance or a fabricated excuse. immanuel.notes: Immanuel is one of the OT's most theologically contested names, appearing chiefly at Isaiah 7:14. Christian tradition reads it as predictive of Christ's incarnation (Matthew 1:23), while historical-critical approaches debate whether it originally referred to a child of Ahaz's era. The name itself—'God with us'—carries the weight of covenant promise and divine presence regardless of historical referent, making it a flashpoint for christological and hermeneutical disagreement.

ov.notes: The word ov carries significant theological weight in OT law and narrative. The most vivid biblical instance is Saul's consultation of the ov at Endor (1 Sam 28), where she conjures Samuel's shade. The practice is consistently condemned as incompatible with covenantal faithfulness; the association with death and forbidden divination makes it a loaded term across prophetic and legal texts.

A familiar spirit or ghost summoned through divination

ovadyah.notes: Obadiah appears first at 1 Ki. 18:3 as Ahab's palace administrator who shelters the prophets during Jezebel's persecution. The book of Obadiah, shortest OT prophetic text, concerns Edom's judgment; historical details about the prophet himself remain sparse. The name itself is compositionally transparent: 'servant of Yahweh.'

The word derives from the verb אָבַד (to be lost/destroyed) and carries straightforward denotational sense without the theological complexity of related terms like שׁאוֹל. Context determines whether the reference is literal ruin or metaphorical ruin of a person's fortune.

In Proverbs and wisdom literature it frequently describes moral or spiritual ruin (Prov. 10:29; 21:28), while in historical texts it can denote military defeat or national collapse. The word has eschatological weight in later theological discourse, though in the OT it remains primarily descriptive of concrete loss.

He represents the Levitical establishment under the United Monarchy and the integration of music and worship into temple administration.

In prophetic contexts (especially Isaiah and Jeremiah), it shifts from personal lament toward divine pronouncement of woe against Israel's enemies or wayward leaders. The word appears prominently in the five woes of Isaiah 5:8–24 and structures much of Ezekiel's judgment speeches. Context is everything: a funeral cry differs sharply from a prophetic oracle, yet both use the same interjection.

The term denotes a large, unclean raptor, but whether osprey, buzzard, or a now-extinct species cannot be determined from the biblical evidence alone.

Unlike later Rabbinic Hebrew צלח, the biblical form emphasizes the achievement or completion of an undertaking rather than mere well-being.
